The IPCC Tier 1 methodology is used to estimate indirect N2O 
emissions due to volatilization and redeposition of nitrogen 
from synthetic N fertilizers and animal manure. The amount of 
synthetic fertilizer and manure nitrogen is multiplied by the

an emission factor. The amount of nitrogen applied is obtained 
from yearly fertilizer sales data, which are available from Statistics 
Canada, and from the amounts of manure nitrogen excreted by 
animals (see Annex 3.3). The amount of nitrogen that volatilizes 
is assumed to be 10% of the total amount of synthetic fertilizer 
applied, 20% of the applied manure nitrogen to cropland, and 
from 12% to 48% of excreted manure nitrogen during handling

Agricultural land comprises both cropland and agricultural grass-
land. Cropland includes all lands in annual crops, summerfallow 
and perennial crops (mostly forage, but also including berries, 
grapes, nursery crops, vegetables, and fruit trees and orchards). 
Agricultural grassland is defined as “unimproved” pasture or 
rangeland that is used only for grazing domestic livestock. It 
occurs only in geographical areas where the grassland would 
not naturally regrow to forest if abandoned: the natural short-
grass prairie in southern Saskatchewan and Alberta and the dry, 
interior mountain valleys of British Columbia. All agricultural land 
that is not grassland is de facto classified as cropland, including 
unimproved pastures where natural vegetation would be forest 
(eastern Canada and most of British Columbia).
Vegetated areas that do not meet the definition of forest land 
or cropland are generally classified as grassland: extensive areas 
of tundra in the Canadian north are considered un-managed 
grassland.
Wetlands are areas where permanent or recurrent saturated con-
ditions allow the establishment of vegetation and soil develop-
ment typical of these conditions and that are not already in forest 
land, cropland or agricultural grasslands. Managed wetlands are 
those where human interventions have altered the water table—
for example, peatlands drained for peat extraction or flooded 
lands (IPCC 2003).

Conducting uncertainty analysis is a significant challenge in com-

forest carbon dynamics, with multiple interactions and depen-

very large number of model inputs and parameters required to 
simulate carbon dynamics. 
Numerical techniques are used to quantify uncertainties about 
the outputs of the CBM-CFS3 (Metsaranta et al. 2014). Careful 
consideration is given to the identification and representation of 
uncertainty sources in the analysis (see Annex A3.4.2.4 for addi-
tional information). Modelling of the entire managed forests of 
Canada is not done as a single run, but in separate “project runs” 
whose output is subsequently assembled. For each “project, ” 100 
insect epidemics have affected a total of over 49 Mha
3 of man-
aged forests, with 83% being located in the Montane Cordillera 
reporting zone and corresponding to the epidemics of Mountain 
Pine Beetle. In contrast, much of the interannual variability of the 
GHG budget of managed forests hinges on the occurrence, loca-
tion and severity of fires. During the 1990–2012 period, annual 
wildfire emissions fluctuated between 11 and 275 Mt. The con-
sumption of DOM by fires accounts for 77% of immediate emis-
sions; much biomass is killed by forest fires and is thus transferred

7.3.2.2. Methodological Issues
The Feasibility Assessment of Afforestation for Carbon Seques-
tration (FAACS) initiative collected and compiled afforestation 
records for 1990–2002 (NRCan 2005a). In this period, softwood 
plantations, especially spruce and pine, accounted for 90% of 
the area planted. Activities for 1970–1989 and 2003–2008 were 
estimated based on activity rates observed in the FAACS data, 
complemented with information from the Forest 2020 Plantation 
Demonstration Assessment (NRCan 2005b). No new afforestation 
activity data were collected for the 2009–2012 inventory years. 
GHG emissions and removals on lands newly converted to 
forests were estimated using CBM-CFS3, as described in Annex 
3.4. Changes in soil carbon stocks are highly uncertain because 
of difficulties in locating data about the carbon stocks prior to 
plantation. It was assumed that the ecosystem would generally 
accumulate soil carbon at a slow rate; the limited time frame of 
this analysis and the scale of the activity relative to other land use 
and land-use change activities suggest that the impact of this 
uncertainty, if any, is minimal.

7.3.2.1. Category Description
This category includes all lands converted to forest land through 
direct human activity. Post-harvest tree planting is not included, 
nor is abandoned farmland where natural vegetation is allowed 
to establish; hence, the category more precisely refers to forest 
establishment where the previous land use was not forest (typi-
cally, abandoned farmland).
The total cumulative area of land converted to forest land 
declined from 174 kha in 1990 to 72 kha in 2012. The trend 
reflects the gradual transfer of lands afforested more than 20 
years ago to the Forest land remaining forest land category, and 
a dearth of recent data on current rates of forest establishment.

in the Prairies (Boreal Shield West, Boreal Plains and Subhumid 
Prairies reporting zones). However, caution must be exerted in 
regard to analysis of afforestation trends due to the absence of a

steadily increased to about 11 Mt CO2 eq in 2006, remaining rela-

7.4.1.4. CO2 Emissions and 
Removals in Woody Biomass
Category Description
Perennial woody biomass is found on cropland planted with vine-
yards, fruit orchards and Christmas trees. It also accumulates on 
abandoned cropland allowed to revert to natural vegetation. In 
the definitional framework adopted in Canada for LULUCF report-
ing, abandoned cropland is still considered “cropland” until there 
is evidence of a new land use; however, there is little information 
on the dynamics of cropland abandonment or recultivation. 
Owing to these data limitations, only vineyards, fruit orchards 
and Christmas trees are considered; for the time being changes in 
woody biomass from “abandoned cropland” on cropland remain-
ing cropland are excluded.
Methodological Issues
Vineyards, fruit orchards and Christmas tree farms are inten-
sively managed for sustained yields. Vineyards and fruit trees 
are pruned annually, and old plants are replaced on a rotating 
basis for disease prevention, stock improvement or introduction 
of new varieties. For all three crops, it is assumed that, because 
of rotating practices and the requirements for sustained yield, 
a uniform age-class distribution is generally found on produc-
tion farms. Hence, there would be no net increase or decrease 
in biomass carbon within existing farms, as carbon lost from 
harvest or replacement would be balanced by gains due to new 
plant growth. The approach therefore was limited to detecting 
changes in areas under vineyards, fruit orchards and Christmas 
tree plantations and estimating the corresponding carbon stock 
changes in total biomass. More information on assumptions and 
parameters can be found in Annex 3.4.
Uncertainties and Time-Series Consistency
Upon a loss of area with perennial woody crops, all carbon in 
woody biomass is assumed to be immediately released. It is 
assumed that the uncertainty for carbon loss equals the uncer-
tainty about mass of woody biomass carbon. The default uncer-
tainty of ±75% (i.e. 95% confidence limits) for woody biomass on 
cropland from the IPCC Good Practice Guidance (IPCC 2003) was 
used.
If the loss in area of fruit trees, vineyards or Christmas trees is 
estimated to have gone to annual crops, there is also a deemed 
perennial to annual crop conversion with associated uncertainty

7.4.1.3. CO2 Emissions from 
Cultivation of Organic Soils
Category Description
In Canada, cultivated organic soils are defined as the conversion 
of organic soils to agriculture for annual crop production, nor-
mally accompanied by artificial drainage, cultivation and liming. 
Organic soils used for agricultural production in Canada include 
the Peaty Phase of Gleysolic soils, Fibrisols over 60 cm thick, and 
Mesisols and Humisols over 40 cm thick (AAFC 1998).
Methodological Issues
The emissions from the cultivation of organic soils were calcu-
lated by multiplying the total area of cultivated histosols by the 
default emission factor of 5 Mg C/ha per year (IPCC 2006). 
Areas of cultivated histosols are not provided by the Census of 
Agriculture; area estimates were based on the expert opinion of 
soil and crop specialists across Canada (Liang et al. 2004). The 
total area of cultivated organic soils in Canada (constant for the 
period 1990–2012) was estimated to be 16 kha, or 0.03% of the 
cropland area. The area of cultivated histosols is mainly located 
in the Atlantic Maritime, Mixedwood Plains and Pacific Maritime 
reporting zones. 
Uncertainties and Time-Series Consistency
The uncertainty associated with emissions from this source is due 
to the uncertainties from the area estimates for the cultivated 
histosols and the emission factor. The 95% confidence limits asso-
ciated with the area estimate of cultivated histosols are assessed 
to be ±50% (Hutchinson et al. 2007). The 95% confidence limits 
of the default emission factor are ±90% (IPCC 2006). The overall 
mean and uncertainties associated with this source of emissions 
were estimated to be 0.3 ± 0.09 Mt CO
2 eq for the level uncertain-

Methodological Issues – Soils
Emissions from soils in this category include the net C stock

Eastern Canada
All agricultural land in the eastern part of the country was 
forested before its conversion to agriculture. Many observations, 
either in the scientific literature or the Canadian Soil Information

7.5. Grassland
Agricultural grassland is defined under the Canadian LULUCF 
framework as pasture or rangeland on which the only agricultural 
land management activity has been the grazing of domestic 
livestock (i.e. the land has never been cultivated). It occurs only in 
geographical areas where the grassland would not naturally grow 
into forest if abandoned: the natural shortgrass prairie in south-
ern Saskatchewan and Alberta and the dry, interior mountain val-
leys of British Columbia. Agricultural grassland is found in three 
reporting zones: Semi-arid Prairies (5207 kha), Montane Cordil-
lera (199 kha), and Pacific Maritime (2 kha). As with cropland, the 
change in management triggers a change in carbon stocks (IPCC 
2003). Very little information is available on management practic-
es on Canadian agricultural grassland, and it is unknown whether 
grazed land is improving or degrading. Therefore, Canada reports 
this grassland remaining grassland category using the IPCC Tier 
1 method based on no change in management practices since 
1990. The subcategory land converted to grassland, within the 
current definitional framework as explained in Section 7.2, is 
reported either as not estimated (wetlands converted to grass-
land) or as not occurring (Table 7–4).

7.6.1. Managed Peatlands
7.6.1.1. Source Category Description 
Of the estimated 123 Mha of peatlands in Canada,8 approxi-
mately 26 kha are, or were at some point in the past, drained for 
peat extraction. Some 14 kha are currently being actively man-
aged. The other 11 kha consist of peatlands that are no longer 
under production. In the Canadian context, generally only bog 
peatlands with a peat thickness of 2 m or greater and an area of 
50 ha or greater are of commercial value for peat extraction (Keys 
1992). Peat production is concentrated in the provinces of New 
Brunswick, Quebec, Alberta and Manitoba. Canada produces only 
horticultural peat.
Since the 1980s, virtually all peat extraction in Canada has relied 
on vacuum harvest technology; approximately 100 t/ha (wet 
basis) of horticultural peat is extracted with this technology 
(Cleary 2003). A drawback of the technology, as opposed to the 
traditional cut-block method, is poor natural vegetation regrowth 
in the post-production phase. Since the 1990s, peatland restora-
tion activities have been pursued with greater interest.
Peat extraction activities expanded during the 1990–2000 period, 
with a 47% increase in the land area under active peat extraction, 
from 9.5 kha in 1990 to 14 kha at the turn of the century. Owing 
to this expansion and to the significant contribution of vegeta-
tion clearing and decay to the overall GHG budget, emissions 
from managed peatlands show a significant increase over the 
first half of the assessment period. Since then, emissions have 
declined (Figure 7-4), from 1.5 Mt in 2000 to 1.1 Mt in 2012. Emis-
sions from managed peatlands are reported under land

The general phases of peat extraction are 1) drainage, 2) vegeta-
tion clearing, 3) extraction, 4) stockpiling, 5) abandonment and 
6) peatland restoration and establishment of natural vegetation.

2 is the dominant GHG emitted from com-
mercial peatlands and the only gas reported under this category. 
The main sources of emissions are vegetation clearing upon 
conversion, the continuing decay of dead organic matter and the 
rapid oxidation of exposed peat, resulting in a threefold increase 
in CO2 emission rates compared to natural peatlands (Wadding-

methodology, based on domestic emission factors. They include 
emissions and removals during all five phases. More information 
on estimation methodology can be found in Annex 3.4.

the peat transported off-site; should these be included, total 
emissions from managed peatlands would significantly increase.

7.8.1. Methodological Issues
Forest conversion to other land categories is still a prevalent 
practice in Canada. This phenomenon is driven by a great variety 
of circumstances across the country, including policy and regula-
tory frameworks, market forces and resource endowment. The 
economic activities causing forest losses are very diverse; they 
result in heterogeneous spatial and temporal patterns of forest 
conversion, which, until recently, were not systematically docu-
mented. The challenge has been to develop an approach that 
would integrate a large variety of information sources to capture 
the various forest conversion patterns across the Canadian 
landscape, while maintaining a consistent approach in order to 
minimize omissions and overlap.
The approach adopted for estimating forest areas converted to 
other uses is based on three main information sources: systemat-
ic or representative sampling of remote sensing imagery, records, 
and expert judgement. The core method involves mapping of for-
est conversion on samples from remotely sensed Landsat images 
dated circa 1975, 1990, 2000 and 2008. For implementation 
purposes, all permanent forest removal wider than 20 m from 
tree base to tree base and at least 1 ha in area was considered 
forest conversion. This convention was adopted as a guide to 
consistently label linear patterns in the landscape. The other main 
information sources consist of databases or other documenta-
tion on forest roads, power lines, oil and gas infrastructure, and 
hydroelectric reservoirs. Expert opinion was called upon when 
the remote sensing sample was insufficient, to resolve differences 
among records and remote sensing information, and to resolve 
apparent discrepancies across the 1975–1990, 1990–2000 and 
2000–2008 area estimates. A more detailed description of the 
approach and data sources is provided in Annex 3.4.

8.1. Overview
This sector includes emissions from the treatment and disposal 
of wastes. Sources include solid waste disposal on land (landfills), 
wastewater treatment and waste incineration. The categories 
evaluated are CH4 emissions from solid waste disposal on land, 
CH4 and N2O emissions from wastewater treatment, and CO2, CH4 
and N2O emissions from waste incineration.
Much of the waste treated or disposed of is biomass or bio-
mass-based. CO2 emissions attributable to such wastes are not 
included in inventory totals but are reported in the inventory as 
a memo item. CO2 emissions of biogenic origin are not reported 
if they are reported elsewhere in the inventory or if the corre-
sponding CO2 uptake is not reported in the inventory (e.g. annual 
crops). Therefore, under these circumstances, the emissions are 
not included in the inventory emission totals, since the absorp-
tion of CO
2 by the harvested vegetation is not estimated by the 
Agriculture Sector and, thus, the inclusion of these emissions in 
the Waste Sector would result in an imbalance. Also, CO
2 emis-
sions from wood and wood products are not included, because 
these emissions are accounted for in the Land Use, Land-use 
Change and Forestry (LULUCF) Sector at the time of tree harvest-
ing. In contrast, CH
4 emissions from anaerobic decomposition 
of wastes are included in inventory totals as part of the Waste 
Sector.
If carbon is lost from forests at an unsustainable rate (i.e. faster 
than annual re-growth), the carbon budget for forest lands will 
be negative for net emissions.
In 2012, the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from the Waste Sec-
tor contributed 21 Mt to the national inventory, compared with 
19 Mt for 1990—an increase of 8.2%. The national total emissions 
increased by 18.2% over the same time interval. The emissions 
from this sector represented 3.2% and 2.9% of the overall Cana-
dian GHG emissions in 1990 and 2012, respectively.

8.2.1. Source Category 
Description
Emissions are estimated from two types of landfills in Canada:
• MSW landfills; and
• wood waste landfills.
In Canada, most waste disposal on land occurs in managed 
municipal or privately owned landfills. Very few, if any, unman-
aged waste disposal sites exist. Therefore, it has been assumed 
that all waste is disposed of in managed facilities. Residential, 
institutional, commercial and industrial wastes are disposed of 
in MSW landfills. Over the past 15 years, dedicated construction 
and demolition (C & D) landfills were established. Typically, these 
landfills do not require CH4 collection systems, as the CH4 genera-
tion rate is very low due to the minimal organic content in the 
waste stream. However, for completeness of this emission source 
and accuracy of emissions from MSW landfills, the waste quanti-
ties now include C & D wastes.
Wood waste landfills are mostly privately owned and operated 
by forest industries, such as saw mills and pulp and paper mills. 
These industries use the landfills to dispose of surplus wood 
residue, such as sawdust, wood shavings, bark and sludges. Some 
industries have shown increasing interest in waste-to-energy 
projects that produce steam and/or electricity by combusting 
these wastes. In recent years, residual wood previously regarded 
as a waste is now being processed as a value-added product—
e.g., wood pellets for residential and commercial pellet stoves 
and furnaces, and hardboard, fibreboard and particle board. 
Wood waste landfills have been identified as a source of CH

The Revised 1996 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas 
Inventories (IPCC/OECD/IEA 1997) provides two methodologies 
for estimating emissions from landfills: a default method and 
a first-order kinetics method, also known as the Scholl Canyon 
model. The default method relates emissions to the quantity of 
waste landfilled in the previous year, whereas the Scholl Canyon 
model relates emissions to the cumulative biologically available 
waste that has been landfilled in previous years.
The composition and amount of waste landfilled in Canada have 
significantly changed over the past several decades, primarily 
as a result of waste diversion initiatives and population growth, 
respectively. For this reason, a static model such as the default 
method is not felt to be appropriate. Therefore, emissions from 
MSW landfills and wood waste landfills are estimated using the 
Scholl Canyon model. The Scholl Canyon model, used to esti-
mate Canada’s CH4 emissions from landfills, has been validated 
independently through a study conducted by the University of 
Manitoba (Thompson et al. 2006).
Landfill gas, which is composed mainly of CH
4 and CO2, is pro-
duced by the anaerobic decomposition of organic wastes. The 
first phase of this process typically begins after waste has been in 
a landfill for 10 to 50 days. Although the majority of the CH4 and 
CO2 gases are generated within 20 years of landfilling, emissions 
can continue for 100 years or more (Levelton 1991).
A number of important site-specific factors contribute to the 
generation of gases within a landfill, including the following:
Waste composition: Waste composition is probably the most 
important factor affecting landfill gas generation rates and 
quantities. The amount of landfill gas produced is dependent on 
the amount of organic matter landfilled. The rate at which gas is 
generated is dependent on the distribution and type of organic 
matter in the landfill.
Moisture content: Water is required for anaerobic degradation 
of organic matter; therefore, moisture content within a landfill 
significantly affects gas generation rates.
Temperature: Anaerobic digestion is an exothermic process. The 
growth rates of bacteria tend to increase with temperature until 
an optimum is reached. Therefore, landfill temperatures may 
be higher than ambient air temperatures. The extent to which 
ambient air temperatures influence the temperature of the 
landfill and gas generation rates depends mainly on the depth of 
the landfill. Temperature variations can af

e until 
an optimum is reached. Therefore, landfill temperatures may 
be higher than ambient air temperatures. The extent to which 
ambient air temperatures influence the temperature of the 
landfill and gas generation rates depends mainly on the depth of 
the landfill. Temperature variations can affect microbial activity,

pH and buffer capacity: The generation of CH4 in landfills is great-
est when neutral pH conditions exist. The activity of methano-
genic bacteria is inhibited in acidic environments.
Availability of nutrients: Certain nutrients are required for anaero-
bic digestion. These include carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen and 
phosphorus. In general, MSW contains the necessary nutrients to 
support the required bacterial populations.
Waste density and particle size: The particle size and density of the 
waste also influences gas generation. Decreasing the particle size 
increases the surface area available for degradation and there-
fore increases the gas production rate. The waste density, which 
is largely controlled by compaction of the waste as it is placed 
in the landfill, affects the transport of moisture and nutrients 
through the landfill, which also affects the gas generation rate.
8.2.2. Methodological Issues
CH4 produced from the decomposition of waste in landfills is 
calculated using the Scholl Canyon model, which is a first-order 
decay model. This reflects the fact that waste degrades in landfills 
over many years. Data pertaining to landfill gas capture were 
obtained directly from the owners/operators of specific landfills 
with landfill gas collection systems.
CH

generated from landfill waste decomposition through the Scholl 
Canyon model, subtracting the CH4 captured through landfill gas 
recovery systems, then adding the quantity of uncombusted CH4 
emitted by the flares for those locations where a portion or all of 
the recovered landfill gas is burned without energy recovery. The 
GHG emissions associated with the combustion of that portion of 
the landfill gas that is captured and utilized for energy genera-
tion purposes are accounted for in the Energy Sector. Annex 3.5 
provides detailed information on the methodologies used for 
various categories covered by this subsector.

CH4 Generation Rate Constant (k)
The CH4 kinetic rate constant (k) represents the first-order rate at 
which CH4 is generated after waste has been landfilled. The value 
of k is affected by four major factors: moisture content, tem-
perature, availability of nutrients and pH. It is assumed that, in a 
typical MSW landfill, the nutrient and pH conditions are attained 
and that, therefore, these factors are not limiting. In many parts 
of Canada, subzero conditions exist for up to seven months of the 
year, with temperatures dropping below −30°C (Thompson et 
al. 2006); however, evidence suggests that ambient temperature 
does not affect landfill decay rates (Maurice and Lagerkvist 2003; 
Thompson and Tanapat 2005). In addition, seasonal temperature 
variations in the waste are minimal when compared with atmo-
spheric temperature variations (Maurice and Lagerkvist 2003). At 
depths exceeding 2 m, the landfill temperature is independent 
of the ambient temperature. It has been shown in Canadian 
field experiments that an insignificant amount of variation in 
landfill CH
4 production occurs between the winter and summer 
seasons (Bingemer and Crutzen 1987; Thompson and Tanapat 
2005). Therefore, of all these factors, moisture content is the most 
influential parameter for Canadian landfills and is largely deter-
mined by the annual precipitation received at the landfills.

The IPCC default method was not used because the required data 
were not available. A method developed for Environment Canada 
(AECOM Canada 2010) was used to calculate an emission factor. 
This country specific methodology provides for the accurate esti-
mation of provincial methane emissions that best suits the avail-
able related activity data. Based on the amount of organic matter

provided in Annex 3.5.
CH4 emissions were calculated by multiplying the emission factor

obtain methane emissions from facilities that treated their efflu-

8.4.1.1. MSW Incineration
A combustion chamber of a typical mass-burn MSW incinerator 
is composed of a grate system on which waste is burned and is 
either water-walled (if the energy is recovered) or refractory-lined 
(if it is not). GHGs that are emitted from MSW incinerators include 
CO2, CH4 and N2O.
As per the Revised 1996 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse 
Gas Inventories (IPCC/OECD/IEA 1997), CO
2 emissions from bio-
mass waste combustion are not included in the inventory totals. 
The only CO
2 emissions detailed in this section are from fossil 
fuel-based carbon waste, such as plastics and rubber.
CH4 emissions from Canadian MSW incinerators are negligible, 
based on the findings from a recent report commissioned by 
Environment Canada (CRA 2011).
8.4.1.2. Hazardous Waste Incineration
There are five hazardous waste incinerators in Canada located in 
Quebec, Ontario and Alberta. CO2, N2O and CH4 are the green-
house gases emitted from this source. The emissions are derived 
from the quantities of hazardous wastes incinerated that were 
provided directly by the facilities in a series of surveys sum-
marized in a report (Environment Canada 2011b). A preliminary 
survey was conducted in 2006, which was followed by surveys 
in 2008, 2010 and 2012 (Environment Canada 2013b) to improve 
completeness of the coverage and data accuracy. 
8.4.1.3. Sewage Sludge Incineration
Two different types of sewage sludge incinerators are used in 
Canada: multiple hearth and fluidized bed. In both types of 
incinerators, the sewage sludge is partially de-watered prior to 
incineration. The de-watering is typically done in a centrifuge or 
using a filter press. Currently, municipalities in Ontario and Que-
bec operate sewage sludge incinerators. GHGs emitted from the 
incineration of sewage sludge include CO
2, CH4, and N2O, as in 
the case of MSW incinerators; however, since the carbon present 
in the wastewater sewage sludge is of biological origin, the CO
2 
emissions are not accounted for in the inventory totals from this 
source.
8.4.2. Methodological Issues
The emission estimation methodology depends on waste type 
and gas emitted. A more detailed discussion of the methodolo-
gies is presented in Annex 3.5.

Inventories (IPCC/OECD/IEA 1997) do not specify a method to 
calculate CO

waste (such as plastics and rubber). Therefore, the following 
three-step method was developed for MSW incineration:
• Calculating the amount of waste incinerated: The amount of 
waste incinerated each year was estimated based on a regres-
sion analysis using data from an Environment Canada (

three-step method was developed for MSW incineration:
• Calculating the amount of waste incinerated: The amount of 
waste incinerated each year was estimated based on a regres-

study, which contains detailed provincial incineration data for

Chapter 9
Recalculations and 
Improvements
Canada’s greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory undergoes a continu-
ous process of updates and improvements in order to ensure 
that the most complete, consistent, comparable, accurate and 
transparent information possible is reported. Section 9.1 of this 
chapter summarizes the recalculations implemented in Canada’s 
national GHG inventory since its 2013 submission, in order to 
facilitate an integrated view of changes in, and impacts on, emis-
sion levels and trends. A description of improvements to the 2014 
submission due to methodological changes or refinements, or 
to address recommendations made by the Expert Review Teams 
(ERTs) as part of the annual review process, can be found in 
Section 9.2 along with a list of planned improvements for future 
inventories. 
Although the quantification of uncertainty for the emission esti-
mates (Annex 7) helps prioritize improvements of future inven-
tories, uncertainty is not an indicator of potential future changes 
resulting from continual improvement activities. 
9.1. Explanations and 
Justifications for 
Recalculations
The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change 
(UNFCCC) requires all Annex I Parties to continually improve their 
national GHG inventories. As new information and data become 
available and more accurate methods are developed, previous 
estimates are updated to provide a consistent and comparable 
trend in emissions and removals. As such, recalculations are 
expected to occur annually, reflecting the principle of continuous 
improvement. The nature, rationale and impact of these recal-
culations are documented in this national inventory report and 
associated data tables. Recalculations can result for any number 
of reasons, including the following:
i. Correction of errors detected by quality control proce-
dures;
ii. Incorporation of updates to activity data including 
changes in data sources;
iii. Reallocation of activities to different categories (although 
this will only affect sub-totals);
iv. Refinements of methodologies and emission factors;
v. Inclusion of categories previously not estimated (which 
improves inventory completeness); and 
vi. Recommendations from UNFCCC reviews.  
On a continuous basis, Environment Canada consults and works 
jointly with key federal and provincial partners along with indus-
try stakeholders, research centres and consultants to improve the 
quality of the underlying variables and scientific information for 
use in the compilation of the national inventory. Where neces-
sary, Environment Canada revises and recalculates the emission 
and removal estimates for all years in the inventory, as good 
inventory preparation practice requires that methodological 
improvements and updates be applied to the entire time series of 
annual estimates (i.e. from 1990 to the most recent year report-
ed). A consistent time series is required to avoid confounding a 
methodological change with an actual change

and 2005 of +1.32%, -0.92% and -0.32%, respectively, relative to

9.1.2. Implications for 
Emission Trends
Overall, the recalculations of the total GHG estimates (excluding 
the LULUCF Sector) had a negligible effect on the trend between 
1990 and 2010, now reported as an 18.7% increase in total GHG 
emissions since 1990 instead of the previously reported 18.6% 
increase. The trend between 1990 and 2012 shows an 18.2% 
increase in GHG emissions.

following agreed-upon UNFCCC review guidelines. Reviews are 
coordinated by the UNFCCC Secretariat, and the ERT is composed

The purpose of the in-depth review, performed by the ERT, is to 
provide a thorough and comprehensive technical assessment 
of the implementation of the Convention and adherence to its 
Reporting Guidelines; the review’s outcome is reflected in an 
annual review report (ARR).

Inventory

The forest inventory and growth & yield information was updated for NIR 2014. The Carbon Accounting Team received a new dataset from the Government of Alberta Sustainable Resource Development (SRD Alberta) department in the summer of 2010. This dataset contains digital information on the forest management areas (FMA) in the province of Alberta. The non-FMA inventory area was filled using the Canfi 2001 dataset. The resulting inventory dataset is a blend of the data provided by the SRD in Alberta and the CanFI2001, as indicated in Table 1-1 and Figure 1.1.

Spatial Stratification

Common Reference Date

The FMA-based dataset was brought to a common reference date of 1990 by the staff at SRD Alberta. The CanFI-based dataset was brought to a common reference date of 1990 according to the procedure described below. As such the entire new Alberta project begins from 1990.

CanFI2001 was compiled from a number of source inventories of varying types and vintages. However, initial conditions for C modelling must represent the state of the forest at a single point in time. A common reference date of 1990 is used for all NIR analyses. Data that were collected prior to 1990 are rolled forward, and data that were collected after 1990 are rolled back. Only age information is updated in this process. This procedure was applied when the current project was created, and has not been updated since NIR2006.

The algorithm used is as follows: 

Step 1: Compile all relevant disturbance monitoring information. This information is used to update the inventory for depletions as it is being rolled forward to 1990. Wherever possible, ArcGIS was used to spatially-reference the disturbance data to the appropriate records in the inventory. The disturbance data compiled for inventory update processing include:
Fires All fires since 1980 that burned more than 200 ha (from the LFDB), will be treated as depletions that must be accounted for in the inventory update process. A discount factor of 0.76 is applied to burn area of each fire in the update process. The discount factor is based on the fact that only 76% of treed land in CanFI is classified as forest. We only consider treed land in this analysis.

Harvesting Alberta SRD provided harvest data (area harvested by year and range/township) for 1990-2005. These will be used to model harvest depletions on stands moving through this period during the update process. However, a large proportion of CanFI records are referenced to dates in the 1980s and 1970s. As these records are rolled forward towards 1990, any depletions that occur must be accounted for. Harvest depletion assumptions must be developed (we have no harvest data for the period prior to 1990). I have set up two harvest depletion scenarios to choose from: (a) assume all harvest depletions prior to 1990 are alrea

olled forward towards 1990, any depletions that occur must be accounted for. Harvest depletion assumptions must be developed (we have no harvest data for the period prior to 1990). I have set up two harvest depletion scenarios to choose from: (a) assume all harvest depletions prior to 1990 are already accounted for in the data, and (b) assume harvest depletions must be accounted for when updating records beyond their reference date and assume that the 1990 harvest level can be used as a base harvest depletion level for years leading up to 1990. This second assumption is basically saying that if 50% of your inventory is referenced to an earlier date than the current date, then account for harvest depletions in the current date using area depletions equivalent to 50% of the 1990 area depletion level.
Insects We are not accounting for insect depletions. Insect impacts are not generally stand-replacing, and we only account for stand-replacing depletions in our inventory update process. This could result in a bias in our estimated 1990 age class structure if there were insect disturbances in ’s history that resulted in significant stand-replacing mortality. Furthermore, we are not adjusting the volume values in the inventory to account for any insect depletions that may have occurred during the lifespan of stands leading up to 1990. We are assuming that the CanFI chronosequence growth curves account for these depletions. (Note that in the CBM runs, we change this assumption and explicitly simulate the impacts of insects on the C budget. This is a methodological inconsistency that we need to examine further.)

Step 2: Assign an age range to each inventory record using the best available information. Where age class information is available, a 20-year age range was assigned (e.g. a record referenced to CanFI age class 2 is assigned an age range of 21 to 40 years old). Where no age class is available, maturity class was used to assign an age range using a genus-specific look-up table (except that separate lookup values were used for black and white spruce). Where neither age class nor maturity class are available, volume was used to estimate the age range using the appropriate growth curve. The attributes of the record are used to select the appropriate growth model, and this model is then solved for age at the given volume. Refer to frmInventoryUpdate code for details.

Table - Information available to determine stand age for AB forests

Step 3: Reference all records in the inventory back to the earliest collection date in the inventory. In , the oldest collection date is 1949. Note that in the Alberta CanFI2001 data, no records are listed as having been updated since collection. Although a few records have update dates listed, these are always the same year as the collection date. For NIR purposes we have only rolled back from 1980 because our fire disturbance data only goes back that far.

Step 4: Step forward one year at a time, applying disturbances

ted since collection. Although a few records have update dates listed, these are always the same year as the collection date. For NIR purposes we have only rolled back from 1980 because our fire disturbance data only goes back that far.

Step 4: Step forward one year at a time, applying disturbances where applicable. Disturb those stands that are eligible for disturbance (i.e. that are referenced to the same spatial entity as the disturbance in question) and give preference to those that could be due for disturbance (i.e. have a current age range that includes 0). Refer to frmInventoryUpdate code for details. Note that I applied a discount factor before applying the fires to the inventory to account for the fact that the fire monitoring data do not distinguish between fires that burn forests versus fires that burn other treed lands. I used a discount factor of 0.76 because 76% of treed lands the FM scenario lands in are forest (as classified in CanFI2001).
 
Step 5: If any records in the inventory were collected or updated after 1990, then these data could contain information on post-disturbance status of records that would have been in a pre-disturbance condition in 1990 (i.e. records that were disturbed after 1990 and updated after the disturbance). Steps 1 through 4 will not revert these stands to their pre-disturbance condition. Therefore, we must estimate how much of the inventory after Steps 1 through 4 has been initialized to the wrong condition (i.e. to post-disturbance condition instead of pre-disturbance condition). We accomplish this as follows:
For each record with a min_age < 0, calculate the age range of the record
Determine both the proportion of the age range that is positive (0 – max_age) and the proportion of the age range that is negative (min_age – 0)
Break each record into two. The first record will contain the proportion of the original record that is positive. The minimum age will be reset to 0 and the area will be adjusted to reflect the proportion of the record that has a positive age. The second record will contain the proportion of the original record that is negative. The minimum and maximum age will be reset to their assumed pre-harvest condition (min_age = 80 and max_age = 360) and the area will be adjusted to reflect the proportion of the record that has a negative age.

Forest inventory and growth & yield compilation

 inventory and growth & yield assumptions have not changed since NIR2007.

Inventory

The NFCMARS forest inventory for derives from two sources. ESSA provided provincial Timber Supply Review (TSR) data for all TSAs, most TFLs and most provincial parks. For all other lands, data were extracted from the Seamless Forest Cover (SFC). These other lands included most of the remaining TFLs, and most national parks. Growth and yield information from the TSR are used to grow Timber Harvesting Land Base (THLB) lands in both the TSR and the SFC inventory records in the model. Growth and yield information for nonTHLB lands were compiled by Timberline and were included in the ESSA dataset.

Spatial Stratification

BC is stratified into 688 spatial units based on administrative and ecological variables. The administrative units are the combination of Timber Supply Areas (TSA), Tree Farm Licenses (TFL) and parks. There are 37 TSAs, 34 TFLs and 4 national and 1 provincial park, for a total of 75 admin units. Most provincial park inventory was assumed to be within the TSA inventory except for which was explicitly included due to known gaps in the TSA inventory and the extensive mountain pine beetle outbreak. (Note that 2 of BC’s 6 national parks are not in the spatial stratification system because there are no data for those parks: and Haida Gwaii). The ecological units in BC are the combination of the Biogeoclimatic Ecological Classification (BEC) system’s subzones (BEC subzones) and the Terrestrial Ecozones of Canada (ecozones).

Note that although provincial parks are assumed to be in the TSR inventory for the purposes of this analysis, it is likely that this is not the case for 100% of provincial park forest lands. However, we have been advised by provincial experts that it is not possible at this time to determine which parks are included and which are not. The reason that provincial parks are not handled consistently is that some regional timber supply analysts do not consider park lands in their assessment of forest resource values while others do.
 
There are a couple of quirky details in the spatial stratification system worth noting. First, there are 1.0 million ha of forest in the TSR data that have no BEC information (i.e. BEC variant = “ZZZZ”). These data will therefore not be mappable in a GIS environment. Second, all TSR data in t

There are a couple of quirky details in the spatial stratification system worth noting. First, there are 1.0 million ha of forest in the TSR data that have no BEC information (i.e. BEC variant = “ZZZZ”). These data will therefore not be mappable in a GIS environment. Second, all TSR data in the and Kingcome TSAs that are in the ESSF BEC zone (approximately 1.8 million ha) are undifferentiated, and have no subzone or variant information. These data were proportionally assigned to the ESSF subzones found in those TSAs. Although the original spatial stratification had 688 units, only 673 have inventory area greater than 2 ha.

To assign the ecological variable, each BEC subzone was mapped to the ecozones on an administrative unit by administrative unit basis. This allows us to say, for example, that BEC subzone ESSFmc is in montane cordillera when it is in administrative unit 14 but is in Boreal cordillera when it is in administrative unit 26. In all but five cases, the BEC subzones in each administrative unit were assigned to ecozones based on their overlapping area. In five cases, the BEC subzones were divided amoung two neighbouring ecozones and the inventory assigned to the ecological variables on a pro-rated basis. Specifically, calculating the geographic area and assuming that the forest area followed the same proportions.

Due to the limits of MS-Access and CBM-CFS3, BC is divided into three CBM projects: Coast, North and South.

Insects

Mountain pine beetle (MPB) disturbance activity data come from two different forest health monitoring data sources. MPB disturbances for the 1999 – 2013 period are taken from the provincially compiled aerial survey data. MPB disturbances for the 1990 – 1996 period come from the CFS Forest Insect and Disease Survey. There are no reliable monitoring data sources for the 1997 – 1998 period, and so area targets for these two years are estimated from the available monitoring data.

Insect disturbances in NFCMARS are derived from these monitoring datasets by spatially overlaying the insect-affected polygons from the monitoring data with the provincial SPU polygons (defined by the intersection of ecozone and provincial forest management administration unit boundary polygons) to determine the area attacked annually within each SPU, by attack severity class. The intent of this step is to make sure that the inventory records selected for disturbance by CBM are located within the appropriate provincial administrative unit and ecozone. The severity class is used to associate each disturbance with the appropriate CBM disturbance matrix. This protocol for preparing the insect disturbance time series for NFCMARS has been in place since at least NIR2010. 

A number of discrepancies between the annual MPB disturbance targets in NFCMARS and the underlying source monitoring data have been identified over the course of the last few NIR cycles. These discrepancies have arisen from past data processing errors, and have made the three BC projects progressively more difficult and cumbersome to work with, and so we have undertaken to clean all of this up for NIR2014. The most current versions of both of the source monitoring datasets were reprocessed from scratch, and the resulting 1990-2013 MPB disturbance time series was reloaded into the project. New 2013 MPB events were also added to the project for NIR2015.

As in previous submissions, CanFI treed lands such as “Open woodlands and Forested Wetlands” have been excluded from the managed forests in . However, in some provinces, forested wetlands are harvested in the winter when equipment can drive in. Furthermore, these treed lands may be treated as deforested areas in remote sensing techniques. Repercussions of excluding these treed lands may include missing targets for deforestation, or missing volume targets, or a biasing the results towards a source due to the excluded forest land.

Spatial Stratification

The spatial stratification system for is done on the basis of forest districts (admin) and terrestrial ecozones (eco). Districts 19a, 20 and 21 are considered to be part of the managed forest because there is forest management planning and commercial forest harvesting activity ongoing in each of these districts. All other districts are assumed to be undeveloped as far as the commercial forest sector is concerned. However, the latest harvest statistics from Boyd Pittman (Newfoundland Forest Service – NFS) indicate that there are small amounts of commercial harvesting starting up in Districts 22 and 23 as of 2000 and 2003, respectively. Given that there is no planning and the harvest permit sales are very limited (especially relative to the large size of these districts), these large districts were not considered to be part of the managed forest. 

A discussion document was prepared on Sept.29, 2006 to solicit feedback from the Newfoundland Forest Service on this proposed implementation of the definition of managed forest (MF). On Oct.2, we received confirmation from Ivan Downton that the approach proposed is appropriate. 

In the NIR2008 submission, some of the forest data was moved from the Boreal Shield East to the Taiga Shield East, and thus the NIR reported areas for these 2 units are slightly incorrect. This is due to a difference in CanFI 2001 data from the CanFI development data that was used in the initial analysis.

Note that the districts are used to make the distinction between managed forest and unmanaged forest. “District” is not available in CanFI as an attribute, so it is brought into the database using a spatial join (GIS overlay). However, the districts GIS layer does not draw the same coastline as the CanFI grid GIS layer. The differences are so large that several CanFI mapsheets are not assigned to a district when the two layers are intersected (refer to district_overlay_issue.jpg – this shows in yellow the CanFI mapsheets that are not assigned to a district). Note that the problem is by far most severe along the shoreline. The problem results in a loss of 20,271 ha of forest from our database (i.e. forest area that exists in CanFI but is not loaded into CBM because of the spatial join issue – failure to associate with any district). Not all of this would be categorized as MF, but some of it certainly would. A decision has been made to simply treat this error as part of our uncertainty because of the relatively small forest area involved. It is felt that this omission will not bias the C outcome in one direction or the other (i.e. towards sink or source). 

The product of the GIS overlay of district boundaries and CanFI grid cells is tblFMU (in the pre-processing database). This table maps each CanFI grid cell to one district. Grid cells that cross district boundaries are assigned to the district where the majority of their area falls (total geographic extent, not forest area – because we do not know where forests are located within the cells). tblFMU_QAQC.jpg shows that each CanFI grid cell has been associated to the appropriate district.

Common Reference Date

CanFI2001 was compiled from a number of source inventories of varying types and vintages. However, initial conditions for C modelling must represent the state of the forest at a single point in time. A common reference date of 1990 is used for all NIR analyses. Most inventory for the managed forest (districts 19a, 20 and 21) was updated within a couple of years of 1990 and we’ve had relatively little disturbance in these forests. Most inventory for the other districts has not been updated since 1972.

Data that were collected prior to 1990 are rolled forward, and data that were collected after 1990 are rolled back. Only age information is updated in this process. This procedure was applied when the current project was created, and has not been updated since NIR2006.

Harvesting Harvest data were acquired for 1969-present from the NFS. These will be used to model harvest depletions on stands moving through this period during the update process. We are assuming that harvest depletions must be accounted for when updating records beyond their reference (update) date towards 1990.
Insects We are not accounting for insect depletions in the inventory common reference date process. Insect impacts are not generally stand-replacing, and we only account for stand-replacing depletions in our inventory common reference process. This could result in a bias in our estimated 1990 age class structure if there were insect disturbances in ’s history that resulted in significant stand-replacing mortality. Furthermore, we are not adjusting the volume values in the inventory to account for any insect depletions that may have occurred during the lifespan of stands leading up to 1990. We are assuming that the CanFI chronosequence growth curves account for these depletions. (Note that in the CBM runs, we make the opposite assumption and explicitly simulate the impacts of insects on the C budget. This is a methodological inconsistency that we need to examine further. But in preprocessing it only affects stocks whereas during CBM run we are measuring fluxes – which is what we are interested in and what we report on to the UNFCCC)

Step 2: Assign an age range to each inventory record using the best available information. Where age class information is available, a 20-year age range was assigned (e.g. a record referenced to CanFI age class 2 is assigned an age range of 21 to 40 years old). Therefore, maturity class is not used. If a record does not have age class, volume was used to estimate the age range using the appropriate growth curve. Fire disturbance events come from two different wildfire monitoring data sources. We accomplish this as follows:
For each record with a min_age < 0, calculate the age range of the record
Determine both the proportion of the age range that is positive (0 – max_age) and the proportion of the age range that is negative (min_age – 0)
Break each record into two. The first record will contain the proportion of the original record that is positive. The minimum age will be reset to 0 and the area will be adjusted to reflect the proportion of the record that has a positive age. The second record will contain the proportion of the original record that is negative. The minimum and maximum age will be reset to their assumed pre-harvest condition (min_age = 70 and max_age = 200) and the area will be adjusted to reflect the proportion of the record that has a negative age.

Chronosequence growth curves were built using chronosequences compiled using data from CanFI2001. The forest area in CanFI was stratified into growth types using 5 CanFI classifiers:

Chronosequences for each growth type were compiled in Access2000 using VBA and Microsoft DAO (refer to code in frmChronoCompiler3 for details). The chronosequences consist of a pair of data points for each age class: average softwood volume and average hardwood volume. Standard deviations were also calculated and reported for each chronosequence data point. 

Growth models were fit to the chronosequences using non-linear regression tools in SigmaPlot (Juha and Murugi are the ones to ask for details). Two growth models were produced for each growth type; one for the softwood component and one for the hardwood component. Overmature decline was only modelled where the data showed a decline in merchantable volume. A default overmature decline assumption is provided as an option that can be applied while generating yield tables from the growth models for import to CBM, but the default is to only model overmature decline where there is evidence of decline in the data.

Inventory

The Newfoundland Forest Service (NFS) provided timber supply analysis data for 17 management units on the (covering districts 1, 2, and 4 through 18). District 3 is not considered to have any productive forest area and is therefore excluded from this analysis. Data for Gros Morne and Terra Nova national parks were extracted from CanFI2001, but these data have not been included in the analysis for either NIR 2006, NIR 2007, NIR 2008 or NIR 2009 because of lack of data. The area of forest in these 2 national parks is ~57 Kha, which amounts to <2% of the forest area on the (2.9 Mha). We do not consider the exclusion of these lands to be a source of positive bias because, as protected areas, they are subject to less disturbance than surrounding forest areas and would therefore be expected to contribute a net C sink to the accounting process (if they were included). Furthermore, the availability of suitable growth and yield data for these forests, which is rather limited, would further contribute to uncertainty if they were included in the accounting. 

The inventory data were updated in NIR 2009 using data provided by the province. 

The data were modified in NIR2010 in order to separate hardwood and softwood yield data. NIR2009 only used single component growth curves, but multiple component growth curves were supplied by NFS. The leading species classifier defined the volume and the other component was set to “unspecified softwood” or “hardwood”.

In total, we have 2.977 Mha of forest in the inventory. Most of this forest is balsam fir (52%) or black spruce (33%). 

Spatial Stratification

The 17 analysis units are the spatial stratification system used in CBM-CFS3. However, there are only 18 districts in (of which one has no productive forest area). The boundaries of these districts can be mapped, but the boundaries of the subregions (administrative units) within the districts cannot. So, even though we have 54 SPUs in the model, we can only map the data (input and/or results) at the resolution of the 18 districts.

Growth and yield compilation

Growth and yield data were updated in NIR 2009 using data provided by the province. NIR2009 only used single component growth curves, but multiple component growth curves were supplied by NFS and have been used since NIR2010. 

In NIR2011, some historic growth curves were found to be incorrectly assigned for ~13 kha. Growth curve mappings were corrected, and the change in 1990 stocks and fluxes was found to be negligible.

Common Reference Date

The inventory is referenced to circa 2006 (beginning of planning period 0) and needed to be rolled back to the start of 1990. The Rollback Tool is used to do this, and was given the fire (from LFDB and NBAC) and clearcut harvest (from NFDP) events (expressed using area targets) to account for depletions. We found that there was substantially more inventory with age <17 years in 2006 than area disturbed by fire and clearcut harvesting during the period 1990-2006, so a choice had to be made – keep the disturbance information as is or preserve the inventory as is? Even after accounting for non-stocked stands that may have age <17 years in 2006 but need not necessarily have been placed at that age by stand-replacing disturbance since 1990, we still found substantial discrepancy. A decision was made to maintain the disturbance data and “add remaining inventory back” (i.e. copy stands from 2006 to 1990 without adjusting their age). Details on the inventory, disturbances, and rollback process are provided in the project log and in the rollback QAQC spreadsheet. The key assumptions are (i) add remaining inventory back (i.e. use 100% of disturbances – no scaling up or down), (ii) do not allow fire or harvest to disturb non-stocked stands, and (iii) give disturbance priority to fire over harvest because it is more spatially specific than NFDP harvest.

Pool Initialization

Soil and dead organic matter pool stocks are initialized prior to a simulation using a spin-up procedure in which iterations of forest growth followed by stand-replacing disturbance are repeated until the difference, between successive iterations, in total C in the aboveground and belowground slow pools is less than 1% (typically 10 to 30 iterations). The historic disturbance regime is assumed to be one of stand-replacing f

forest growth followed by stand-replacing disturbance are repeated until the difference, between successive iterations, in total C in the aboveground and belowground slow pools is less than 1% (typically 10 to 30 iterations). The historic disturbance regime is assumed to be one of stand-replacing fire with return intervals ranging from 75 to 300 years by terrestrial ecozone (Kurz et al. 2009). Once the iteration termination condition is met, a final stand-replacing disturbance event and subsequent regrowth to the age of the stand as recorded in the inventory are simulated, and the soil and dead organic matter pool C stocks at that age are added to the biomass C pools of the corresponding stand record.

A discrepancy was noted in previous analyses between the utilization rate used for final stand-replacing harvest disturbances during the spin-up (97%) and for harvesting events during the 1990-2011 reporting period simulations (85%). This discrepancy has been fixed for NIR2013 so that harvest disturbances consistently remove 85% of merchantable biomass during both the spin-up and simulation phases of the analysis.

The CanFI information for NWT does not provide the type of volume data required to compile chronosequence growth curves, so curves were borrowed from adjacent jurisdictions. Cordilleran growth curves were borrowed from and all other growth curves were borrowed from . For detailed description of the growth curve compilation methods, please refer to the documentation for these jurisdictions.

This approach to simulating growth in NWT is recognized as a potentially important source of uncertainty. However, there are few alternatives because there is very little growth and yield information gathered in ’s north, and satellite remote sensing inventory methods do not provide rich attribute information from which accurate estimates of stand volume or even stand age can be derived. 

Common Reference Date

CanFI2001 was compiled from a number of source inventories of varying types and vintages. However, initial conditions for C modelling must represent the state of the forest at a single point in time, and each record must be referenced to the same age classes that are used for loading the yield tables into the Standard Import Tool (we use 5 year age classes). A tool was developed in VBA to bring all records to a common reference date. This tool also organizes the CanFI records into the classifier sets that are used in CBM-CFS3 and assigns age class values to each record. 

All CanFI 2001 inventory data were collected in 1995 using satelite remote sensing methods, so the common reference date processing is simply a matter of rolling the inventory back 5 years while updating for stand-replacing disturbances. Since this work was already undertaken for the NFSC FM C Risk Analysis before the development of the Rollback Tool, the methods are those of the common reference date processing, and not the Rollback Tool. 

The algorithm used to roll the inventory to 1990 is as follows:

Step 1: Compile all relevant disturbance monitoring information. This information is used to update the inventory for depletions. Wherever possible, ArcGIS was used to spatially-reference the disturbance data to the appropriate records in the inventory. The disturbance data compiled for inventory update processing include:
Fires All fires since 1980 that burned more than 200 ha (from the LFDB-polygon), will be treated as depletions that must be accounted for in the inventory update process. A discount factor of 0.38 is applied to

in the inventory. The disturbance data compiled for inventory update processing include:
Fires All fires since 1980 that burned more than 200 ha (from the LFDB-polygon), will be treated as depletions that must be accounted for in the inventory update process. A discount factor of 0.38 is applied to burn area of each fire in the update process to account for the fact that the fire record tells us total area burned while we are interested only in forest area burned. The discount factor is usually calculated by determining the amount of treed land that is forest. In the NWT many of the fires burn on land classes other than treed lands, such as shrub, mosses and low-density conifers. For this reason the discount fire factor was calculated using additional land classes, which included some naturally vegetated non-treed land classes. The total area burned in NWT included the following land classes:

Scattered vegetated treed 
Recent unproductive burn
Moss 
Tundra, shrub and lichen (including low density conifers) 
Brush/avalanche/riparian banks

In NWT the discount factor was calculated using only area that was burned in the fire polygons dataset, instead of calculating the discount from the total area of each land class of interest in the territory. This was done to ensure that the model did not target areas outside of the known fires and over-burn forest or other land classes. 
Harvesting Harvest data were acquired for 1970-2002 from the territory. These were used to model harvest depletions on stands moving through this period during the update process. We are assuming that harvest depletions must be accounted for when updating records beyond their reference (update) date towards 1990.
Insects We are not accounting for insect depletions in the inventory common reference date process. Insect impacts are not generally stand-replacing, and we only account for stand-replacing depletions in this process. This could result in a bias in our estimated 1990 age class structure if there were insect disturbances in ’s history that resulted in significant stand-replacing mortality. Furthermore, we are not adjusting the volume values in the inventory to account for any insect depletions that may have occurred during the lifespan of stands leading up to 1990. 

Step 2: Assign an age range to each inventory record using the best available information. No records in NWT have an age class, so volume was used to estimate the age range by looking up the appropriate CanFI chronosequence growth curve. The attributes of the record are used to select the appropriate growth curve, and this curve’s equation is then solved for age at the given volume (refer to frmInventoryUpdate code for details). After the age is estimated using volume, there were a disproportionate number of records with age 110-130 years old. In order to more accurately reflect the age-class distribution of NWT forests, the age ranges of these records was adjusted to 100 –250 years old.

Step 3: Reference all records in the inventory back to the earliest collection date in the inventory. In , all records were collected in 1995. It would appear that rolling the inventory back to 1990 should be a trivial task in this situation – however, this is not the case. We cannot know from the inventory how much of the area in the 1-20 age class circa 1995 was disturbed between 1990 and 1995. We need to reference the disturbance history to determine this. The most effective way to accurately reconstruct the young portions of the age class structure circa 1990 is to roll back to a year well before 1990 and step forward while applying the disturbances that produce the age class structure that we ought to see in 1990. The disturbance history in NWT only goes back to 1980 in a form that is sufficiently complete to provide information into this process, so we hard-coded the start date of the inventory roll-back process to 1980 (instead of using the earliest collection date).

Step 4: Step forward one year at a time, applying disturbances where applicable. Disturb those stands that are eligible for disturbance (i.e. that are referenced to the same spatial entity as the disturbance in question) and give preference to those that could be due for disturbance (i.e. have a current age range that includes 0). Refer to frmInventoryUpdate code for details. Note that we apply a discount factor before applying the fires to the inventory to account for the fact that the fire monitoring data do not distinguish between fires that burn forests versus fires that burn other lands. A discount factor of 0.38 was used because 38% of non-arctic (or recently burned) lands in NWT are classified as forest in CanFI2001.

Note that while undertaking the common reference date processing, we found that we were unable to locate enough CanFI forest are to burn in the mapsheets where fires occured in the 1980s. It turns out that the inventory for NWT, having been conducted by low-resolution satellite remote sensing, identifies recently burned areas mostly as land_class 21140 (naturally non-vegetated recent/unproductive burn) rather than forest, although there is also some forest land with stocking_class 211 (unstocked burn). There are in fact over seven million ha of 21140 and half a million ha of 211. We therefore updated our processing m

eas mostly as land_class 21140 (naturally non-vegetated recent/unproductive burn) rather than forest, although there is also some forest land with stocking_class 211 (unstocked burn). There are in fact over seven million ha of 21140 and half a million ha of 211. We therefore updated our processing methods and developed a special approach for handling these lands:
When updating to common reference date 1990, prioritize 21140 and 211 lands for burning. These lands should coincide with the fire polygons and we expect the majority of them to be burned by our scripts. Where fire polygons are larger than the area of 21140 and 211 lands (or are in locations with no 21140 or 211 lands), then these may burn stocked forest. Where 21140 or 211 lands are burned by our scripts, the scripts will update the classifiers to partially stocked softwood forest (land_class 22340, stocking_class 320, site_quality –8, forest_type 1, predominant_genus 8). This will ensure that these lands are assigned to the most appropriate growth curve for their post-fire regeneration in CBM-CFS3. This choice of assumed post-fire conditions was made on the basis an analysis of the inventory to determine what the most common growth types are. 
As anticipated, our scripts were not be able to find fires to burn all 21140 and 211 lands. Since the inventory was done in 1995, it is most likely that these lands were therefore burned between 1990 and 1995 (because they appear as fire scars in the 1995 remote sensing data and we know that they didn’t burn between 1980 and 1989 because the LFDB does not have fire polygons from before 1990 in the locations of these scars). This means that our scripts need to initialize these lands to their pre-fire condition in 1990 and they must somehow be identified as highest priority lands for burning in the first 5 years of the CBM-CFS3 model simulation. This was done as a pre-processing step after the common reference date, but before importing the data into CBM-CFS3. We located the fires in the fire data that are to burn the remaining 21140 and 211 lands and set these fires up as events that specifically target the 21140 and 211 lands. However, these lands had to first have their classifiers adjusted to the pre-fire conditions (i.e. 22340 and 320, not 21140 and 211). We have set the pre-fire conditions to a classifier set that is recognizable and set the fires’ eligibility criteria such that these stands are targeted. If there are left-over fires for the first 5 years, these can simply be treated as regular fires (i.e. fires that burn using a random sort type). After 1995, everything goes back to normal. 

Step 5: After the inventory is set to 1990 all records with a minimum age less than zero need to have their age adjusted. These records are split into two records, one representing the positive component and one representing the negative component. The positive component has its minimum age reset to zero. with a minimum age less than zero need to have their age adjusted. These records are split into two records, one representing the positive component and one representing the negative component. The positive component has its minimum age reset to zero. The negative component has both its minimum and maximum age reset to its pre-harvest state, the minimum age = 80 and maximum age = 250. ally compiled National Burn Area Composite (NBAC) data product. Growth and yield compilation
Each of the two types of forest inventory data have associated growth and yield information that are used to project forest growth in CBM-CFS3. The SFMM inventory has an associated library of growth curves and a library of pseudochronosequence growth curves were compiled for the CanFI2001 data (the pseudochronosequence growth curve compilation procedure is described elsewhere).

The preliminary C risk analysis results reduced our confidence in the CanFI pseudo-chronosequence curves. Both CFS and OFRI scientists agreed that the CanFI curves were likely responsible for an overestimation of the sink strength of forest lands being modelled using CanFI data (these are the FMS 2 and FMS 3 lands in the C risk analysis). Follow-up analyses revealed that the CanFI curves are more optimistic about growth rates than the growth and yield community feels is warranted given our current knowledge. It was therefore determined that the growth assumptions for the CanFI lands needed to be modified. CFS and OMNR agreed that the most viable way to improve our growth assumptions for the CanFI lands is to use SFMM curves in place of the CanFI ones.

Inventory
Forest Inventory data for ’s () forest management are derived from a provincial timber supply analysis dataset compiled for the modelling software framework. Data were exported from the modeling framework into an Access2003 database for loading into NFCMARS by Lindsay W. in October of 2008.

Spatial Stratification
All of is treated as a single spatial unit, as the entire province is within a single ecozone and administrative unit. 

Classifiers
Classifiers are used for mapping inventory records into the spatial stratification system, mapping to growth curves, and for setting criteria and eligibility in the model. 

The following classifiers are used in the project:

Cover Type
Treatment

Cover type identifies the species composition of stand types, and Treatment identifies the stand originating disturbance. 

Growth and yield compilation
Chronosequence growth curves were built by the PEI Department of Natural Resources (DNR). Growth curves were compiled by the PEI DNR and loaded into the modeling environment. growth curves were generally divided into naturally regenerated stand types and plantations.

Growth and yield were imported into the CBM-CFS3 via the Woodstock Import Tool (WIT). The chronosequences consist of a pair of data points for each age class: softwood volume and hardwood volume. 

Common Reference Date
The reference date of the inventory provided by PEI DNR is assumed to be 2000, and was therefore rolled back to the start of 1990. The rollback tool has been documented in previous versions of the NIR. The key assumptions are (i) add remaining inventory back (i.e. use 100% of disturbances – no scaling up or down), (ii) do not allow fire or harvest to disturb non-stocked stands, and (iii) give disturbance priority to fire over harvest because it is more spatially specific than NFDP harvest.

Common Reference Date
Initial conditions for C modelling must represent the state of the forest at a single point in time. A common reference date of 1990 is used for all NIR analyses. The reference date of the aggregated inventory data was 2000, therefore all three projects were ‘rolled back’ to 1990. The ‘Rollback tool’ software attempts to match inventory from 2000 via disturbance events from 1990-1999. Assumptions about which disturbances target which inventory are made at the age level, instead of the species and stand type level.

Fire

Fire disturbance events come from two different wildfire monitoring data sources. Fires for the years 1990-2003 come from the Canadian National Fire Database (Canadian Forest Service, 2010), and fires for the years 2004-2011 come from the annually compiled National Burn Area Composite (NBAC) data product. Fire disturbances in NFCMARS are derived from these monitoring datasets by spatially overlaying the burned area polygons in the monitoring data with polygons defining the ecozone/provincial forest management administration unit boundary polygons (polygonal spatial planning unit - PSPSU) for each province to determine the area burned annually within each PSPU. The intent of this step is to make sure that fire disturbances are associated with the disturbance matrix for the correct ecozone, and that the inventory records selected for burning by CBM are located within the appropriate provincial administrative unit. This protocol for preparing the fire disturbance time series for NFCMARS has been in place since at least NIR2010.

The most current versions of both of these datasets were pre-processed from scratch, and the resulting 1990-2011 fire disturbance time series was reloaded into the project. This step cleans up an accumulation of data processing errors from previous NIR cycles, and brings the fire disturbance targets in NFCMARS back in line with the current vintages of the fire monitoring datasets.

The NIR2014 NBAC product included new events for 2013 (but no updates to previous NBAC products) and these were also added to the project.

Appendix – Inventory Aggregation

In NIR2006, was run as 43 contiguous “blocks”. The Sylva data was at a complexity level that was not effective under given time constraints. The Sylva data received had forest data characterized in greater than ten classifiers. For NIR2006, we reduced the classifiers to ten for each of the 43 blocks. However, this left us with 43 project databases simulating one province. A decision was made in February, 2006 to aggregate the data structure of the input databases to remove unneeded classifiers. was divided into three regions, which were named “”, “Rupert”, and “Laurentians”. The three regions do not necessarily fall within the actual boundaries of the , but more or less are contained within these areas. 
 
Aggregations goals:

Generate a dataset that is compact and efficient enough to be set up and run as 3 projects for all of instead of 43 blocks:

Aggregations goals:

Generate a dataset that is compact and efficient enough to be set up and run as 3 projects for all of instead of 43 blocks:
need to reduce the size of the output files in order to make the step of loading results possible for large regions. This is best accomplished by reducing the number disturbance types and the number of classifier sets (which can be done either by reducing the number of classifiers or the number of classifier values or both);
need to reduce the size of the SIT tables and set up the structure of the data contained in those tables in order to make the step of importing possible for large regions. This may be best accomplished by making sure that there are not too many SPUs or complicated disturbance groups – also need to keep the size of the files down (inventory, events, TRs).
Realize C results that are the same (i.e. that are the ‘same’ within an acceptable tolerance) as the results generated by the fully detailed dataset built using Sylva data and instructions.

Aggregation tests:

need to be able to confirm that the results are not unduly affected by the aggregation process. Runs conducted at the block level will be used to compare results from fully detailed data against results from aggregated data;
need to be able to confirm that the aggregation will provide us with the performance that we need. Aggregation trials will be conducted at the regional level to ensure that the performance is sufficiently enhanced (or to indicated that further aggregations are required).

Reduce the number of growth curves:
