Simulation territory is essentially the administrative boundary for . This level of spatial complexity was retained after aggregation. Ecozone was also retained during the aggregation process. Ecozone is important from a carbon modeling perspective as many of the dead organic matter parameters are linked to terrestrial ecozone. Calculation group was also retained throughout the aggregation process as it was a link from disturbances to spatial boundaries.

We found that the “rate-model” (model to simulate partial cut growth responses) growth curves contributed to computational complexity problems. Each inventory record in the rate model was associated with its own growth curve. Each rate model inventory record also had its own disturbance event and transition rules associated with it. The data overhead for the increase in precision was outweighing the benefits in model run detail.

We aggregated the growth curves using an area weighted approach. Firstly, we tallied the area from the inventory (ha) of forest with growth expectations described by rate model growth curves. 
We then multiplied this total by the growth rates as defined in age classes (m3/ha). This gave us total volume of area in simulation territories and calculation group that was assigned to the rate model growth curves. Using “group by” queries, each simulation territory, ecozone, calculation group and leading species was left with only one set (hardwood and softwood components) of total volumes. 

In essence, we have taken small portions of area and conglomerated them into larger, aspatial forest zones that are identified by the ecozone in which they live, the species composition and growth rates. We found that species generally followed similar growth rates. For example, yellow birch-dominated stands all generally followed a growth rate of ~ 2.5 m3/ha/yr. By using the area weighted average growth rate, we adjusted the model to have one inventory record in each simulation territory with one growth rate. Instead of hundreds, sometime thousands of growth curves, we are now using one growth curve per inventory record. However, the one aggregated inventory record contains thousands of tiny Sylva records, conglomerated into one. 

Our process interpolates a linear curve from year 0 to year 150 based on the average rate of growth that would be needed to have the area weighted average volume per ha at age 150. We chose 150 years of age for “Rate Model” area as an arbitrary age for partial cut stands. The “Rate Model” does not require stands to have ages, though the CBM-CFS3 requires stands to have an age in order to calculate DOM stocks. For reference on the Rate Model see:

(Volume (m3/ha) @ age 150) / (150 yr) = x m3/ha/yr

We then apply this growth rate from year 0 to year 150 to create curves that

te Model” does not require stands to have ages, though the CBM-CFS3 requires stands to have an age in order to calculate DOM stocks. For reference on the Rate Model see:

(Volume (m3/ha) @ age 150) / (150 yr) = x m3/ha/yr

We then apply this growth rate from year 0 to year 150 to create curves that end up at the area weighted average volume at year 150. Curves from year 150 and beyond are calculated by taking the weighted average per ha amounts of volume from each simulation territory, ecozone, calculation group and species type. The aggregation process resulted in reductions of thousands of growth curves into hundreds. This led to an exponential decrease in database size and subsequent improvement in data import times, model run times and results exporting times. 

The outcome is less stand-level detail, yet same total disturbance area and, essentially, the same carbon stock changes. Modelling at the regional scale, of 37 million ha of forest, we could not afford, due to modelling overhead, having such a fine grained system. We have assumed that, at the strategic level, there were really only a few distinct growth rates by species types in the regions of . For example, yellow birch, on productive soils, we are assuming to have a general growth rate in . What we found was that there were thousands of slightly different growth rates for yellow birch in selected ecozones and calculation groups. At a regional scale, we have assumed all yellow birch will follow similar growth expectancy. Our aggregation takes into account high and low growth rates and finds the average by amount of area in each level of stand productivity. This is the basis for our aggregation of growth curves.

Some forest areas in the inventory are listed as “not stocked”. These records need to be mapped to a growth curve, even through they are not stocked, and assumptions must be made regarding the fate of these lands during the simulation period. Our options are (i) leave these lands out of the analysis (i.e. assume that they will see no regeneration during the simulation period), or (ii) map these lands to a generic growth curve, thereby assuming that they will regenerate during the simulation period. For the purposes of this analysis, we assume that these lands will all regenerate to forest, and we have mapped them to the most generic growth curve available for the region in which they are located (given the lack of information in the inventory indicating what type of forests to expect on these lands when they regenerate) and set their age to zero. Note that this may result in an overestimate of biomass production on these sites, but it will also move these lands into the pool of lands available for disturbance. Therefore, it is not guaranteed that these assumptions will bias the C outcome towards a greater sink.

Introduction

This document summarizes the updates to Canada’s National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System (NFCMARS) for Canada’s 2015 national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory submission to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), covering the reporting period 1990-2013.

No changes to the emissions estimation methodology have been introduced for NIR2015. NFCMARS updates for the current National Inventory Report (NIR) were limited to changes in input data:

Updated wildfire activity data for 1990-2012 in Ontario, to capture updates to the underlying data sources and to correct an accumulation of past data processing errors;
Updated slash burning activity data for 1990-2012 in Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Ontario, Quebec and Northwest Territor

1990-2012 in Ontario, to capture updates to the underlying data sources and to correct an accumulation of past data processing errors;
Updated slash burning activity data for 1990-2012 in Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Ontario, Quebec and Northwest Territories, to capture all updates to the underlying National Forestry Database Program (NFDP) prescribed burning statistics;
Update global warming potential (GWP) factors to IPCC 2006 values; 
Updating harvest activity data for 2008-2012, to capture recent changes to the underlying NFDP harvest statistics; and
Addition of new activity data for 2013 wildfires, insect disturbances, harvesting, slashburning and deforestation.

These updates and the implications for changes in GHG emisisons and removals estimates are described in more detail in the remainder of this document.

Section 2 describes the sequential updates of activity data and other model parameters from NIR2014 for the 1990-2012 time series. Section 3 summarises the activity data updates for the reporting year 2013. Section 4 summarises the results for NIR2015 and Section 5 details the changes in the emission and removal time series for each step in the recalculations due to updated activity data for the period 1990 to 2013.

All analyses in this report are conducted assuming instant oxidation of wood transferred to forest products. The implications of using the new harvested wood products model will be reported elsewhere.

The issues that prevented updating Ontario fire disturbance activity data have been resolved and we have updated 1990 – 2013 fire disturbance events in Ontario for NIR2015.

Implementing these changes increased the area burned in some of the historic years (1995 and 1996 in particular). Harvest activity data in the NIR are specified in units of target volume (carbon), not in terms of area. The NIR 2014 was the first year in which we used the available NFDP statistics for the reporting year. Results

GHG Emissions and Removals in the Managed Forest

Figure 4.1 shows the annual GHG emissions from, and areas affected by, disturbance in the managed forest for the period 1990 to 2013. Canada’s managed forest was a net sink of carbon emissions in 2013 (19 Mt CO2e), while with the updated disturbance information, 2012 was a bigger source of C (34 Mt CO2e) than in NIR2014.

Figure 4.1: Emissions and removals from Canada’s managed forest, NIR2015 vs NIR2014

Fire

The total area burned in 2013 was 455,000 hectares (Figure 3.1). Direct emissions from wildfire in 2013 were 60 Mt CO2e, down from 121 Mt CO2e in 2012 (Figure 4.2). 

Figure 4.2: Wildfire emissions, NIR2015 vs NIR2014 

The area burned in 2013 is below average compared to the rest of the timeseries. 1995 remains the most instense fire year within the past 23 years. Emissions differ am

wildfire in 2013 were 60 Mt CO2e, down from 121 Mt CO2e in 2012 (Figure 4.2). 

Figure 4.2: Wildfire emissions, NIR2015 vs NIR2014 

The area burned in 2013 is below average compared to the rest of the timeseries. 1995 remains the most instense fire year within the past 23 years. Emissions differ among the two NIR time series as the model selects different records to burn due to the random selection of stands within each spatial unit. This is a well-documented consequence of the modelling approach in the CBM-CFS3 and contributes to the estimated uncertainty of the NIR time series. 

Insects

The CBM-CFS3 represents two types of insects: defoliators and bark beetles. Herbivory by defoliators contributes a small amount of direct emissions to the GHG balance in each year (Figure 4.3). Bark beetles, including the Mountain Pine Bettle, do not contribute to direct emisisons in the year of disturbance but cause large transfers of live biomass to dead organic matter pools from where emissions result in subsequent years due to decay (heterotrophic respiration) of organic matter. 

Figure 4.3: Direct emissions from defoliating insects, NIR2015 vs NIR2014. 

The area disturbed by insects continued to decline in 2012 due to the waning extent and severity of the Mountain Pine Beetle epidemic in British Columbia. The total realized area disturbed by insects in 2012 was 1,735 kHa, down from 2,971 kHa in 2011 (figure 3.2.1). The realized disturbances are less than the area targets in 2013 and 2012 because there is simply not enough inventory with identifiable host tree species (i.e. not enough inventory in BC with an identifiable or inferrable pine component, and not enough inventory in Alberta with an identifiable or inferable aspen component) to satisfy the areas prescribed in the insect monitoring data. Also, data received from the province of British Columbia in 2014 indicated that severe and very severe impacts occurred in areas where there has been no low or moderate beetle impact in previous years. Disturbance rules in the CBM-CFS3 for Mountain Pine Beetle currently define that severe and very severe impacts can only occur in stands which, in the previous 5 years, had been affected by the beetle. This issue will be examined further for NIR2016 and may require revisions to the current disturbance rules. 

Forest Management

1. Introduction 
 
This document summarizes the updates to Canada’s National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and 
Reporting System (NFCMARS) for Canada’s 2015 national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory submission 
to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), covering the reporting 
period 1990-2013. 
 
No changes to the emissions estimation methodology have been introduced for NIR2015. NFCMARS 
updates for the current National Inventory Report (NIR) were limited to changes in input data: 
 
 Updated wildfire activity data for 1990-2012 in Ontario, to capture updates to the underlying data 
sources and to correct an accumulation of past data processing errors; 
 Updated slash burning activity data for 1990-2012 in Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, New 
Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Ontario, Quebec and Northwest Territories, to capture all 
updates to the underlying National Forestry Database Program (NFDP) prescribed burning 
statistics; 
 Update global warming potential (GWP) factors to IPCC 2006 values1; 
 Updating harvest activity data for 2008-2012, to capture recent changes to the underlying NFDP 
harvest statistics; and 
 Addition of new activity data for 2013 wildfires, insect disturbances, harvesting, slashburning and 
deforestation. 
 
These updates and the implications for changes in GHG emisisons and removals estimates are described 
in more detail in the remainder of this document. 
 
Section 2 describes the sequential updates of activity data and other model parameters from NIR2014 for 
the 1990-2012 time series. Section 3 summarises the activity data updates for the reporting year 2013.

4.3. Insects 
 
The CBM-CFS3 represents two types of insects: defoliators and bark beetles. Herbivory by defoliators 
contributes a small amount of direct emissions to the GHG balance in each year (Figure 4.3). Bark 
beetles, including the Mountain Pine Bettle, do not contribute to direct emisisons in the year of 
disturbance but cause large transfers of live biomass to dead organic matter pools from where emissions 
result in subsequent years due to decay (heterotrophic respiration) of organic matter. 
 
 
 
Figure 4.3: Direct emissions from defoliating insects, NIR2015 vs NIR2014. 
 
The area disturbed by insects continued to decline in 2012 due to the waning extent and severity of the 
Mountain Pine Beetle epidemic in British Columbia. The total realized area disturbed by insects in 2012 
was 1,735 kHa, down from 2,971 kHa in 2011 (figure 3.2.1). The realized disturbances are less than the 
area targets in 2013 and 2012 because there is simply not enough inventory with identifiable host tree 
species (i.e. not enough inventory in BC with an identifiable or inferrable pine component, and not 
enough inventory in Alberta with an identifiable or inferable aspen component) to satisfy the areas 
prescribed in the insect monitoring data. Also, data received from the province of British Columbia in 
2014 indicated that severe and very severe impacts occurred in areas where there has been no low or 
moderate beetle impact in previous years. Disturbance rules in the CBM-CFS3 for Mountain Pine Beetle 
currently define that severe and very severe impacts can only occur in stands which, in the previous 5 
years, had been affected by the beetle. This issue will be examined further for NIR2016 and may require 
revisions to the current disturbance rules.

Introduction

This document summarizes the updates to Canada’s National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System (NFCMARS) for Canada’s 2015 national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory submission to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), covering the reporting period 1990-2013.

No changes to the emissions estimation methodology have been introduced for NIR2015. NFCMARS updates for the current National Inventory Report (NIR) were limited to changes in input data:

Updated wildfire activity data for 1990-2012 in Ontario, to capture updates to the underlying data sources and to correct an accumulation of past data processing errors;
Updated slash burning activity data for 1990-2012 in Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Ontario, Quebec and Northwest Territories, to capture all updates to the underlying National Forestry Database Program (NFDP) prescribed burning statistics;
Update global warming potential (GWP) factors to IPCC 2006 values; 
Updating harvest activity data for 2008-2012, to capture recent changes to the underlying NFDP harvest statistics; and
Addition of new activity data for 2013 wildfires, insect disturbances, harvesting and deforestation.

These updates and the implications for changes in GHG emisisons and removals estimates are described in more detail in the remainder of this document.

Section 2 describes the sequential updates of activity data and other model parameters from NIR2014 for the 1990-2012 time series. Section 3 summarised the activity data updates for the reporting year 2013. Section 4 summarises the results for NIR2015 and Section 5 details the changes in the emission and removal time series for each step in the recalculations due to updated activity data for the period 1990 to 2013.

Recalculations Updates
Wildfire activity data

For NIR 2014, to correct a number of data processing errors from prior years and to capture updates to the underlying wildfire monitoring data, a complete 1990 – 2011 time series of wildfire disturbances was re-assembled from the official monitoring datasets. Fire disturbance activity data were re-loaded for all provinces except Ontario because of issues in relating GIS wildfire polygons to aspatial Ontario inventory records. The issues that prevented updating Ontario fire disturbance activity data have been resolved and we have updated 1990 – 2013 fire disturbance events in Ontario for NIR2015.

Figure 2.1 compares the area annually burned in Ontario after updating the Ontario fire disturbances with the area annually burned in NIR2014 for Ontario only. Implementing these changes increased the area burned in some of the historic years (1995 and 1996 in particular). The area burned in Ontario in the NIR2015 now more closely matches the statistics found in the CFS Large Fire Database.

Slash burning activity data

Slash burning activity data for Alberta, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Labrador, and the Northwest Territories are taken from the prescribed burning statistics provided by the NFDP. A number of discrepancies between the slash burning disturbance targets used in NIR2014 and the current NFDP statistics were noted during a recent review. We have updated the 1990 – 2013 slash burning targets for these provinces in order to re-establish consistency between NFCMARS and the NFDP statistics.

Global warming potentials

Global warming potentials (GWP) for methane and nitrous oxide have been updated to the IPCC 2006 values. Specifically, the GWP for methane (CH4) has increased from 21 to 25, while the GWP for nitrous oxide (N2O) has decreased from 310 to 298.

Recent activity data updates

The NIR 2015 incorporated the following new activity data: 
Fire activity data for the year 2013
Harvest activity data for years 2008 to 2013
Mountain Pine Beetle infestation data in British Columbia for year 2013
New Slash burning data for years 1990-2013

No other new activity data were incorporated into the NIR 2015 submission.Deforestation data for 2013 have not been updated and 2012 deforestation rates were extended to 2013. No new afforestation data are available and afforestation rates in 2013 were assumed zero, as in 2012.

Forest Management Activity Data

Harvest activity data in the NIR are specified in units of target volume (carbon), not in terms of area. The NIR 2014 was the first year in which we used the available NFDP statistics for the reporting year. Because some of the provincial data were incomplete statistics, this unfortunately resulted in underestimated harvest rates for some regions of the country, in particular for Quebec. These NFDP data have been updated since NIR2014 and when the harvest time series for NIR2015 is compared to NIR2014 (Fig 3.3), substantial increases in the area harvested for 2012 can be seen. 

For NIR 2015 we decided to use only the most recent year with complete statistics (in this case 2012) and to apply the 2012 value in 2013. This resulted in two years of identical harvest targets (2012 and 2013), yet updates the time-series with the most recent available complete data. It is anticipated that in NIR2016, the harvest rates for 2013 will differ from those in 2012.

Insects

The CBM represents two types of insects: defoliators and bark beetles. Herbivory by defoliators contributes a small amount of direct emissions to the GHG balance in each year (
Figure 4.2). Bark beetles, including the Mountain Pine Bettle, do not contribute to direct emisisons in the year of disturbance but cause large transfers of live biomass to dead organic matter pools from where emissions result in subsequent years due to decay (hetertrophic respiration) of organic matter. 

Figure 4.3: Direct emissions from defoliating insects, NIR2015 vs NIR2014. 
Note that the y-axis scale on this graph is t, while all other emissions graphs show Mt – a difference in scale of six orders of magnitude (one million).

The area disturbed by insects continued to decline in 2012 due to the waning extent and severity of the Mountain Pine Beetle epidemic in British Columbia. The total realized area disturbed by insects in 2012 was 1,735 kHa, down from 2,971 kHa in 2011. The realized disturbances are less than the area targets in 2013 and 2012 because there is simply not enough inventory with identifiable host tree species (i.e. not enough inventory in BC with an identifiable or inferrable pine component, and not enough inventory in Alberta with an identifiable or inferable aspen component) to satisfy the areas prescribed in the insect monitoring data. Also, data received from the province of British Columbia in 2014 indicated that severe and very severe impacts occurred in areas where there has been no low or moderate beetle impact in previous years. Disturbance rules in the CBM-CFS3 for Mountain Pine Beetle currently define that severe and very severe impacts can only occur in stands which, in the previous 5 years, had been affected by the beetle. This issue will be examined further for NIR2016 and may require revisions to the current disturbance rules.

Introduction
This document describes Canada’s National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System (NFCMARS), as implemented for Canada’s 2014 national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory submission (the National Inventory Report, or NIR) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), covering the reporting period 1990-2012. The system is documented herein at a summary level of detail, and includes numerous references to peer-reviewed literature and technical reports that describe various aspects of NFCMARS in significantly greater detail. 
NFCMARS is designed for both the monitoring and projection of forest carbon (C) stocks and GHG emissions

NFCMARS is designed for both the monitoring and projection of forest carbon (C) stocks and GHG emissions and removals. In addition to providing annual estimates and reporting of the Canadian forest sector greenhouse gas budget to meet Canada’s international UNFCCC reporting obligations, NFCMARS is actively used to inform federal policy development such as the design of improved forest C reporting and accounting methods (e.g. forward-looking reference levels), the evaluation of Canadian forest sector mitigation potential, and to assist in meeting the forest C policy and reporting needs of provincial and territorial governments.
The document structure and content is consistent with Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) guidance for documenting tier 3 model-based inventory reporting systems (IPCC, 2011).
National Circumstances
Forests play a significant role in the global C cycle, sequestering the equivalent of roughly one-third of total fossil fuel emissions annually (Pan et al. 2011). Global forest C stocks are currently estimated at 861±66 Pg C, distributed 55% in tropical forests, 32% in boreal forests, and 14% in temperate forests. Over the last two decades the world’s 1135 million hectares of boreal forest have contributed, on average, 21% (0.5 Pg C yr-1) of the global C sink in established forests. Similarly, 767 million hectares of temperate forests have contributed 31% (0.75 Pg C yr-1) of the global forest C sink over the same period (Pan et al. 2011).
The geographic extent of Canada’s forests is shown in Figure 1-1. Canada’s estimated 350 million hectares of forest land (NRCan, 2013) constitute 10% of the world’s total forest area, and 20% of the circumpolar boreal forest biome (Stinson et al. 2011). Canadian forests are composed of approximately 68% coniferous, 16% mixed wood, 11% broadleaf, and 6% non-treed forest types. The predominant tree genera by volume are spruce (53%), poplar (12%), and pine (9%) (NRCan, 2013). 
Canada’s managed forests are defined and delineated using an area-based approach consistent with IPCC Good Practice Guidance (IPCC, 2003), and include lands managed for sustainable production of wood fibre or wood-based bioenergy, protection from and suppression of natural disturbance agents, and conservation of forest ecological values (Stinson et al. 2011). Forest within these areas is defined according to Canada’s implementation of the Marrakesh Accord as areas 1 hectare or greater that are at least 20 metres wide (from tree base to tree base), having a minimum of 25% crown closure and the potential to reach a minimum tree height at maturity in situ of 5 metres (Government of Canada, 2007). Under this definition, the managed forest covers 2.3 x 106 of Canada’s estimated 3.5 x 106 km2 total forest area (Stinson et al.

Canadian forests are impacted by a variety of disturbance agents, including wildfire, insects and other factors affecting forest health, wind damage, and numerous industrial activities such as logging, road construction, non-renewable resource exploration and extraction, and other human activities. Both natural and anthropogenic disturbances are an integral part of forest ecosystem dynamics, including C dynamics, and each influences the other through the actions of forest managers who increasingly seek to develop silvicultural systems that mimic natural disturbance characteristics, and to salvage timber resources damaged by natural agents. Spatial Representation Framework
NFCMARS incorporates a hierarchically nested spatial framework. At the highest level are 15 terrestrial ecozones. Twelve of these contain managed forest, and GHG statistics in the LULUCF sector are reported at this resolution. Terrestrial ecozones are intersected by provincial and territorial boundaries to create 50 reconciliation units. Land area change accounts from various sectors are reconciled at this scale. Finally, reconciliation units are intersected with the boundaries of provincial and territorial forest management units, creating a total of 635 spatial analysis units (SPUs). Forest inventory and disturbance data are spatially referenced to these SPUs, though the exact location of each forest stand within each SPU is not tracked in the model. Nearly 3 million stands are tracked in NFCMARS. Analyses are conducted at this spatial resolution, and results are then aggregated into the 15 larger ecozone units for reporting (Stinson et al. 2011).

Science background: Forest C Modelling
Though the forest C sink strength has been relatively consistent over the past two decades at global scales, significant regional and temporal differences exist at regional and local scales due to the inherent heterogeneity of forest ecosystems. The large spatial and temporal scales over which the forest C cycle operates make capturing the heterogeneity in C stocks and stock changes through measurement alone impractical, if not impossible. Thus field measurements and remote sensing data are typically augmented with computer models in forest C monitoring systems for large landscapes. The NFCMARS is such a system.
General model description: type, scope
The analytical foundation of the NFCMARS is the Carbon Budget Model of the Canadian Forest Sector (CBM-CFS3) (Kurz et al. 2009), an internationally recognized forest carbon dynamics modelling framework that has been used in several other countries, including Russia, Mexico, and several European countries. NFCMARS implements the IPCC Tier 3 “default” method of adding growth and subtracting depletions from an initial inventory for estimating forest C stock changes (IPCC, 2003), and CBM-CFS3 is used to calculate annual changes in forest carbon stocks, and emissions of non-CO2 GHGs, resulting from forest management activities, natural disturbances and natural (non-disturbance) forest processes. This approach allows for the quantification of annual C-impacts from different disturbance processes, facilitating the attribution of C-impacts to anthropogenic versus non-anthropogenic causal agents. Natural forest processes, such as net primary productivity (NPP) and heterotrophic respiration (Rh), however, are influenced by biotic and abiotic drivers as well as direct and indirect anthropogenic impacts. Factoring out the direct anthropogenic effects from all others in the largest ecosystem C fluxes, such as NPP and Rh, cannot yet be done in NFCMARS.
The CBM-CFS3 is a wood volume yield data driven model that explicitly simulates the C dynamics of five IPCC-recommended ecosystem C pools – aboveground biomass, belowground biomass, dead wood, litter, and soil organic matter (IPCC, 2003) – and can represent forest C dynamics at both the stand and landscape scales. It tracks C stocks, transfers between pools, and emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), and carbon monoxide (CO) (Kurz et al. 2002).
CBM-CFS3 is described in detail in Kurz et al. 2009, and NFCMARS is described in further detail in Stinson et al. 2011.
Main processes represented and equations
Forest and Forest Carbon state description
CBM-CFS3 tracks forest carbon in 22 distinct pools – 12 biomass and 10 DOM – for each forest stand (Kurz et al. 2009). Softwood (SW) and hardwood (HW) tree genera are tracked separately for all biomass components and for stem and branch snags. These pools are then aggregated into the five

escription
CBM-CFS3 tracks forest carbon in 22 distinct pools – 12 biomass and 10 DOM – for each forest stand (Kurz et al. 2009). Softwood (SW) and hardwood (HW) tree genera are tracked separately for all biomass components and for stem and branch snags. These pools are then aggregated into the five IPCC-recommended pools. The pools are listed in Table 2-1.
Each stand is described by its area, age, UNFCCC land class (IPCC, 2003), and up to 10 user-defined classifiers. The classifier definitions used in NFCMARS are specific to each jurisdiction, and include information such as site productivity, leading species, management unit and ownership. Classifiers are used to associate stands with the appropriate yield tables, and to identify suitable candidate stands for disturbances. Each stand is also referenced to the spatial unit in which it is located (see section 1.2).
Table - CBM-CFS3 carbon pools

Stand growth, mortality and decay dynamics
The CBM-CFS3 simulates the annual C-stock changes in each of the 22 pools in each stand resulting from growth, biomass turnover, litterfall, decomposition, and – where applicable – C transfers caused by natural and anthropogenic disturbance processes.
Forest growth is driven by gross merchantable volume (including decay, waste and breakage) versus age tables, of the type typically developed by provincial and territorial forest management agencies. Stand yields are converted from merchantable volume units to total living aboveground C mass using a comprehensive set of volume-to-biomass equations developed for all Canadian forest types from a large number of permanent and temporary sample plots representing all provinces and the Yukon territories (Boudewyn et al. 2007). Merchantability criteria are used to allocate the stemwood biomass into tops, stumps and merchantable stemwood pools. For immature growth stages having little or no merchantable volume, a curve smoothing algorithm is used to estimate aboveground biomass dynamics from stand establishment to the first available measurements. 
Tree, foliage, branch, and root mortality are represented using annual biomass turnover rates up to the time of stand breakup, (as indicated by declining yield curves) after which time the biomass pool turnover is considered incremental to the biomass losses from stand-breakup. Litterfall transfer rates are used to partition the C from biomass turnover processes into the different DOM pools. Litterfall transfer and biomass turnover rates are as described by Kurz et al. (1992) and Kurz and Apps (1999), except for fine root turnover rates which are from Li et al. (2003).
The annual amount of organic matter decomposed in each DOM pool is controlled by a temperature-dependent decay rate (yr-1):

ak = BDRk × Tmod × Smod

where ak is the actual decay rate, BDRk is the base decay rate, and Tmod and Smod are temperature and stand modifiers, respectively (Kurz et al. 2009).
The temperature modifier acts to reduce the decay rate for mean a

controlled by a temperature-dependent decay rate (yr-1):

ak = BDRk × Tmod × Smod

where ak is the actual decay rate, BDRk is the base decay rate, and Tmod and Smod are temperature and stand modifiers, respectively (Kurz et al. 2009).
The temperature modifier acts to reduce the decay rate for mean annual temperatures below the reference temperature, and the stand modifier acts to increase decomposition rates in open-canopied stands:

Tmod = e((MATi-RefTemp) × ln(Q10) × 0.1)

Smod = 1 + (MaxDecayMult - 1)e(-b × TotBio/MaxBio)

where MATi is the mean annual temperature in spatial unit i, RefTemp is the reference mean annual temperature, Q10 is a temperature coefficient, MaxDecayMult is the open canopy decay rate multiplier, TotBio and MaxBio are, respectively, the total and maximum aboveground biomass for the stand type, and b is a constant (6.93; see Kurz and Apps 1999). MATi is the average of 1961 to 1990 mean annual temperatures within each spatial unit from interpolated climate surface data (McKenney et al. 2001). The temperature modifier thus results in decay rate temperature sensitivity that is spatially variable but temporally constant. MaxDecayMult is set to 1 in current applications of the model, effectively removing any dependency of decay rates on stand density.
In all but the slow DOM pools, some of the decomposed material is released to the atmosphere and the remainder is transferred to the more stable slow DOM pools. All decomposed material in the slow DOM pools is released to the atmosphere. Decomposition rates are as described in Kurz et al. (2009) and Smyth et al (2010).
The CBM-CFS3 representation of forest growth, mortality and decay dynamics is described in significantly greater detail in Kurz et al. 2009.
Disturbance dynamics
IPCC Good Practice Guidance (IPCC, 2003) encourages explicit reporting of both natural and anthropogenic disturbances, and both are represented in NFCMARS.
Disturbance dynamics are characterized in CBM-CFS3 by five essential elements: candidate stand characteristics, disturbance extent, disturbance impacts on forest C transfers between the C pools or out of the ecosystem altogether, post-disturbance stand regeneration regime, and land-use change accounting in the case of afforestation (L-FL) or deforestation (FL-L) disturbance events (Kurz et al. 2009).
The collection of candidate stands for each disturbance type may be controlled through: geography, via targeting of specific groups of one or more spatial units (section 1.2); biophysical forest characteristics via targeting of specific stand attributes such as species, age, disturbance history, and C profile; order of selection from the collection of candidate stands via various sorting criteria such as random, or decreasing order of merchantable C biomass or age.
The extent of disturbance activity is defined through explicit targets expressed in terms of area-per-year or carbon mass-per-year.

The impacts of disturbances on the C profile (i.e. the distribution of C mass in the 22 pools) of the disturbed stand are characterized by a disturbance matrix (Kurz et al. 2009). These two dimensional transition matrices specify the proportion of existing C in each pool that is transferred to other pools, to the atmosphere, or to the forest products sector. Disturbance matrices are specific to each disturbance type, and may be varied both geographically and temporally. Table 2-2 shows an example of a CBM-CFS3 disturbance matrix for wildfire in the Boreal Shield West ecozone.
CBM-CFS3 includes a flexible suite of options for controlling post-disturbance stand recovery dynamics. Disturbances can be specified as either full or partial stand mortality events, and transition rules can be applied to control the post-disturbance stand type, regeneration delay, and growth trajectory. Up to four distinct post-disturbance regeneration regimes can be specified for a given pre-disturbance stand type and disturbance combination. Any disturbed area not explicitly assigned a post-disturbance regime is regenerated to the original stand type.
The impacts of land-use change can be both positive and negative. Deforestation accounts for roughly 12% of anthropogenic GHG emissions (van der Werf et al. 2009). The IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories (IPCC, 2006) distinguish between emissions from lands subject to the same land-use for more than 20 years and emissions from lands that have experienced a change in land-use in the preceding 20 years. The CBM-CFS3 supports this distinction by representing both deforestation and afforestation land-use change events as distinct disturbance types with their own unique disturbance matrices and transition rules. Post-disturbance C dynamics are simulated in the same manner as for all other disturbance types, except that deforestation and afforestation events trigger a change in land-use classification prior to the evaluation of disturbance impacts so that the impacts are reported in the new land-use class.

Key Assumptions
The CBM-CFS3 is designed primarily for forested upland sites, and thus there is a higher degree of uncertainty in the predicted C stocks and emissions resulting from deep organic soils, low-lying forested peatlands, and sites underlain with permafrost (Kurz et al. 2012).
Soil and dead organic matter pool stocks are initialized prior to a simulation using a spin-up procedure in which iterations of forest growth followed by stand-replacing disturbance are repeated until the difference, between successive iteratio

and sites underlain with permafrost (Kurz et al. 2012).
Soil and dead organic matter pool stocks are initialized prior to a simulation using a spin-up procedure in which iterations of forest growth followed by stand-replacing disturbance are repeated until the difference, between successive iterations, in total C in the aboveground and belowground slow pools is less than 1% (typically 10 to 30 iterations). The historic disturbance regime is assumed to be one of stand-replacing fire with return intervals ranging from 75 to 300 years by terrestrial ecozone (Kurz et al. 2009). This approach yields non-equilibrium soil conditions that reflect changes in disturbance regime, management or species at the start of the simulation, relative to historical conditions. Once the iteration termination condition is met, a final stand-replacing disturbance event and subsequent regrowth to the age of the stand as recorded in the inventory are simulated, and the soil and dead organic matter pool C stocks at that age are added to the biomass C pools of the corresponding stand record. 
The spin-up initialization procedure described above cannot be applied to afforested areas because CBM-CFS3 is not designed to simulate growth of agricultural crops or other non-woody species. The initialization assumptions for dead organic matter pools in afforested areas are described in section 3.2.2.2.
of Application
The of application of the NFCMARS is the managed forest landbase of Canada (shown in Figure 1-1, and defined in section 3.1), and those (very small) portions of the unmanaged forest that have been subject to deforestation events.
Though NFCMARS provides nearly complete coverage for all managed forest lands in Canada, there remain several known gaps with a total estimated area of approximately 3 million hectares (1.3% of the total managed forest area in Canada). The managed forest lands not presently accounted for fall into three categories.
Forests in national parks and park reserves administered by Parks Canada are not presently accounted before because inventory information does not exist for these areas at the present time.
Privately owned forest lands are only included to the extent that they are present in the forest inventory source information (Table 3-1) from which the NFCMARS inventory database is assembled and private land information is not consistently incorporated in provincial forest estate planning datasets from various jurisdictions.
Shade tolerant hardwood forests on public lands in Ontario that are managed using selection harvest silviculture systems are a special case. Though these forests are present in Ontario’s forest estate planning inventories, their representation is not readily translatable into the NFCMARS inventory framework. It was decided jointly by the CFS and the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources to exclude these data from NFCMARS.

Model Calibration
Slow pools decay parameters
The calibration of base decay rates for the slow pools used an iterative process to minimize the mean bias (Smith et al. 1997) between modelled estimates and measured values for stand-level data. The data used were 599 measurements of forest floor and mineral soil C, including percent carbon or percent organic matter by horizon, horizon thickness, and soil profile classification from a forest ecosystem C database (Shaw et al. 2005) and from the Ontario Terrestrial Assessment Program (ELCG, 2005). The calibrated base decay rates (at 10°C) were 1.5% yr-1 for the aboveground slow pool, 0.33% yr-1 for the belowground slow pool, and an assumed transfer rate (from aboveground slow to belowground slow) of 0.6% yr-1. The value of the temperature quotient (Q10) for the aboveground slow pool was assumed to be the same as for the aboveground very fast pool (Q10=2.65). Since the base decay rates calibrated for individual plots exhibited no discernable trend with mean annual temperature, the Q10 for the belowground slow pool was set to one. See Shaw et al. (2006) for a full description of the calibration procedure.
Very fast aboveground pool decay parameters
Dead organic matter submodel parameters were estimated using litterbag decomposition data from the Canadian Intersite Decomposition Experiment (CIDET) (Smyth et al. 2010). This national experiment provided 12 years of decomposition time series data from 18 sites across Canada for calibration of decay parameters for foliar litter (very fast decay pool) and fine woody debris (fast decay pool). Time series of measured carbon remaining were compared to model predictions to calibrate the base decay rates, temperature quotients, and the proportion of carbon transferred from quickly decaying dead organic matter pools to the slow pools. A statistical approach was developed to optimize several model parameters simultaneously by minimizing residual errors. 
For foliar litter decay, which is synonymous with aboveground very fast pool in the CBM-CFS3, the asymptotic form of the decay function used in the model was consistent with the measured time series for both needle and leaf litter. Calibrated decay parameters had a base decay rate of 35.5 % yr-1 at a 10° C reference temperature, a temperature quotient (Q10) of 2.65, and a proportion transferred to the slow pool of 0.185. 
Fast pools decay parameters
Fast pool decay parameters were calibrated using fine woody debris decomposition data from the CIDET (Smyth et al. 2010). Wood block decay time series were not well represented by the model’s asymptotic form of decay. Instead, the coldest sites had a linear deca

f 0.185. 
Fast pools decay parameters
Fast pool decay parameters were calibrated using fine woody debris decomposition data from the CIDET (Smyth et al. 2010). Wood block decay time series were not well represented by the model’s asymptotic form of decay. Instead, the coldest sites had a linear decay rate and the remaining sites had a variable decay rate that was better fit by a sigmoidal function. Four potential modifications to the decay algorithm were tested to estimate improvements in model predictions of fast pool decay. These included a temperature-dependent time delay, a sigmoidal function for decay, and the addition of a holding pool that had either a delayed transfer of C to the fast pool or a decayed transfer of C. The implementation of these modifications in the model would, however, require the introduction and simulation of the age structure of the DOM pools for each stand. This effort would be justifiable only if more long-term decay data were available to improve model parameterization. At present, NFCMARS uses a base decay rate of 14.35 % yr-1 at a 10° C reference temperature, a temperature quotient (Q10) of 2.0, and a proportion transferred to the slow pool of 0.17. 
Decay of all other pools, including standing dead organic matter, is described in Kurz et al. (2009).
Model evaluation
Roots indicators and root parameter evaluation
The contribution of roots to the C budget was estimated for Canada’s managed forests from 1990 to 2008. The estimated average net primary production (NPP) during this period was 809 Tg C yr-1 (352 g C m2 yr-1) with roots contributing 39.8 % of this production, mostly through replacement of fine root turnover. The estimated belowground NPP (NPPBG) of 140 g C m2 yr-1 for the CBM-CFS3, was very close to the NPPBG by Gower et al. (2001) of 144±25 g C m2 yr-1 (standard error), and within the range of NPPBG values (69 g C m2 yr-1 to 166 g C m2 yr-1) for the boreal (Luyssaert et al. 2007). The ratio of NPPBG/NPP estimated by the CBM-CFS3 was 39.8%, which was similar to the estimates by Gower et al. (2001) of 33%±3%. Fine root NPP was 31%, which was similar to the global estimate of 33% (Jackson et al. 1997).
Estimated average root C stocks were 2383 Tg (1235 g C m-2), mostly from coarse roots (≥ 5 mm diameter), and had an average root to shoot percentage of 25.6%.
For the Boreal region, Mokany et al. (2006) found a slightly higher root to shoot percentage of 39%±6% versus the model’s predicted value of 31.2% for low aboveground biomass (<7500 Mg m-2), but was consistent with the root to shoot percentage for high aboveground biomass (>7500 Mg m-2); 24%±2% versus the model’s predicted value of 24.7%. Estimates of root to shoot percentages from Cairns et al. (1997) and Gower et al. (2001) for the boreal region were 27%±1% and 28±11%, respectively, which were similar to the overall root to shoot percentage of 25.6% predicted by the national-scale run.

to shoot percentages from Cairns et al. (1997) and Gower et al. (2001) for the boreal region were 27%±1% and 28±11%, respectively, which were similar to the overall root to shoot percentage of 25.6% predicted by the national-scale run.
Impacts of varying root parameters on stocks and fluxes were assessed through three national-scale simulations. Varying the root turnovers and fine root recalcitrant percentage had small impacts on estimated primary production and net ecosystem production, but estimates of dead organic matter stocks and corresponding heterotrophic respiration were affected. General data inputs
Information describing the initial state of the forest inventory, expected forest growth and wood volume yield over time, anthropogenic and natural disturbances to the forest inventory, and land-use change are the primary data inputs that drive CBM-CFS3 simulations. Each of these is discussed in more detail in section 3. 
Sensitivity Analysis
Ground plot sensitivity analysis (5% change)
A sensitivity study was conducted on predicted C stocks matching the ground plot data (from section 2.5.1) to rank the importance of decay parameters in the CBM-CFS3. The analysis included 40 parameters: eleven base decay rates, eleven temperature quotients, ten proportions transferred to the slow pools, and eight fire retention percentages of the aboveground dead organic matter pools. Parameter impact was assessed by estimating the percent difference in the aboveground and belowground slow pool C stocks for a 5% change in parameter value. The parameters with the highest impact on the predicted soil C stocks were the slow pool base decay rates, the belowground slow pool temperature quotient and the transfer rate to the belowground slow pool. Also important were the aboveground slow pool fire retention percentage, its temperature quotient, and transfers from the very fast and fast dead organic matter pools. See Smyth et al. (2011) for a full description of the sensitivity analysis.
Stand sensitivity analysis (Bayesian)
The sensitivity of the dead organic matter stocks and fluxes to variation in model parameters was assessed by varying parameters that controlled biomass turnover, dead organic matter decay and model initialization. Four different landscapes were simulated, three with different species but the same rotation length and one using the same species with two different rotation lengths, to evaluate interactions between modeled scenarios and assumptions about parameter variability. Parameter sensitivity was assessed using Bayesian statistics to estimate the contribution of each parameter to the overall variation. National-scale impacts assessment: root parameters
The impact of adjusting tree root turnover and decay parameters was assessed in three national-scale simulations from 1990 to 2008 (Stinson et al. 2011). Three parameters were adjusted: the fine root turnover rate was decreased from 64.1% yr-1 to 51% yr-1, the coarse root turnover rate was increased from 2% yr-1 to 4.24% yr-1, and the percentage transferred to the atmosphere during decomposition from the very fast belowground pool was decreased from 83% to 67.3%.
For all three simulations, the changes in net primary production and heterotrophic respiration were small (<7%), and the change in net ecosystem production was less than 4%. Adjustment of the root annual turnovers changed net primary production and heterotrophic respiration indicators by roughly 22 g C m-2 yr-1 with increased fluxes for the increased coarse root turnover, and reduced fluxes for the reduced fine root turnover. Changing the percentage of decayed fine roots emitted to the atmosphere had no impact on the NPP estimates, and only a small impact on heterotrophic respiration estimates. See Smyth et al. (2012) for a full description of the impact assessment.
National-scale impacts assessment: slow pool parameters
The impact of adjusting slow pool parameters was assessed in ten national-scale simulations from 1990-2100. Five parameters were adjusted including the base decay rates of the slow pools, their temperature coefficients, and the transfer rate between the slow pools. Ten combinations of these five parameters were determined by minimizing the error between model predictions to soil stock estimates from 597 ground plots (section 2.5.1). 
In 1990, the average heterotrophic respiration emissions for all ten parameter combinations was 323.9 g C m-2 yr-1 (745.3 Tg C yr-1), and the range in emissions estimates for the ten simulations was small: 2.6 g C m-2 yr-1 (5.88 Tg C yr-1), or 0.78%. Managed Forests
As is shown in Figure 1-1, the majority of the managed forest is found in the more southerly areas with fewer contiguous areas in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. 
Forest Inventories
Forest inventories describe the area, age-class and species composition of the managed forest of Canada. These are typically derived from photo interpretation where forest areas are delineated and stand attributes are stored in geographic information systems (GIS).
In Canada, forest inventory data collection is predominantly done by the provinces and territories. These data were periodically incorporated into a Canadian Forest Inventory (CanFI), and areas not inventoried by the provinces were evaluated using best available satellite remote sensing data to provide reporting on all forests in Canada. The last such national compilation was completed by Power and Gillis (2006). 
The provincial and territorial inventory methods are broadly similar, with stereo aerial photography at scales ranging from 1:10,000 to 1:20,000 interpreted to delineate stands and estimate stand attributes such as species composition, tree height, density, volume and age. Interpretation is supported by ground plots to ensure accuracy. In some provinces, inventories are conducted on a 10 year re-measurement cycle, such that forest inventory data in these provinces are no more than 10 years old. In other provinces, the data may be several decades old and simply updated to reflect known depletions (harvesting and natural disturbances) and expected growth. The data are stored in GIS repositories and are typically aggregated prior to being used in the timber supply analyses that inform the determination of annual harvest rates. For some provinces, these data are shared with the Canadian Forest Service for integration into NFCMARS. The transfer of data from provincial forest inventory or timber supply analysis databases into NFCMARS can be complex, depending on the structure of the data in their native system. The transfer is conducted collaboratively by CFS and provincial experts to ensure that the process does not introduce errors. The source datasets are aggregated and spatially referenced to the 635 spatial analysis units of the NFCMARS spatial representation framework (see section 1.2) (Stinson et al. 2011). In total, there are approximately 3 million records in the NFCMARS inventory database. In some cases, the work has been conducted in close coopera

gated and spatially referenced to the 635 spatial analysis units of the NFCMARS spatial representation framework (see section 1.2) (Stinson et al. 2011). In total, there are approximately 3 million records in the NFCMARS inventory database. In some cases, the work has been conducted in close cooperation with provincial inventory specialists who have expertise in CBM-CFS3 modelling and analysis. Table 3-1 lists the source datasets upon which the NFCMARS forest inventory is currently based (after Stinson et al. 2011).
As the various component inventories have different reference dates, they are all adjusted to reflect the age-class structure of the forest in 1990, the common reference year for all UNFCCC reporting. The adjustment, commonly referred to as a “roll-back”, alters the age of all stand records whose pre-adjustment age is less than the roll-back period (inventory reference year – 1990), taking into account all stand-replacing disturbances known to have occurred during the roll-back period.

In Quebec, 97% removal is required by legislation, so clearcut harvesting is parameterized accordingly for Quebec. In Alberta, clear-cut harvesting removes 94% of merchantable biomass.
By default, shelterwood harvesting is represented in CBM-CFS3 as a stand-replacing harvest. This allows the model to establish a new stand after first entry, and start its growth. In practice, shelterwood harvesting involves multiple entries into a stand, removing first a large proportion of merchantable timber, and then coming back one or more times to remove the remainder after these trees have served a period of time providing seed-source and shelter for the regenerating cohort that was established after the first entry. The CBM-CFS3, however, must simulate total removal of the overstory canopy in order to permit establishment of the regenerating cohort. In effect, this compresses all harvest entries into one – compressing several years of activity on one site into one year. This overestimates the impacts on a site in the first year, and underestimates it in subsequent years. However, because this cutting type occurs every year the resulting errors cancel out.

Wildfire
NFCMARS obtains fire area data from the Canadian Wildland Fire Information System (CWFIS) . CWFIS combines wildfire monitoring data from the Canadian National Fire Database (CNFDB) (Stocks et al. 2002) and the National Burned Area Composite (NBAC). The CNFDB provides information on fires for the period 1990-2003, while the NBAC is an annual (beginning in 2004) spatially explicit compilation of coarse resolution SPOT-VGT satellite mapping, medium resolution Landsat-TM satellite mapping (de Groot et al. 2007), and provincial and territorial government fire agency mapping. Gross burn areas from the CNFDB and NBAC are netted down to account for fires in sparsely treed areas that do not meet the definition of forest (see section 3.1) (Stinson et al. 2011).
The NBAC compilation process applies decision-based rules to remove redundancies between the three data sources and assemble the final national product. The rule set applied for NIR compilation purposes selects fire polygons in the following priority order: 1) Landsat-TM 2) fire agency, and 3) SPOT-VGT (R. Landry, personal communication, 2009). Theil-Sen non-parametric modelling (Fernandes and Leblanc, 2005) is used to provide estimates of the fire polygon areas that are free from any bias introduced by the lower resolution data sources. In addition to providing spatially-explicit fire area data for the current reporting year, the NBAC compilation process frequently produces refinements to the fire area data for previously reported years.
The CNFDB and NBAC fire polygons are geo-referenced to the 635 spatial units of the NFCMARS spatial framework (see section 1.2), and fire disturbance events are then randomly assigned to eligible forest stands within the appropriate spatial analysis unit during CBM-CFS3 simulation runs (Stinson et al. 2011). 
To represent the C impacts of fire, CBM-CFS3 disturbance matrices (DMs) are created for each unique province (or territory) and ecozone stratum (Anderson and Simpson, 2010). For example, the Boreal Plains West ecozone, which spans 4 provinces and one territory, is split into 5 province-ecozone strata. The derivation of fire DMs is a four-step process.
The annual area burned and average annual fire weather conditions are first calculated for each province-ecozone stratum for all satellite-detected fire hotspots within the stratum for each year in the time series (1990 to current inventory year), using information from the Canadian Wildland Fire Information System (CWFIS; http://cwfis.cfs.nrcan.gc.ca/, accessed on August 13, 2014).
DMs are calculated for every stand from the final forest inventory at the end of the previous inventory analysis by using the CANFIRE model (de Groot et al. 2007) to simulate the burning of, and determine the fuel consumption and biomass transfers between C pools for, each stand.
The stand-level DMs for each province-ecozone stratum are averaged (weighted by stand size) to produce two DMs for each stratum, for eac

sing the CANFIRE model (de Groot et al. 2007) to simulate the burning of, and determine the fuel consumption and biomass transfers between C pools for, each stand.
The stand-level DMs for each province-ecozone stratum are averaged (weighted by stand size) to produce two DMs for each stratum, for each year, describing the impacts of crown and surface fires, respectively.
A single representative DM is calculated for each province-ecozone stratum by combining the annual DMs, weighted according to the annual area burned calculated in step 1.
The method for calculating fire DMs for GHG inventory reporting has evolved somewhat over the years, primarily through the refinement of fuel consumption calculation algorithms within CANFIRE, and the development of the annual area weighting of DMs described above, to better capture the annual variability fire weather conditions. Though the application of new DMs in each inventory reporting year has resulted in some instability in fire emissions estimates from one reporting cycle to the next, the system is now approaching stability as length of the averaging period has increased. Fire DMs need no longer be updated annually, but only when significant changes within the CBM-CFS3 model occur.
The wildfire disturbance matrices are provided in Appendix B.

Windthrow
The representation of wind-throw disturbances in NFCMARS is currently limited to Hurricane Juan, the 2003 storm that resulted in substantial forest damage in Nova Scotia. The storm damage was characterized with two damage classes: class 1 represents areas where there was 30-69% blow down (6,055 hectares), and; class 2 represents areas where there was 70-100% blow down (9,807 hectares). These classes are represented in NFCMARS as 50% and 85% mortality, respectively. While there is anecdotal evidence of other local windthrow events, no systematic data are available. The impact of such events is currently believed to be well within overall model uncertainties.
Forest-related land-use change
Forest conversion
This section provides a brief overview of the deforestation estimation procedure for NFCMARS. A more detailed and comprehensive description is available in Dyk et al. (in review).
Deforestation occurs when humans clear forested areas permanently to use the land for another purpose, like agriculture or urban development. From 1990 to 2008, approximately one million hectares of forest in Canada (approximately 0.3 % of Canada’s total forest area) have been converted to other uses. Primary drivers of forest conversion include agricultural expansion, mineral and fossil energy resource extraction, and hydroelectric development (Kurz et al. 2012). 
A consistent approach was applied to monitor forest land converted to cropland, wetlands, other lands, and to settlements thereby minimizing omissions and overlaps, and maintaining spatial consistency between these land-use categories. The Deforestation Monitoring Group at Natural Resources Canada tracks deforestation using data from Landsat and other satellites, aerial photos, Google Earth imagery, provincial records and expert judgment. The official estimates of Canada’s deforestation appear in the annual State of Canada’s Forests report, provincial government summaries and Canada’s annual reporting on greenhouse gas emissions to the United Nations.

All mapping agencies, including provincial partners and contractors, are required to follow the standardized methodology for deforestation mapping as laid out in the Deforestation Interpretation Guide (Leckie et al. 2010). This methodology adheres to IPCC Good Practice Guidance (IPCC, 2003). Quality control is performed during mapping projects, returning revision requests to the interpreters, and subsequently inspecting all revisions. Construction of the University of Northern British Columbia (UNBC)

Landsat imagery is used to identify potential deforestation. Circa 1975 conditions are evaluated from Landsat multispectral scanner data (MSS), with Thematic Mapper (TM) and Enhanced Thematic Mapper (ETM+) data for the subsequent time periods. The mapping of deforestation candidate events employs additional data as available, whether publicly available or from federal, provincial, or municipal data sets. These may include high-resolution imagery, aerial photography, Google Earth, records data, mapping of large events, and ancillary GIS databases. Confirmation of forest prior to change is often made using winter Landsat MSS and TM imagery.
Landsat images define the core periods within which events are mapped: MSS for circa 1975, TM for 1990, ETM+ for 2000, TM (again) for 2008 and potentially the next Landsat for 2012. The core images are selected from best available images (i.e. seasonality and low cloud cover) close to these dates.
The mapped polygons are summarized to estimate a deforestation rate (ha/yr) within spatial, land-use class and temporal units.
For reporting on the NFCMARS and the LULUCF sector of the GHG inventory reports the data are aggregated into the 15 reporting zones (Figure 1-4) and 12 industrial classes (Table 3-4) on an annual basis.
Spatial Summary
Deforestation mapping is done on a sampling basis. The landbase of Canada is divided into deforestation strata based on the nature of regional deforestation activity, and different sampling densities are employed in each stratum as needed to obtain rigourous estimates. Mapping areas are based on Landsat scene units. Full-area mapping is performed within “grid cells” on the order of 3.5 km on a side, separated by 10 to 20 km depending on the location, throughout the sample area (see Figure 3-2). Minimum area of deforestation mapped is 1 ha. Linear events less than 20 m wide from tree base to tree base are not mapped. 
Depending on the expected spatial patterns and rates of forest conversion, sampling approaches range from complete coverage mapping, to mapping of cells within a sample grid overlaid on Landsat scenes.

Initial Soil Carbon
All afforestation in Canada is assumed to occur on cropland, and since most Canadian agricultural regions have chernozemic soils, initial soil carbon on afforested sites is assumed to be 101 t C ha-1, the CBM-CFS3 default for non-forested chernozemic dark brown soils. All initial soil carbon is assumed to be in the slowly decomposing below ground soil pool, and all other pools are assumed to be empty prior to tree planting.
Yield Curves
Yield curves for species planted were taken from a variety of sources, depending on the spatial unit. Most provinces do not have yield curve information for all afforestation species established on agricultural lands.
Where species do not have their own yield curve, they are given the yield curve of another species with similar growth characteristics (for example, most of the southern hardwoods in Ontario use the sugar maple or tolerant hardwood curve). In some cases, species were listed as being “unknown” softwood or hardwood, or occasionally unknown “genus”. In these cases, the species were attributed to the species most likely to have been planted in that area (softwoods were typically modeled as white spruce; hardwoods might be poplar or tolerant hardwood depending on province and ecozone).

Institutional Arrangements 
Most forest management in Canada takes place on provincially managed Crown lands. Provinces and territories maintain detailed forest resource inventory databases, forest harvesting and silvicultural activity tracking systems, and disturbance and forest heath monitoring programs. Most of the data inputs needed for inventory preparation by the Canadian federal government (Canadian Forest Service) are drawn from these sources. Many of these data are provided under formal institutional arrangements. Many others are provided freely without formal arrangements. 
A federal/provincial/territorial committee was struck in 2001 to oversee all aspects of federal/provincial/territorial collaboration on matters relating to forest carbon and climate change mitigation, including the development of NFCMARS and its application to reporting and policy analysis. This National Forest Sinks Committee (NFSC) meets regularly to exchange knowledge and ensure that the necessary institutional arrangements are in place to provide the Canadian Forest Service (CFS) with the data needed for inventory preparation. Provinces, territories and the CFS also coordinate forest information collection, management and dissemination through the National Forestry Database (nfdp.ccfm.org), which also serves as a source of centralized national forest management activity data for inventory preparation.
Canada’s NFCMARS uses forest inventory data extracted from provincial databases, as described in Section 3.1.1. Data sharing agreements have been put in place to make it possible for provinces to share these data, and associated tree volume yield tables, with the CFS for the purpose of GHG inventory preparation. These agreements put strict limitations on the use of data and on the dissemination of derived products in order to protect the interests of the data providers. 
Other data needed for inventory preparation are provided to CFS freely, without formal institutional arrangements. Informal agreements are made by the NFSC membership on how data are to be used, and how products derived from those data are to be disseminated. 
Years of fruitful collaboration between federal, provincial and territorial government agencies active in the NFSC since its inception have built a foundation of mutual trust that makes it possible for the inventory preparation, and provision of data for this purpose, to occur with remarkably limited need for formal

collaboration between federal, provincial and territorial government agencies active in the NFSC since its inception have built a foundation of mutual trust that makes it possible for the inventory preparation, and provision of data for this purpose, to occur with remarkably limited need for formal institutional arrangements. All parties abide by the letter and spirit of agreements reached by the NFSC membership at its meetings. One such agreement is that outputs of NFCMARS into the GHG inventory be reported at the spatial resolution of Reporting Zones, which makes the LULUCF sector unique from other sectors in Canada’s GHG inventory because it is the only sector where data are not reported by province and territory. 
Data collection, processing and storage
All data are collected, processed and stored on secure Natural Resources Canada (NRCAN) servers located at the Pacific Forestry Centre in Victoria, BC. These servers are maintained and backed up by the informatics personnel of NRCAN’s Shared Services Office. 
Each year, the inventory preparation process begins with the creation of that year’s inventory preparation directory structure on the designated file server system. Consistent directory structure and naming conventions are used each year, making navigation through the structure easy and straight forward. Raw incoming data and metadata (where available) are saved to designated directory folders and archived before any processing work is done. Data are archived after each major processing stage has been completed. Quality control checks are documented and archived alongside the data. Documentation is compiled, with particular emphasis on documenting changes that have been implemented for the new inventory preparation (i.e., changes relative to the previous year’s inventory preparation). All software applications and utilities used during the processing are also archived alongside the data every year.
Quality assurance and quality control
QAQC procedures are categorized into 4 areas:
Workflow Checks. 
These checks are performed by analysts during inventory estimate preparation, and include the verification of data completeness and reasonableness, and of the data processing and transformation steps applied in the preparation of new data for NFCMARS updates.
Model Checks. 
A variety of checks are performed automatically by the CBM-CFS3 software to determine if model inputs are well formed. The outputs of the checks are reported to the analyst.
Benchmark Checks.
These checks are performed manually by analysts. They typically comprise comparing an estimated quantity produced by the model against an independent estimate of the same quantity.
External Reviews.
These involve contacting individuals not directly involved in the preparation of estimates to review the estimates

Workflow checks
Much of the workflow is project based, where a project consists of compiling and preparing data and running CBM for a defined geographic region. Each project is assigned a lead analyst, who has responsibility for completing a project, including the workflow checks. Each project is also assigned a review analyst, who is responsible for verifying the work of the lead analyst, including the workflow checks.
Workflow checks are documented in one of the following document types:
Project log spreadsheet, used by analysts to keep a record of all project activities; 
RollbackChecks spreadsheet - a semi-automated excel spreadsheet that facilitates verifying that the inventory rollback procedure has been correctly applied;
Deforestation Checks spreadsheet - a semi-automated excel spreadsheet that facilitates verifying that deforestation data have been imported correctly into a CBM project database;
DeluxeQAQC spreadsheet - a semi-automated excel spreadsheet that generates standardized tabular and graphical reports of CBM data loading, inputs and results for review by an analyst.

The various spreadsheets listed above are completed by analysts for each project, checked by the review analyst, and archived along with all other annual NIR production information for future reference. 
Model Checks
A variety of checks are performed automatically by the various software components of NFCMARS to determine if model inputs are well formed. In total, there are over 290 checks that cause the model to fail if an invalid condition is detected. Examples of the checks performed include:
Does each stand have a valid growth curve?
Is area conserved between timesteps?
Is carbon mass conserved between timesteps?
Do disturbance matrix parameters for each source pool sum to 1?
Are model parameters within scientifically valid ranges?

A failure is usually fatal, in that the model will fail to produce output or will produce incomplete output. In these circumstances an analyst will correct the error and run the model again. Non-fatal errors can occur and are recorded as errors or warnings in a log file produced by CBM. The analyst will check the log file for warnings or errors, and decide if the model needs to be run again. 
The model also produces diagnostic outputs that may indicate a problem with model inputs. An example is the area of disturbances the model was not able to achieve because of conflicts between disturbance targets and available inventory. Analysts review these diagnostic outputs to determine if model inputs need to be adjusted.
Benchmark Checks
Benchmark checks involve comparing an estimated quantity produced by the model against an independent estimate of the same or similar quantity. These checks are opportunistic, rather than systematic, in that they depend on the availability of an independent dataset to verify against.
