Uncertainty
The purpose of uncertainty assessments in GHG inventories is to provide guidance as to where to apply effort for reducing future uncertainty. IPCC Good Practice Guidance requires that uncertainties be identified, quantified, and reduced as far as practicable (IPCC, 2003). 
Assessment Methodology
Two methods of analysis are employed in assessing the uncertainty of GHG emissions estimates from NFCMARS.
Comprehensive
100 Monte Carlo simulations are conducted for each of the 22 CBM-CFS3 projects that constitute NFCMARS, requiring approximately 1 month of computing time using 10 PCs. Because of the practical storage space and time limitations imposed by this computationally intensive process, a bootstrap sampling procedure is used to increase the sample size for the national sums by randomly sampling combinations of the 100 Monte Carlo runs for each CBM-CFS3 project to obtain 10,000 bootstrap samples of national totals. 
Extrapolation
The computationally intensive nature of the comprehensive analysis and the variable availability of resources make it infeasible to repeat the full analysis for each NIR reporting year. Consequently, in years with relatively minor updates to the NFCMARS, uncertainty estimates are approximated by extrapolation. Values of the 2.5th, 50th (median) and 97.5th uncertainty percentiles are estimated by linear regression, using the following model and the reporting values (kt CO2e) and years from the most recent comprehensive analysis results as predictors:

Uncertainty Percentileyear = Intercept + ReportingYear + Reported Valueyear

A more detailed description of the NFCMARS uncertainty assessment procedures and their results is currently in preparation for publication in the peer-reviewed scientific literature.

Sources of Uncertainty
Uncertainty about the C balance of managed forests in Canada as estimated using NFCMARS arises from uncertainties in several broad categories (Metsaranta et al. 2011):
Model inputs,
Model parameters, 
Model structure, and 
Human error.

Model inputs
Three main input data sources used in NFCMARS are: (1) a forest inventory that describes the extent, condition, and composition of the forest; (2) merchantable volume yield curves that describe forest productivity; and (3) activity data that describe the location and quantity of forest management activities and natural disturbance events (Metsaranta et al. 2011).
The NFCMARS is an integrative user of many different data sources collected across Canada, but does not itself collect any of these data, and so errors in these are not under the system’s control. Jurisdictional data sources are used where available, and national data sets when they are not (Kurz and Apps, 2006; Stinson et al. 2011). In the CBM-CFS3 modelling framework, uncertainty about forest inventory and growth and yield data, in addition to the allometric equations used to estimate biomass, primarily affects model results through the

lable, and national data sets when they are not (Kurz and Apps, 2006; Stinson et al. 2011). In the CBM-CFS3 modelling framework, uncertainty about forest inventory and growth and yield data, in addition to the allometric equations used to estimate biomass, primarily affects model results through the net growth portion of net primary production. We estimated the uncertainty of all of these factors taken together by assuming an uncertainty of ± 50% in the simulated biomass increment.
Annual targets of carbon mass to be harvested in each jurisdiction (province and territory) are developed from harvest volume statistics compiled and provided by the Canadian Council of Forest Ministers’ National Forestry Database (NFD). These volume harvest statistics are assumed to have an error of ±1%. 
An analysis of uncertainty in annual rates of deforestation by Leckie (2011) suggests that uncertainty in deforested area could range from ± 20% to ± 30%. In order to be conservative, the most pessimistic estimate is assumed in the assessment of overall uncertainty in NFCMARS emissions estimates.
As described in section 3.1.3.1, annual estimates of burned area are provided by the CWFIS. An uncertainty of ± 10% of the area burned is assumed for the purposes of this analysis.
Data describing the extent and impact of major defoliating insect and bark beetle outbreaks are compiled from available federal, provincial and territorial forest health and disease survey programs. These data are typically compiled using aerial overview survey sketch mapping methods, and also need to be adjusted so that only the portion occurring in ‘forest’ and in susceptible stand types is simulated. We assumed an uncertainty of ± 25% in the area impacted by insects.
Model parameters
In addition to inherent uncertainty in the allometric equations used to estimate biomass (accounted for in the ± 50% uncertainty applied to the simulated biomass increment), the models and parameters used to simulate dead organic matter decay, and biomass turnover (White et al. 2008), and the disturbance matrices used to represent the impact of different activities on carbon dynamics are key sources of uncertainty in NFCMARS estimates (Metsaranta et al. 2011).
The impact of uncertainty in the ecological parameters that control litterfall, decay, and C transfer rates is assessed by allowing these parameters to vary independently for each of 100 Monte Carlo simulation runs. Parameter values for each run a drawn from a triangular distribution centered on the CBM-CFS3 default value.
The uncertainty arising from disturbance matrix parameters is not currently assessed because it is not possible to systematically vary these within the NFCMARS modelling framework.
Model structure
Uncertainty also arises because processes in nature are highly variable and because our understanding of them, and our ability to represent them computationally, is imperfect. NFCMARS estimates are influenced by both (Metsaranta et al. 2011).

Model structure
Uncertainty also arises because processes in nature are highly variable and because our understanding of them, and our ability to represent them computationally, is imperfect. NFCMARS estimates are influenced by both (Metsaranta et al. 2011).
The uncertainty associated with incorrectly or incompletely specified or excluded processes is directly included in our assessments, as it is not presently possible to simply substitute one method of modelling a particular ecological process with another in NFCMARS. Assessing and reducing uncertainty of this type continues to be addressed by ongoing model validation and model inter-comparison exercises, such as Wang et al. 2011, and through research activities into methods by which the excluded processes may be incorporated in the future (e.g. Smyth et al. 2011).
Uncertainty resulting from the computational methods used by NFCMARS arises from two particular algorithms: (1) the methods used to select stands for disturbance, and (2) the initialization procedure used by the model to populate soil and DOM C pools.
Disturbance events are referenced to spatial unit boundaries, but it is not known which stands within those units are affected by these events and so the system uses sorting and eligibility rules to select records for disturbance (Kurz et al. 2008a). In the case of both insect and forest management disturbances, sufficient information is available to apply deterministic rules; however in the case of fire, pre-burn fuel conditions are not known and so records for burning are selected at random from all eligible stands within the geographic area for which the target area is defined. The random selection of stands to burn can therefore produce different simulation results for a given set of inputs, because more C emissions will result if high biomass stands are selected than if low biomass stands are selected. For NIR analyses, repeatable results are produced by ensuring the use of consistent random seed values, however the results produced are only one of many possible outcomes thus contributing to uncertainty in the C dynamics of large landscapes with significant levels of fire disturbance. This source of uncertainty is quantified by allowing the random seed value to vary for each of 100 Monte Carlo simulation runs.
Soil and dead organic matter pools are initialized via a spin-up process of repeated iterations of growth followed by stand-replacing disturbance until the difference between the slow soil C pools between successive iterations is less than 1%, using an assumed historic disturbance regime of stand-replacing fire with return intervals ranging from 75 to 300 years by terrestrial ecozone (Kurz et al. 2009). However, any estimate of the historical average disturbance rate inferred from observational data is highly uncertain due to the large inter-annual variability in area burned (Armstrong 1999; Metsaranta 2010), and CBM-CFS3 results are sensi

75 to 300 years by terrestrial ecozone (Kurz et al. 2009). However, any estimate of the historical average disturbance rate inferred from observational data is highly uncertain due to the large inter-annual variability in area burned (Armstrong 1999; Metsaranta 2010), and CBM-CFS3 results are sensitive to assumptions made about the long-term disturbance return interval (White et al. 2008). This source of uncertainty is quantified by randomly selecting fire return intervals from an ecozone-specific gamma distribution during the spin-up initialization for each of 100 Monte Carlo simulation runs (Metsaranta et al. 2011).
Human error
The annual process of generating estimates from NFCMARS contains several quality assurance and control steps to minimize human errors, nonetheless such errors are inevitable in complex analytical systems that process many gigabytes of data from multiple, disparate information sources. 
NFCMARS has been used for estimating GHG emissions and removals in Canada’s managed forest since the 2006 reporting year, and repeated application of the quality control procedures discussed in section 4.3 has significantly reduced the uncertainty due to human errors over time. 
Refinements to workflow and quality assurance procedures are made on an ongoing basis to further reduce the impact of human error over time as the system continues to mature (Metsaranta et al. 2011).

Introduction
This document summarizes the updates to Canada’s National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System (NFCMARS) for Canada’s 2015 national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory submission to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), covering the reporting period 1990-2013.

No changes to the emissions estimation methodology have been introduced for NIR2015. NFCMARS updates for the current national inventory report (NIR) were limited to:

Updated wildfire activity data for 1990-2012 in Ontario, to capture updates to the underlying data sources and to correct an accumulation of past data processing errors
Updated slash burning activity data for 1990-2012 in Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Ontario, Quebec and Northwest Territories, to capture all updates to the underlying National Forestry Database Program (NFDP) prescribed burning statistics
Update global warming potential (GWP) factors to IPCC 2006 values 
Updating harvest activity data for 2008-2012, to capture recent changes to the underlying NFDP harvest statistics
Addition of new activity data for 2013 wildfires, insect disturbances, harvesting and deforestation.

These updates are described in more detail in the remainder of this document.

Recalculation Updates
Wildfire activity data

To correct a number of past data processing errors and capture updates to the underlying wildfire monitoring data, a complete 1990 – 2011 time series of wildfire disturbances was re-assembled from the official monitoring datasets, and fire disturbances were re-loaded in NIR2014 for all provinces except Ontario (because of issues in relating GIS wildfire polygons to aspatial Ontario inventory records). The issues that prevented updating Ontario fire disturbances have now been resolved and so for NIR2015 we have updated 1990 – 2013 fire disturbance events in Ontario.

Figure 2-1 compares the total area burned annually after updating the Ontario fire disturbances with the total area burned annually in NIR2014 for Ontario only. Implementing these changes increased the area burned in some of the historic years (1995 and 1996 in particular). The area burned in Ontario in the NIR2015 now more closely matches the statistics found in the Large Fire Database. 

Figure 2-1: Area burned in Ontario for 1990-2013, NIR2015 vs NIR2014

Slash burning activity data
Slash burning activity data for Alberta, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Labrador, and the Northwest Territories are taken from the prescribed burning statistics provided by the NFDP. A number of discrepancies between the slash burning disturbance targets used in NIR2014 and the current NFDP statistics were noted during a recent review. We have updated the 1990 – 2013 slash burning targets for these provinces in order to re-establish consistency between NFCMARS and the NFDP

NFDP. A number of discrepancies between the slash burning disturbance targets used in NIR2014 and the current NFDP statistics were noted during a recent review. We have updated the 1990 – 2013 slash burning targets for these provinces in order to re-establish consistency between NFCMARS and the NFDP statistics.

Figure 2-2 compares the total area slash-burned annually after updating the NFCMARS targets with the total area slash-burned annually in NIR2014.

Figure 2-2: Area slash burned 1990-2012, NIR2015 vs NIR2014

Global warming potentials
Global warming potentials (GWP) for methane and nitrous oxide have been updated to the IPCC 2006 values. Specifically, the GWP for methane (CH4) has increased from 21 to 25, while the GWP for nitrous oxide (N2O) has decreased from 310 to 298.
Recent activity data updates

The NIR 2015 incorporated new data in the following forms: 
Fire activity data for the year 2013
Harvesting activity for years 2008 to 2013
Mountain Pine Beetle infestation data in British Columbia for year 2013
New Slash burning data for years 1990-2013

No other new activity data were incorporated into the NIR 2015 submission. There hasn’t been a significant update of deforestation data for 2013, as such; the 2013 values were extrapolated from the 2012 dataset.
Wildfire Activity Data
Data for the NIR 2015 was compiled by the National Forest Burn Area Composite at the Northern Forestry Centre in Edmonton. This year’s submission included a new class of burn, a partial burn category for the province of Alberta only. All other provinces and territories were reporting complete burns as in previous NIRs. The partial burn status was applied to about 900 ha in Alberta in the year 2013. The entire area burned statistics are shown in Figure 3-1. 

Figure 3.1. Area burned NIR2015 vs NIR2014.

We received updated data for mountain pine beetle infestation for the province of British Columbia for 2013. Following a pattern of the previous years, the total area infested in British Columbia is declining, with total area infested in 2013 as simulated in the NIR 2015 1.3 M ha. Most of the infestation was classified as low impact and very little area infested as severe defoliation. The insect impacts in the NIR 2015 are relatively benign when compared to NIR of the past, as seen in figure 3.2.1.

Results

GHG Emissions and Removals in the Managed Forest
Figure 4-1 shows the annual GHG emissions from, and areas affected by disturbance in, the managed forest for the current reporting period. Canada’s managed forest was a net sink of carbon emissions in 2013 (19 Mt CO2e), while with the updated disturbance information, 2012 was a bigger source of C (34 Mt CO2e).

Figure 4-1: Emissions from Canada’s managed forest, NIR2015 vs NIR2014

Fire
The total area burned in 2013 was 895,093 hectares (see Figure 2-1). Direct emissions from wildfire in 2013 were 60 Mt CO2e, down from 121 Mt CO2e in 2012, as illustrated by Figure 4-2. 

Figure 4-2: Wildfire emissions, NIR2015 vs NIR2014 

The area burned in 2013 is relatively benign when compared to the rest of the timeseries. 1995 remains the most instense fire year within the past 23 years. Emissions differ in the two NIR time series as the model finds different records due to the selectioning of specific forest stands which burn at random within the CBM-CFS3. As such, it is relatively difficult to reproduce exactly the emissions in year to year NIRs when slight changes in the datasets are introduced.
Insects
Damage by defoliators contributes direct emissions to the GHG balance in each year, as sh

ic forest stands which burn at random within the CBM-CFS3. As such, it is relatively difficult to reproduce exactly the emissions in year to year NIRs when slight changes in the datasets are introduced.
Insects
Damage by defoliators contributes direct emissions to the GHG balance in each year, as shown in Figure 4-3. There were very little direct emissions in the NIR 2015 as the only influential insect disturbances are from mountain pine beetle. Emissions from mountain pine beetle are, in effect, residual in the years following disturbance as dead and decaying wood resources begin to break up and decay through heterotrophic respiration. 

Figure 4-3: Emissions from defoliating insects, NIR2015 vs NIR2014

The area disturbed by insects continued to decline in 2012 due to the waning extent and severity of the mountain pine beetle epidemic in British Columbia. The total realized area disturbed by insects in 2012 was 1,735 kHa, down from 2,971 kHa in 2011 (Figure 4-4). The realized disturbances are less than the area targets in 2013 and 2012 because there is simply not enough inventory with identifiable host tree species (i.e. not enough inventory in BC with an identifiable or inferrable pine component, and not enough inventory in Alberta with an identifiable or inferable aspen component) to satisfy the areas prescribed in the insect monitoring data. Also, data received from the province of British Columbia in 2014 indicated some severe and very severe impacts in areas where there has been no Low or Moderate impact beetle in previous years. This countervenes a number of disturbance rules within the CBM-CFS3 that state that no severe or greater impact can hit stands that have not had a pine beetle infestation within the past 5 years. This indicates that some of the aerial surveys are not quite representing what is feasible within our modelling environment. 

Figure 4-4: Area attacked by insects 1990-2013, NIR2015 vs NIR2014

The changes in Ontario resulted in visibly different overall emissions (figure 5.1), which was expected. Any underlying changes in the conditions of the input projects will inevitably result in differences in overall emissions between two identical runs as different stand records will be selected by the CBM-CFS3. Also, since the spatial location of the fires was shifted slightly in Ontario (the targetted area was unchanged), the emissions changed slightly. When looking at the national perspective (figure 5.2), there is little overall change in emissions, which is good.

The slash burning targets in the NIR2015 were completely redone to mimic as closely as possible the NFDP statistics. As such there were differences in the direct emissions from slash burning as evidenced in figured 5.3. Given that the area of slash burning has increased this year relative to the NIR2014, it is not surprising and completely expected that the emissions would increase in the NIR2015 relative to the NIR2014.

As shown in figure 5.4, the overall impact of implementing the slash burning changes had a minor effect in the emissions trends of the NIR2015 compared to the NIR2014. Generally the emissions were higher in the NIR2015 with these changes due to the fact that the targets for slashburning were higher than the NIR2014.

The NIR2015 also saw the introduction of new GWP values for calculation of GHG emissions from CH4, CO and N2O. Specifically, the GWP for methane (CH4) has increased from 21 to 25, while the GWP for nitrous oxide (N2O) has decreased from 310 to 298 as highlighted in section 2.3. At the national level, the impacts of implementing the new GWP values are evidenced in figure 5.5.

As shown in figure 5.7, the fire updates do not contribute to changes in the historic period (1990-2012), however, the impact of the updates can be seen in figure 5.8 which reflect in the 2013 reporting year. 2013 was a relatively benign fire year as seen in figure 3.1, and as such, it appears that 2013 will be a small sink of GHG in the FLFL.

Harvest disturbance targets were updated for the years 2008-2012. The 2013 years targets were set to equal those of 2012 as we did not receive new silvicultural statistics for the year 2013 from the NFDP at the time of processing this analysis. Changing the harvest targets in the NIR2015 resulted in some “visible” changes to the timeseries, as seen in figure 5.8. The harvest targets for the reporting year 2012 for Quebec used in the NIR2014 were found to be about 50% of what the NFDP reported this year. That meant that the total volume harvest in the NIR2014 was too low, and as such the impacts of the changes are evident in the figure 5.8 in 2012 especially. By making the corrections to the 2012 harves targets in Quebec, the NIR2015 is reporting a slightly larger source of GHG in 2012 (48Mt CO2e in NIR2015 vs about 31 Mt CO2e in the NIR2014 for reporting year 2012). Other provinces and territories had relatively minor changes implemented in the NIR2015 for years from 2008-2012, though none were as large as the changes in Quebec. 

Figure 5-8: Incremental changes of all of the disturbance updates, vs the NIR2014. 

When comparing the NIR2014 and the NIR2015 the major sources of change are evidenced in Figure 5.9. Mainly the differences revolve around the differences in the fire emissions throughout the historic period (figure 5.9). Unfortunately, must of this source of difference is due to the random selection of forest inventory records done by the CBM-CFS3. There is no good way for us to constrain the CBM-CFS3 to select precisely the same stands to burn in the NIR2014 vs the NIR2015 due to the fact that some of the underlying disturbances have changes (Ontario spatial location of fires, changes to historical slashburning implementation). As such, must of this difference is “noise” within the system. The most legitimate source of change is seen in the difference in emissions caused by forest management (red triangles, figure 5.9), especially in the year 2012. As mentioned earlier, the source of this difference largely resides in the changes in harvest targets for Quebec (which used the most recent year of disturbance from the NFDP available at the time of processing, year 2012). As it turns out, this does not seem to be a terrific practice as we’ve since found that the reported numbers for 2012 that were used in the NIR2014 were about 50% of what was reported for 2012 in the NFDP this year. We have to assume that the statistics were updated with better figures for 2012, and that we will not use the most recent year’s statistics as a target in subsequent NIRs. The NIR2015 avoids this “issue” by extending the 2012 harvest targets to the 2013 reporting year. 

Figure 5-9: Differences between the NIR2014 and the NIR2015 by major disturbance agents.

The update to the implementation of slash burning also contr

year’s statistics as a target in subsequent NIRs. The NIR2015 avoids this “issue” by extending the 2012 harvest targets to the 2013 reporting year. 

Figure 5-9: Differences between the NIR2014 and the NIR2015 by major disturbance agents.

The update to the implementation of slash burning also contributed to some of the major differences between the NIR2014 and the NIR2015. As evidenced in the figure 5.9, the yellow circles, show differences in the 1992-1997 range due to the increases in the targeted slash burns (figure 2.2). This, combined with the differences in emissions burned, result in the major contributors of difference between the NIR2014 and the NIR2015.

Introduction

This document summarizes the updates to Canada’s National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System (NFCMARS) for Canada’s 2015 national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory submission to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), covering the reporting period 1990-2013.

No changes to the emissions estimation methodology have been introduced for NIR2015. NFCMARS updates for the current National Inventory Report (NIR) were limited to changes in i

ubmission to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), covering the reporting period 1990-2013.

No changes to the emissions estimation methodology have been introduced for NIR2015. NFCMARS updates for the current National Inventory Report (NIR) were limited to changes in input data:

Updated wildfire activity data for 1990-2012 in Ontario, to capture updates to the underlying data sources and to correct an accumulation of past data processing errors;
Updated slash burning activity data for 1990-2012 in Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Ontario, Quebec and Northwest Territories, to capture all updates to the underlying National Forestry Database Program (NFDP) prescribed burning statistics;
Update global warming potential (GWP) factors to IPCC 2006 values; 
Updating harvest activity data for 2008-2012, to capture recent changes to the underlying NFDP harvest statistics; and
Addition of new activity data for 2013 wildfires, insect disturbances, harvesting and deforestation.

These updates and the implications for changes in GHG emisisons and removals estimates are described in more detail in the remainder of this document.

Section 2 describes the sequential updates of activity data and other model parameters from NIR2014 for the 1990-2012 time series. Section 3 summarised the activity data updates for the reporting year 2013. Section 4 summarises the results for NIR2015 and Section 5 details the changes in the emission and removal time series for each step in the recalculations due to updated activity data for the period 1990 to 2013.

Recalculation Updates
Wildfire activity data

For NIR 2014, to correct a number of data processing errors from prior years and to capture updates to the underlying wildfire monitoring data, a complete 1990 – 2011 time series of wildfire disturbances was re-assembled from the official monitoring datasets. Fire disturbance activity data were re-loaded for all provinces except Ontario because of issues in relating GIS wildfire polygons to aspatial Ontario inventory records. The issues that prevented updating Ontario fire disturbance activity data have been resolved and we have updated 1990 – 2013 fire disturbance events in Ontario for NIR2015.

Figure 2.1 compares the area annually burned in Ontario after updating the Ontario fire disturbances with the area annually burned in NIR2014 for Ontario only. Implementing these changes increased the area burned in some of the historic years (1995 and 1996 in particular). The area burned in Ontario in the NIR2015 now more closely matches the statistics found in the CFS Large Fire Database.

Forest Management Activity Data

Harvest activity data in the NIR are specified in units of target volume (carbon), not in terms of area. The NIR 2014 was the first year in which we used the available NFDP statistics for the reporting year. Because some of the provincial data were incomplete statistics, this unfortunately resulted in underestimated harvest rates for some regions of the country, in particular for Quebec. These NFDP data have been updated since NIR2014 and when the harvest time series for NIR2015 is compared to NIR2014 (Fig 3.3), substantial increases in the area harvested for 2012 can be seen. 

For NIR 2015 we decided to use only the most recent year with complete statistics (in this case 2012) and to apply the 2012 value in 2013. This resulted in two years of identical harvest targets (2012 and 2013), yet updates the time-series with the most recent available complete data. It is anticipated that in NIR2016, the harvest rates for 2013 will differ from those in 2012.

Insects
The CBM represents two types of insects: defoliators and bark beetles. Herbivory by defoliators contributes a small amount of direct emissions to the GHG balance in each year (
Figure 4.2). Bark beetles, including the Mountain Pine Bettle, do not contribute to direct emisisons in the year of disturbance but cause large transfers of live biomass to dead organic matter pools from where emissions result in subsequent years due to decay (hetertrophic respiration) of organic matter. 

Figure 4.2: Direct emissions from defoliating insects, NIR2015 vs NIR2014. 
Note that the y-axis scale on this graph is t, while all other emissions graphs show Mt – a difference in scale of six orders of magnitude (one million).

The area disturbed by insects continued to decline in 2012 due to the waning extent and severity of the Mountain Pine Beetle epidemic in British Columbia. The total realized area disturbed by insects in 2012 was 1,735 kHa, down from 2,971 kHa in 2011 (Error! Reference source not found.). The realized disturbances are less than the area targets in 2013 and 2012 because there is simply not enough inventory with identifiable host tree species (i.e. not enough inventory in BC with an identifiable or inferrable pine component, and not enough inventory in Alberta with an identifiable or inferable aspen component) to satisfy the areas prescribed in the insect monitoring data. Also, data received from the province of British Columbia in 2014 indicated that severe and very severe impacts occurred in areas where there has been no low or moderate beetle impact in previous years. Disturbance rules in the CBM-CFS3 for Mountain Pine Beetle currently define that severe and very severe impacts can only occur in stands which, in the previous 5 years, had been affected by the beetle. This issue will be examined further for NIR2016 and may require revisions to the current disturbance rules.

Insects
The CBM represents two types of insects: defoliators and bark beetles. Herbivory by defoliators contributes a small amount of direct emissions to the GHG balance in each year (Fig. 4.3). Bark beetles, including the Mountain Pine Bettle, do not contribute to direct emisisons in the year of disturbance but cause large transfers of live biomass to dead organic matter pools from where emissions result in subsequent years due to decay (hetertrophic respiration) of organic matter. 

Figure 4.3: Direct emissions from defoliating insects, NIR2015 vs NIR2014. 
Note that the y-axis scale on this graph is t, while all other emissions graphs show Mt – a difference in scale of six orders of magnitude (one million).

The area disturbed by insects continued to decline in 2012 due to the waning extent and severity of the Mountain Pine Beetle epidemic in British Columbia. The total realized area disturbed by insects in 2012 was 1,735 kHa, down from 2,971 kHa in 2011 (Figure 3.2.1). The realized disturbances are less than the area targets in 2013 and 2012 because there is simply not enough inventory with identifiable host tree species (i.e. not enough inventory in BC with an identifiable or inferrable pine component, and not enough inventory in Alberta with an identifiable or inferable aspen component) to satisfy the areas prescribed in the insect monitoring data. Also, data received from the province of British Columbia in 2014 indicated that severe and very severe impacts occurred in areas where there has been no low or moderate beetle impact in previous years. Disturbance rules in the CBM-CFS3 for Mountain Pine Beetle currently define that severe and very severe impacts can only occur in stands which, in the previous 5 years, had been affected by the beetle. This issue will be examined further for NIR2016 and may require revisions to the current disturbance rules.

Introduction

This document summarizes the updates to Canada’s National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System (NFCMARS) for Canada’s 2015 national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory submission to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), covering the reporting period 1990-2013.

No changes to the emissions estimation methodology have been introduced for NIR2015. NFCMARS updates for the current National Inventory Report (NIR) were limited to changes in input data:

Updated wildfire activity data for 1990-2012 in Ontario, to capture updates to the underlying data sources and to correct an accumulation of past data processing errors;
Updated slash burning activity data for 1990-2012 in Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Ontario, Quebec and Northwest Territor

1990-2012 in Ontario, to capture updates to the underlying data sources and to correct an accumulation of past data processing errors;
Updated slash burning activity data for 1990-2012 in Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Ontario, Quebec and Northwest Territories, to capture all updates to the underlying National Forestry Database Program (NFDP) prescribed burning statistics;
Update global warming potential (GWP) factors to IPCC 2006 values; 
Updating harvest activity data for 2008-2012, to capture recent changes to the underlying NFDP harvest statistics; and
Addition of new activity data for 2013 wildfires, insect disturbances, harvesting, slashburning and deforestation.

These updates and the implications for changes in GHG emisisons and removals estimates are described in more detail in the remainder of this document.

Section 2 describes the sequential updates of activity data and other model parameters from NIR2014 for the 1990-2012 time series. Section 3 summarises the activity data updates for the reporting year 2013. Section 4 summarises the results for NIR2015 and Section 5 details the changes in the emission and removal time series for each step in the recalculations due to updated activity data for the period 1990 to 2013.

All analyses in this report are conducted assuming instant oxidation of wood transferred to forest products. The implications of using the new harvested wood products model will be reported elsewhere.

1. Introduction 
 
This document summarizes the updates to Canada’s National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and 
Reporting System (NFCMARS) for Canada’s 2015 national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory submission 
to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), covering the reporting 
period 1990-2013. 
 
No changes to the emissions estimation methodology have been introduced for NIR2015. NFCMARS 
updates for the current National Inventory Report (NIR) were limited to changes in input data: 
 
 Updated wildfire activity data for 1990-2012 in Ontario, to capture updates to the underlying data 
sources and to correct an accumulation of past data processing errors; 
 Updated slash burning activity data for 1990-2012 in Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, New 
Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Ontario, Quebec and Northwest Territories, to capture all 
updates to the underlying National Forestry Database Program (NFDP) prescribed burning 
statistics; 
 Update global warming potential (GWP) factors to IPCC 2006 values1; 
 Updating harvest activity data for 2008-2012, to capture recent changes to the underlying NFDP 
harvest statistics; and 
 Addition of new activity data for 2013 wildfires, insect disturbances, harvesting, slashburning and 
deforestation.

underlying wildfire monitoring data, a complete 1990 – 2011 time series of wildfire disturbances was re-

provinces except Ontario because of issues in relating GIS wildfire polygons to aspatial Ontario

3.3. Forest Management Activity Data 
 
Harvest activity data in the NIR are specified in units of target volume (carbon), not in terms of area. The 
NIR 2014 was the first year in which we used the available NFDP statistics for the reporting year. 
Because some of the provincial data were incomplete statistics, this unfortunately resulted in 
underestimated harvest rates for some regions of the country, in particular for Quebec. These NFDP data 
have been updated since NIR2014 and when the harvest time series for NIR2015 is compared to NIR2014 
(Fig 3.3), substantial increases in the area harvested for 2012 can be seen. 
 
For NIR 2015 we decided to use only the most recent year with complete statistics (in this case 2012) and 
to apply the 2012 value in 2013. This resulted in two years of identical harvest targets (2012 and 2013), 
yet updates the time-series with the most recent available complete data. It is anticipated that in NIR2016, 
the harvest rates for 2013 will differ from those in 2012.

4.3. Insects 
 
The CBM-CFS3 represents two types of insects: defoliators and bark beetles. Herbivory by defoliators 
contributes a small amount of direct emissions to the GHG balance in each year (Figure 4.3). Bark 
beetles, including the Mountain Pine Bettle, do not contribute to direct emisisons in the year of 
disturbance but cause large transfers of live biomass to dead organic matter pools from where emissions 
result in subsequent years due to decay (heterotrophic respiration) of organic matter. 
 
 
 
Figure 4.3: Direct emissions from defoliating insects, NIR2015 vs NIR2014. 
 
The area disturbed by insects continued to decline in 2012 due to the waning extent and severity of the 
Mountain Pine Beetle epidemic in British Columbia. The total realized area disturbed by insects in 2012 
was 1,735 kHa, down from 2,971 kHa in 2011 (figure 3.2.1). The realized disturbances are less than the 
area targets in 2013 and 2012 because there is simply not enough inventory with identifiable host tree 
species (i.e. not enough inventory in BC with an identifiable or inferrable pine component, and not 
enough inventory in Alberta with an identifiable or inferable aspen component) to satisfy the areas 
prescribed in the insect monitoring data. Also, data received from the province of British Columbia in 
2014 indicated that severe and very severe impacts occurred in areas where there has been no low or 
moderate beetle impact in previous years.

Introduction
This document summarizes the updates to Canada’s National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System (NFCMARS) for Canada’s 2015 national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory submission to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), covering the reporting period 1990-2013.

No changes to the emissions estimation methodology have been introduced for NIR2015. NFCMARS updates for the current national inventory report (NIR) were limited to:

Updated wildfire activity data for 1990-2012 in Ontario, to capture updates to the underlying data sources and to correct an accumulation of past data processing errors
Updated slash burning activity data for 1990-2012 in Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Ontario, Quebec and Northwest Territories, to capture all updates to the underlying National Forestry Database Program (NFDP) prescribed burning statistics
Update global warming potential (GWP) factors to IPCC 2006 values 
Updating harvest activity data for 2008-2012, to capture recent changes to the underlying NFDP harvest statistics
Addition of new activity data fo

the underlying National Forestry Database Program (NFDP) prescribed burning statistics
Update global warming potential (GWP) factors to IPCC 2006 values 
Updating harvest activity data for 2008-2012, to capture recent changes to the underlying NFDP harvest statistics
Addition of new activity data for 2013 wildfires, insect disturbances, harvesting and deforestation.

These updates are described in more detail in the remainder of this document.

Recalculation Updates
Wildfire activity data

To correct a number of past data processing errors and capture updates to the underlying wildfire monitoring data, a complete 1990 – 2011 time series of wildfire disturbances was reassembled from the official monitoring datasets, and fire disturbances were reloaded in NIR2014 for all provinces except Ontario (because of issues in relating GIS wildfire polygons to aspatial Ontario inventory records). The issues that prevented updating Ontario fire disturbances have now been resolved and so for NIR2015 we have updated 1990 – 2012 fire disturbance events in Ontario.

Figure 2-1 compares the total area burned annually after updating the Ontario fire disturbances with the total area burned annually in NIR2014.

Figure 2-1: Area burned 1990-2012, NIR2015 vs NIR2014

Slash burning activity data
Slash burning activity data for Alberta, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Labrador, and the Northwest Territories are taken from the prescribed burning statistics provided by the NFDP. A number of discrepancies between the slash burning disturbance targets used in NIR2014 and the current NFDP statistics were noted during a recent review. We have updated the 1990 – 2012 slash burning targets for these provinces in order to re-establish consistency between NFCMARS and the NFDP statistics.

Figure 2-2 compares the total area slash-burned annually after updating the NFCMARS targets with the total area slash-burned annually in NIR2014.

Figure 2-2: Area slash burned 1990-2012, NIR2015 vs NIR2014

Global warming potentials
Global warming potentials (GWP) for methane and nitrous oxide have been updated to the IPCC 2006 values. Specifically, the GWP for methane (CH4) has increased from 21 to 25, while the GWP for nitrous oxide (N2O) has decreased from 310 to 297.
Recent activity data updates
The NIR2015 included new data for forest fires, mountain pine beetle and forest management activities. Updates to forest management were implemented from 2008-2012. Fire and mountain pine beetle data was implemented for 2013. The NFDP did not have an accurate account of the 2013 forest management as of time of the analysis (mid-September, 2014), as such all of the 2013 forest management targets were assumed to equal the 2012 targets. This is a similar approach as was employed in the NIR2014.

Introduction
This document summarizes the updates to Canada’s National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System (NFCMARS) for Canada’s 2015 national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory submission to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), covering the reporting period 1990-2013.

No changes to the emissions estimation methodology have been introduced for NIR2015. NFCMARS updates for the current national inventory report (NIR) were limited to:

Updated wildfire activity data for 1990-2012 in Ontario, to capture updates to the underlying data sources and to correct an accumulation of past data processing errors
Updated slash burning activity data for 1990-2012 in Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Ontario, Quebec and Northwest Territories, to capture all updates to the underlying National Forestry Database Program (NFDP) prescribed burning statistics
Updating harvest activity data for 2008-2012, to capture recent changes to the underlying NFDP harvest statistics
Addition of new activity data for 2013 wildfires, insect disturbances, harvesting and deforestation.

These updates are described in

The issues that prevented updating Ontario fire disturbances have now been resolved and so for NIR2015 we have updated 1990 – 2012 fire disturbance events in Ontario.

We have updated the 1990 – 2012 slash burning targets for these provinces in order to re-establish consistency between NFCMARS and the NFDP statistics.

Revision of C.F.S volume-to-biomass equations for B.C.
Feb. 2019

All the procedures used to develop the most recent version of the CFS volume-to-biomass models for B.C. (2014) were reviewed during the spring of 2018, as part of a larger comparison between BCMFLNR and CFS volume-to-biomass models.

During the review, it was discovered that the compilation of the older ‘S’ type plots in the biomass database still had some issues (these ‘S’ type plots are large, temporary sample plots used for inventory in B.C. during the 1950’s, 1960’s and 1970’s - there are over 20,000 in the database). Most of them are actually a cluster of 2 separate plots, but are combined and treated as 1 large plot for analysis and modeling. However, during this phase, the individual plot areas were not combined and ended up being half the size in the final database (e.g. plot area of 0.08 ha was used instead of 0.16 ha). 

The compilation procedures have been revised to combine the plot areas correctly, and all the B.C. volume-to-biomass models have been updated (May, 2018). An overall effect of this change on the models is to reduce the biomass they estimate by a small amount, usually < 10%. However, some ecozone-species combinations that contain a high proportion of ‘S’ plots have greater changes (e.g. white pine stands can show a 20% or more reduction in estimated biomass), or even have small increases in biomass estimates.

Overview
The Land Use, Land-Use Change and Forestry (LULUCF) Sector reports greenhouse gas (GHG) fluxes between the atmosphere and Canada’s managed lands as well as those associated with land-use change and emissions from harvested wood products (HWP) derived from these lands. The assessment includes emissions and removals of carbon dioxide (CO2); additional emissions of methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O) and carbon monoxide (CO) due to controlled biomass burning; CH4 and N2O emissions from wetland drainage and rewetting due to peat extraction; and N2O released following Land converted to Cropland. 
The estimated net GHG flux in the LULUCF Sector, calculated as the sum of CO2 and non-CO2 emissions and CO2 removals, amounted to a net removal of 68 Mt in 1990, 21 Mt in 2005 and 24 Mt in 2017. When applied to the national totals, they decrease the total Canadian GHG emissions by 11%, 2.9% and 3.3% in 1990, 2005 and 2016, respectively. Land Category Definition and Representation of Managed Lands
In order to harmonize all land-based estimates, common working definitions were developed and adopted by all groups involved in estimate preparation. Definitions are consistent with the IPCC (2006) land categories, while remaining relevant to land management practices, prevailing environmental conditions and available data sources in Canada. This framework applies to all LULUCF estimates reported under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).
Forest Land includes all areas of trees of 1 ha or more, with a minimum tree crown cover of 25% and trees of 5 m in height – or having the potential to reach this height. Not all Canadian forests are under the direct influence of human activities, prompting the non-trivial question “what areas properly embody ‘managed forests’?” Briefly, for the purpose of the GHG inventory, managed forests are those managed for timber and non-timber resources (including parks) or subject to fire protection. Annex 3.5 provides more detail on the implementation of the “managed forests” definition.
Agricultural land comprises both Cropland and agricultural Grassland. Cropland includes all lands in annual crops, summerfallow and perennial crops (mostly forage, but also including berries, grapes, nursery crops, vegetables, and fruit trees and orchards). Agricultural Grassland is defined as “unimproved” pasture or rangeland that is used only for grazing domestic livestock. It occurs only in geographical areas where the grassland would not naturally regrow to forest if abandoned, i.e. the natural shortgrass prairie in southern Saskatchewan and Alberta and the dry, interior mountain valleys of British Columbia. All agricultural land that is not grassland is de facto classified as Cropland, including unimproved pastures where natural vegetation would be forest (Eastern Canada and most of British Columbia).
Vegetated areas that do not meet the definition of Forest Land or Cropland are generally classified as Grassland. Extensive areas of tundra in the Canadian North are considered unmanaged grassland.
Wetlands are areas where permanent or recurrent saturated conditions allow the establishment of vegetation and soil development typical of these conditions and that are not already included in the Forest Land, Cropland or agricultural Grassland categories. Currently, managed lands included in the Wetlands category are those where human interventions have directly altered the water table—which include peatlands drained for peat extraction and flooded lands (hydroelectric reservoirs) (IPCC 2006).

and categories. Currently, managed lands included in the Wetlands category are those where human interventions have directly altered the water table—which include peatlands drained for peat extraction and flooded lands (hydroelectric reservoirs) (IPCC 2006).
The Settlements category includes all built-up land: urban, rural residential, land devoted to industrial and recreational use; roads, rights-of-way and other transportation infrastructure; and resource exploration, extraction and distribution (mining, oil and gas). The diversity of this category has so far precluded a complete assessment of its extent in the Canadian landscape. However, the conversion of Forest Land, Cropland and unmanaged Grassland (tundra) to Settlements and the area of urban trees are assessed in this GHG inventory. 
Other Land comprises areas of rock, ice or bare soil, and all land areas that do not fall into any of the other five categories. Currently, only emissions from the conversion of Other Land to reservoirs and peat extraction are reported, under the Wetlands category.
As a consequence of the land categorization scheme, some land-use transitions cannot occur—for example, forest conversion to agricultural grassland—since by definition these exclude areas where forests can grow naturally. Since grassland is defined as “native,” creation of grassland does not occur.
The IPCC default land-use change transition period of 20 years is used for all land-use change categories except for land conversion to flooded lands (reservoirs), for which a 10-year transition period is used (IPCC 2006), and for land conversion for peat extraction, for which a land-use change period of one year is used to represent the land conversion practices of draining and clearing of the surface vegetation layer (acrotelm) in preparation for peat extraction. However, the use of the 20-year land transition period for reporting land areas is simply procedural since higher tier estimation methods are utilized for developing emission and removal estimates.

Forest Land (CRF Category 4.A)
Forest and other wooded lands cover 400 million hectares (Mha) of Canadian territory; forest lands alone occupy 350 Mha (NRCan 2018). Managed forests account for 230 Mha, or 65% of all forests. Four reporting zones (Boreal Shield East, Boreal Plains, Montane Cordillera and Boreal Shield West) account for 69% of managed forests.
In 2017, the net GHG balance of managed Forest Land amounted to removals of 150 Mt (Table 6-1 and CRF Table 4), while emissions from wood products originating from Canada’s managed forests amounted to 125 Mt. 
The Forest Land estimate includes net emissions and removals of CO2, as well as N2O and CH4 emissions from slash burning. For the purpose of UNFCCC reporting, managed Forest Land is divided into the subcategories Forest Land remaining Forest Land (230 Mha, net removals of 150 Mt in 2017) and Land converted to Forest Land (0.04 Mha, net removals of 0.4 Mt in 2017).
Forest Land Remaining Forest Land (CRF Category 4.A.1)
Sink Category Description
As trees grow, they absorb CO2 from the atmosphere through photosynthesis, and some of this carbon is stored in vegetation (biomass), dead organic matter (DOM) and soils. Carbon dioxide and other GHGs are returned to the atmosphere by respiration and the decay and burning of organic matter. Human interactions with the land can directly alter the size and rate of these natural exchanges of GHGs in both the immediate and long term. Land-use change and land-use practices in the past still affect current GHG fluxes to and from the managed forest. This long-term effect is a unique characteristic of the LULUCF Sector, which makes it very distinct from other inventory sectors.
Forest planning, harvest operations and subsequent forest regeneration are the primary direct human influences on emissions and removals in forests. Forest harvest transfers carbon to Harvested Wood Products (HWP) (Section 6.4) and produces harvest residues (branches, foliage and non-commercial species) which are left to decay or are burned. Clear-cut harvesting resets stand age to 0; this changes the rate of carbon accumulation in biomass as young trees accumulate little biomass in the first 30 to 40 years. The combination of emissions and removals in Forest Land and emissions of carbon harvested from the forest represent the net flux between managed forests and the atmosphere (Figure 6-2).
Estimates for the net removals from Forest Land exclude the impacts of non-anthropogenic natural disturbances (wildfires, insect infestations and wind throw). Net removals from Forest Land decreased from 210 Mt in 1990 to 150 Mt in 2007 and remained relatively constant thereafter (Figure 6-2). The decrease in removals that occurred between 2000 and 2007 is mainly due to trends in the Montane Cordillera and Boreal Plains reporting zones. In the Montane Cordillera, ins

from Forest Land decreased from 210 Mt in 1990 to 150 Mt in 2007 and remained relatively constant thereafter (Figure 6-2). The decrease in removals that occurred between 2000 and 2007 is mainly due to trends in the Montane Cordillera and Boreal Plains reporting zones. In the Montane Cordillera, insect infestations and salvage harvesting of infested stands resulted in a shift in the average age of the forests of this region to younger age classes and an overall decrease in the rate of carbon accumulation in biomass in the reporting zone. At the same time, low-level insect infestations increased tree mortality over large areas, increasing emissions from decomposition. In the Boreal Plain, harvest rates also resulted in a shift in the average age of forests of that reporting zone, but insect infestation and fire also caused a reduction in the area of commercially mature forest stands and, consequently, a reduction in the rate of carbon uptake for the region. Reduced carbon uptake and increased emissions from decomposition in these regions resulted in a decrease large enough in removals to impact the national trend.

Methodological Issues
Canada applies a Tier 3 methodology for estimating GHG emissions and removals in managed forests. Canada’s National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System (NFCMARS) includes a model-based approach (Carbon Budget Model of the Canadian Forest Sector, or CBM-CFS3) (Kull et al. 2014; Kurz et al. 2009). This model integrates forest inventory data and yield curves with spatially referenced activity data on forest management and natural disturbances to estimate forest carbon stocks, stock changes and CO2 emissions and removals. The model uses regional ecological and climate parameters to simulate carbon transfers among pools, to harvested wood products and to the atmosphere. A more detailed description of forest carbon modelling can be found in Annex 3.5.2.1. 
Prior to the 2017 inventory edition, emissions and removals of Forest Land displayed large interannual variability due to the impact of natural disturbances that masked the impact of forest management activities. The IPCC has recognized the issue of reporting emissions from natural disturbances for some countries and encouraged countries that use Tier 3 methodologies to work towards the development of new approaches that can improve the isolation of anthropogenic impacts (IPCC 2010). It is understood that in Canada, natural disturbances are responsible for significant emissions and subsequent removals when forests regrow after the disturbances occur (Table 6-5). However in Canada, a Tier 3 approach to isolate the effect of anthropogenic activities on managed forests has been developed. This approach is based on the monitoring of forest stands impacted by anthropogenic and natural drivers separ

ls when forests regrow after the disturbances occur (Table 6-5). However in Canada, a Tier 3 approach to isolate the effect of anthropogenic activities on managed forests has been developed. This approach is based on the monitoring of forest stands impacted by anthropogenic and natural drivers separately (Figure 6-3). For transparency, all emissions and removals are presented in this report, but reporting is based on stands associated with anthropogenic drivers in an effort to better capture emissions and removals (Figure 6-3) more closely linked to land management decisions and to provide information to better inform policy. Emissions and removals from stands dominated by the impacts of recent natural disturbances are not reported until the stands have reached commercial maturity for a given region; however they are displayed in Table 6-5 for reference and transparency purposes. When stands have reached a regionally determined minimum operable age and, as a consequence, are considered within forest management planning or are directly affected by forest management activities, they are reclassified as stands under anthropogenic influence. Direct forest management activities include commercial clear-cut and partial harvest, commercial and pre-commercial thinning, and salvage logging. Additional information on the estimation approach is provided in Annex 3.5.2.3.
Carbon stock changes in managed forests are reported in CRF Table 4.A, by reporting zone. For any given pool, carbon stock changes include not only exchanges of GHG with the atmosphere, but also the carbon transfers to and from pools, for example its transfer from living biomass to dead organic matter upon stand mortality. Therefore, individual carbon stock changes give no indication of the net fluxes between carbon pools in managed forests and the atmosphere. 
Harvesting wood from managed forests results in both a transfer of carbon from the Forest Land category to the Harvested Wood Products category (Figure 6-2, Table 6-5) and in debris or residues that remain on site and decompose. The fate of the carbon embedded in wood material taken off-site is tracked in the HWP pool and reported in the Harvested Wood Products category, and the emissions from the carbon that decomposes on site are reported in Forest Land. Due to limitations in the current design of the CRF tables, the carbon transferred from the forest to the HWP pool is not reported in CRF Table 4.A since it would result in an automatic calculation of CO2 emissions in the “net CO2 emissions/removals” column of that table, which would amount to using the instant oxidation approach for HWP. Instead, and for transparency purposes, this carbon transfer is reported as carbon input into the HWP in-use pool in CRF Table 4.G without removing it from the emissions reported in the “Net emissions/ removals from HWP in use” column of CRF Table 4.G. For this reason, it is important to caution against interpreting the net carbon stock change in

Uncertainties and Time-Series Consistency
Uncertainty Estimates
Numerical techniques are used to quantify uncertainties about the outputs of the CBM-CFS3 (Metsaranta et al. 2017). Modelling of the entire managed forests of Canada is not done as a single run, but in separate “project runs” whose output is subsequently assembled. For each “project,” 100 Monte Carlo runs are conducted using the base input data for the 2019 submission (covering the entire 1990–2017 time series). Confidence intervals are obtained for each inventory year by randomly sampling 10 000 combinations of all the project runs for that year. Separate uncertainty estimates are produced for each gas. 
Throughout the entire time series, the uncertainties associated with annual estimates are expressed as a 95% confidence interval, bound by 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the Monte Carlo run outputs. The uncertain range of the CO2 estimates is 76 Mt in 1990, 82 Mt in 2005 and 83 Mt in 2017 (Table 6-6). On average, uncertainty was ±58 Mt of the median result from the Monte Carlo runs over the entire time series. Non-CO2 emissions contribute little to total uncertainty. Probability distributions are asymmetrical around the net flux estimate and are skewed to the lower bound (greater sink), representative of the nature of the distributions of the activity data and parameters tested in the Monte Carlo analysis as they are expressed in the model. More information on the general approach used to conduct this analysis is provided in Annex A3.5.2.4 and a detailed description of methods, assumptions and discussions of the skewed nature of uncertain distribution can be found in Metsaranta et al. (2017).

Time-Series Consistency
All estimates have been developed in a consistent manner, but some sources of activity data do not provide full coverage for the entire reporting period. Estimates of wildfire areas burned in the managed forest for the 1990–2003 period were derived from the Canadian National Fire Database (CNFDB), which comprises information from provincial resource management agencies, compiled and updated by the Canadian Forest Service. Estimates of area burned for the period 2004–2017 were obtained from the National Burned Area Composite (NBAC). This composite of data is derived from various remote sensing sources, monitoring data collected by provincial resource management agencies, and a rule set that, for each fire, identifies the most accurate available data source. An analysis of the period of overlap in the data shows that the differences between the two time series are small and not biased. The processes used to quantify the area burned estimates in NBAC generate improved estimates of the area burned of individual fires, because, in general, more detailed information about unburned areas within the fire perimeter is generated. Individual fire events may thus generate less burned area, but the total number of events included in the NBAC can be higher. 
The forest inventory data incorporated in the analyses were not all collected in the same year across the country. Annex 3.5 explains how forest inventory data from various sources were processed to provide complete, coherent and consistent forest data for 1990.
Quality Assurance / Quality Control and Verification
Systematic and documented quality assurance/quality control (QA/QC) procedures are performed in four areas: workflow checks (manual), model checks (automated), benchmark checks (manual) and external reviews. Check results are systematically documented; an issue logging system identifies each issue and facilitates tracking and managing its resolution. Tier 2 QC checks (White and Dymond 2008; Dymond 2008) specifically address estimate development in the Forest Land category.
Environment and Climate Change Canada, while maintaining its own QA/QC procedures for estimates developed internally (refer to Section 1.3, Chapter 1), has implemented category-specific Tier 2 checks for estimates obtained from partners, as well as for all estimates and activity data contained in the LULUCF data warehouse and entered into the CRF reporter. These procedures and their outcome are fully documented in the centralized archives.
Shaw et al. (2014) compared the carbon stocks predicted by the CBM-CFS3 with ground plot-based estimates of ecosystem carbon stocks from Canada’s new National Forest Inventory (NFI). ted by the CBM-CFS3 with ground plot-based estimates of ecosystem carbon stocks from Canada’s new National Forest Inventory (NFI). Data sets from the NFI of carbon stocks were entirely independent of the input data used for model simulations for each ground plot. The mean error in total ecosystem stocks between model predictions and ground plot measurements was 1%, while the error in aboveground biomass, deadwood, litter and mineral soil pools was 7.5%, 30.8%, 9.9% and 8.4%, respectively. The contribution of aboveground biomass and deadwood to the error in ecosystem subtotal pools was small. However, the contribution from soils was large. As part of quality assurance efforts, the 2017 NIR approach for estimating anthropogenic emissions and removals was reviewed by an international panel of forest scientists convened by Environment and Climate Change Canada in October 2016. The panel found that the new approach effectively isolates anthropogenic emissions and removals due to forest management from the impacts of natural disturbances. The panel also stated that the criterion established to classify stands impacted by insect infestations as under anthropogenic or natural influence was justifiable. However, it recommended that the threshold criterion used to differentiate anthropogenic or natural emissions and removals after stand-replacing natural disturbances should be regionally specific to incorporate regional variations in forest ecology. Changes have been implemented in this submission and, once implemented in the model, the revised approach was reviewed and approved by provincial forest experts.

Land Converted to Forest Land (CRF Category 4.A.2)
Category Description
This category includes all lands converted to Forest Land through direct human activity. Post-harvest tree planting is not included, nor is abandoned farmland where natural vegetation is allowed to establish; hence, the category more precisely refers to forest establishment where the previous land use was not forest (typically, abandoned farmland).
The total cumulative area reported under the Land converted to Forest Land category declined from 170 kha in 1990 to 36 kha in 2017. The trend reflects the gradual transfer of lands afforested more than 20 years ago to the Forest Land remaining Forest Land category and a lack of recent data on rates of forest establishment. Eighty percent of all farmland converted to forest land over the last 20 years occurred in Eastern Canada (Atlantic Maritime, Mixedwood Plains and Boreal Shield East reporting zones), with only 15% in the Prairie provinces (Boreal Shield West, Boreal Plains and Subhumid Prairies reporting zones) and the remaining 7% in Western Canada (Pacific Maritime and Montane Cordillera).
Net removals declined throughout the period, from 1.1 Mt in 1990 to 0.4 Mt in 2017. Net carbon accumulation largely occurs in biomass (90 Gg C in 2017 – CRF Table 4.A); soil carbon sequestration is negligible and will remain so because this category is restricted to plantations that are younger than 20 years. For the same reason, and considering the relatively low net increment of planted trees in the early years, the sub-category as a whole is not expected to contribute significantly to the net greenhouse gas balance of Forest Land. In considering these trends, it must also be noted that the data used in this analysis are not comprehensive.
Methodological Issues
The Feasibility Assessment of Afforestation for Carbon Sequestration (FAACS) initiative collected and compiled afforestation records for 1990–2002 (NRCan 2005a). In that period, softwood plantations, especially spruce and pine, accounted for 90% of the area planted. Activities for 1970–1989 and 2003–2008 were estimated based on activity rates observed in the FAACS data, complemented with information from the Forest 2020 Plantation Demonstration Assessment (NRCan 2005b). No new afforestation activity data were collected for the 2009–2017 inventory years.

8 were estimated based on activity rates observed in the FAACS data, complemented with information from the Forest 2020 Plantation Demonstration Assessment (NRCan 2005b). No new afforestation activity data were collected for the 2009–2017 inventory years. 
GHG emissions and removals on lands newly converted to Forest Land were estimated using CBM-CFS3, as described in Annex 3.5. Changes in soil carbon stocks are highly uncertain because of difficulties in locating data about the carbon stocks prior to plantation. It was assumed that the ecosystem would generally accumulate soil carbon at a slow rate. The limited time frame of this analysis and the scale of the activity relative to other land use and land-use change activities suggest that the impact of this uncertainty, if any, is minimal.
Uncertainties and Time-Series Consistency
Significant challenges remain in estimating uncertainty for this category due to the lack of a consistent national system for tracking afforestation and because it is currently not possible to run a Monte Carlo simulation using the model data input structure for this category. Given these limitations, initial uncertainty estimates were developed based on expert judgement. It was assumed that the 95% confidence intervals for this category could be estimated at 10% smaller or 200% larger than the reported value. 
Quality Assurance / Quality Control and Verification

Environment and Climate Change Canada, while maintaining its own QA/QC procedures for estimates developed internally (refer to Section 1.3, Chapter 1), has implemented specific procedures for estimates obtained from data partners, as well as for all estimates and activity data contained in the LULUCF data warehouse and entered into the CRF reporter.

The Harvested Wood Products category is reported following the Simple Decay Approach as described in the Annex to Volume 4, Chapter 12, of the 2006 IPCC Guidelines (IPCC 2006). The approach is similar to, but differs from the Production Approach in that the HWP pool is treated as a carbon transfer related to forest harvest and hence does not assume instant oxidation of wood in the year of harvest (more details provided in Annex 3.5).

Emissions associated with this category result from the use and disposal of HWP manufactured from wood resulting from forest harvest and forest conversion activities in Canada and consumed either domestically or elsewhere in the world. Products disposed of at the end of their useful life are assumed to be immediately oxidized.
Emissions from this source are mainly influenced by the trend in forest harvest rates and the long-term impact of harvest levels starting in the year that carbon begins to be stored in a pool of HWP that are in use. As a result, emissions fluctuated between 120 Mt in 2009 (lowest harvest year) and a peak of 150 Mt in 1995. In 2017, HWP amounted to total emissions of 130 Mt, similar to 1990 (Table 6-7).
Harvested Wood Products emissions are inextricably linked to emissions/removals from Forest Land, such that the sum of net emissions/removals from Forest Land and emissions from HWP provides an estimate of total net emissions/removals from the managed forest (Figure 6-2).

Methodological Issues
A country-specific model, the National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System for Harvested Wood Products (NFCMARS-HWP), is used to monitor and quantify the fate of carbon off-site from the point of forest harvest or forest conversion. The model tracks HWP sub-pools and carbon flows between sub-pools through the life-cycle of wood products (e.g. manufacturing, use, trade and disposal).
In more concrete terms, the harvested wood products model takes the carbon output from harvested wood from the ecosystem model, exports a portion as roundwood, converts all the rest of the harvested wood into commodities, exports some of the commodities produced, and keeps track of the additions to and removals from HWP in-use and bioenergy. 
Inputs to the model (Table 6-7) include the annual mass of carbon from conventional contemporary harvest and residential firewood collection in Forest Land and a relatively small amount from forest conversion activities (around 2.4% of all inputs in any year) transferred from the CBM-CFS3 model (see Section 6.3.1.2). For the historical harvest, the input comes from the historical commodity production from Statistics Canada at a national level of spatial resolution, covering the 1900–1989 period.
Data on the annual volume of residential firewood and industrial wood waste are provided by the Energy Sector. Residential firewood data come from the 1996, 2006 and 2012 TNS Global/Canadian Facts Surveys, while data on industrial consumption of firewood comes from the annual Report on Energy Supply and Demand in Canada (RESD). More information on the estimation methodology, data sources and parameters used in the model are available in Annex 3.1 (data sources) and Annex 3.5.

For the amounts of C associated with volumes of residential firewood provided by the Energy Sector, 87% of the total firewood volume is used as input to simulate the harvest of firewood from the managed forest. The remaining 13% of the Energy Sector wood volumes comes from post-consumer products (details are provided in Annex 3.5). 
The trend in emissions from HWP disposal results from historical commodity production combined with the duration of the life cycle of various commodities (Table 6-7). The impact of any significant changes in harvest levels or in the mix of products is therefore redistributed over several subsequent years and decades as commodities are gradually retired from use. Activity data and annual estimates of carbon inputs, stock changes in the HWP pool and resulting net emissions for each commodity are reported in CRF Table 4.G.

Cropland (CRF Category 4.B)
Cropland covers approximately 47 Mha of the Canadian territory. In 2017, the net GHG balance in the Cropland category amounted to removals of 6.8 Mt (Table 6-1). For the purpose of reporting under the UNFCCC, Cropland is divided into Cropland remaining Cropland (net removals of 9.6 Mt in 2017) and Land (either forest or grassland) converted to Cropland (net emissions of 2.6 Mt and 0.2 Mt, respectively, in 2017). The estimates of Land converted to Cropland include net emissions and removals of CO2, as well as N2O and CH4 emissions.
Cropland Remaining Cropland (CRF Category 4.B.1)
Cultivated agricultural land in Canada includes areas of field crops, summerfallow, hay fields and tame or seeded pasture. Cropland is found mainly in the nine southernmost reporting zones. About 83% of Canada’s cropland is in the interior plains of Western Canada, made up of the Semi-arid Prairies, Subhumid Prairies and Boreal Plains reporting zones. Another 12% of cropland is found in the Mixedwood Plains reporting zone.
Cropland remaining Cropland includes CO2 emissions/removals in mineral soils, CO2 emissions from cultivation of organic soils and CO2 emissions/removals resulting from changes in woody biomass from specialty crops, trees and shrubs and lands not fulfilling the definition of a forest. An enhanced Tier 2 approach is used for estimating CO2 emissions from and removals by mineral soils triggered by changes in land management practices.
