Methodological Updates 
Improvement Project 2021_10 –Refine estimates of BC slash-burning activity
Prior to NIR2025, the proportion of harvest area in BC where slash pile burning (SPB) is applied was estimated using an “expert opinion” of 15% for coastal regions and 50% for the interior. For NIR2025, the proportions determined by “expert opinion” have been replaced by new proportions using a data-driven approach.
 A statistical analysis using very high resolution imagery was conducted to assess the rates of slash pile burning in BC. In the study, harvest events from around BC were randomly selected and assessed for their association with SPB occurrence rates. The updated proportions for SPB occurrence developed from the study are 15% for the coast and 59% for the interior, and these new proportions have been applied for BC in NIR2025.The methods and results of this improvement project have been submitted for publication (Nesdoly et al. In preparation)
BC Harvest conditions update 
This project revised the selection criteria for harvesting in BC in order to better reflect the temporal and spatial occurrence of salvage following the Mountain Pine Beetle (MPB) outbreak. The prior assumption in CBM modelling had been to use a snag-priority harvest rule for all harvesting in BC to represent salvage harvesting associated with the MPB outbreak. This update used evidence from the Forestry Practice Board of BC to limit the snag-priority harvesting to the years and spatial areas where mountain pine beetle had the greatest impact. For the Montane regions of BC, evidence from billing records and the shelf life of beetle-killed wood supported the retention of the snag priority rule between 2002 and 2020, while the remaining years were reassigned to a volume-priority rule. Boreal and Pacific regions of BC, which were not as impacted by the MPB outbreak, were also converted to a volume-priority harvest rule. 
Computing architecture update
CBM-CFS3 carbon dynamics, input data, events and record tracking were migrated to a more modern computing architecture that provides advantages in run time and level of detail, while replicating all previous science and model features. Transitioning to a modern computing architecture paves the way for future improvements that were unable to be implemented in the previous architecture paradigm. 
Quebec insect classifier update
For multiple years, large areas of Spruce Budworm disturbance in Quebec have been unable to be realized during modelling, leading to shortfalls in achieved insect attack targets. Spruce Budworm disturbances have specific host tree species, and limitations in the data have meant that tree species in Quebec have not been robustly represented in the inventories. Reforestation bug fix
A bug fix was implemented to ensure records selected for reforestation were not eligible for subsequent wildfire or firewood collection disturbances. 
 Update to Forest Land and Harvested Wood Products reporting methods
Canada’s 2025 National GHG Inventory Report (NIR2025) is incorporating a major change to its reporting structure for emissions and removals from the managed forest and harvested wood products (HWP). This change is not a modelling change, and is in response to recommendations from a UNFCCC expert review team released following their review of the Canada’s NIR in fall 2023. However, the change in approach does alter the communication and representation of modelling results. 
Under the current reporting approach, the transfer of carbon from harvested stands between the managed forest and HWP is not treated as an emission nor removal. Instead, it is counted as a carbon stock change from the managed forest carbon pool to the HWP carbon pool. Under the revised approach, carbon stock changes are equated to emissions and removals. As such, when a forest stand is harvested, the transfer of carbon out of the managed forest carbon pool is treated as an emission within the managed forest and correspondingly the transfer of carbon into the HWP carbon pool is treated as a removal. This approach significantly changes the individual timeseries data for both the managed forest and HWP, however net emissions for the forest sector (i.e. the sum of manage forest and HWP emissions/removals) remain identical under the current and revised approach (see figure below). Updated Waste Incineration Activity Data
Activity data describing waste incineration levels for the period 1941 – 2022 period were provided by ECCC. There were no changes in the wood waste incineration activity from 1990-2021. No waste incineration activity data was provided for 2023, and so waste incineration targets were set to 0 tC for 2023. 
The ‘contemporary’ HWP model scenario that runs from 1990 onward to estimate end-of-life emissions associated with Canada’s domestic harvest since 1990 has been updated to capture the new year (2022) of waste incineration activity data. 
HWP estimates prepared for the NIR include the post-1989 end-of-life emissions from domestic wood products originally harvested as early as 1900. Although the emissions from wood and paper waste incinerated in years 1941 through 1989 do not contribute to the post-1989 HWP emissions, they do alter the C stocks that would otherwise be present in landfills and that would in turn influence post-1989 emissions from landfills. Therefore the ‘historic’ HWP model scenario that runs from 1900 onward to estimate post-1989 end-of-life emissions from pre-1990 HWP-in-use stocks in included, however no changes to the 1941-1989 waste incineration activity data relative to NIR2025 have been made. Recalculations
NFCMARS updates for NIR2025 resulted in recalculation of previously reported emissions estimates for 1990 – 2022 estimates. Table 5-1 summarizes the overall difference between emissions/removals reported for NIR2025 and NIR2024 for the period 1990 – 2022, to the nearest 0.1 Mt CO2e. 
Figure 5-1 shows the net emissions/removals from the anthropogenic portion of the FLFL landbase for the period 1990 – 2022. The top panel shows net emissions as reported in NIR2025 and NIR2024, and the difference between them under the old reporting format. The middle panel shows the incremental contribution of the various NIR2024 improvement projects and activity data updates to the overall differences. The bottom panel shows the net emissions for NIR2025, NIR2024, and the difference between them under the new reporting format. The dominant driver of recalculations from 1990 to 2022 are the improvements to the BC harvest sorting condition. In this improvement, the prior assumption of snag-priority harvest was limited to the years and regions where the mountain pine beetle epidemic occurred. The remaining years and areas were re-assigned to a volume-priority harvest condition. This means that a smaller area was needed to meet the harvest targets, and lowered emissions because there was more undisturbed forest left on the landscape. Additional recalculations came from increased emissions from the slash-pile burn update, which lead to more emissions because more area was burned and the Quebec spruce budworm update. The latter project caused increased emissions because increased insect targets were realized and so more emissions from decomposition occurred as the biomass was transferred to dead organic matter pools. The computing architecture update also led to recalculations throughout the time series due to reshuffling of records and changed interpretation of growth curves. 
Figure 5-2 shows the FLFL Anthropogenic partition area for the period 1990 – 2022. The top panel shows the FLFL Anthro area as reported in NIR2025 and NIR2024 and the difference between them. The bottom panel shows the incremental contribution of the various NIR2025 improvement projects and activity data updates to the overall differences. The primary driver of the change in anthropogenic area was the change in BC sort conditions, because this update changed the amount of land are needed to meet harvest targets. 
Recalculations in the HWP category are illustrated in Figure 5-3. The top panel shows the HWP emissions of CO2 as reported in NIR2025 and NIR2024, and the difference between them. The bottom panel shows the incremental contribution of the various emission types to the overall differences. HWP emissions of CO2 as reported in NIR2025 and NIR2024, and the difference between them. The bottom panel shows the incremental contribution of the various emission types to the overall differences. CO2 emissions from HWP in 2022 show an increase of 1.4 Mt CO2 relative to the NIR2024 estimate, and CO2 emissions from HWP in 2021 show an increase of 0.6 Mt CO2 relative to NIR2024. Methodological Updates 
Improvement Project 2021_10 –Refine estimates of BC slash-burning activity
Prior to NIR2025, the proportion of harvest area in BC where slash pile burning (SPB) is applied was estimated using an “expert opinion” of 15% for coastal regions and 50% for the interior. For NIR2025, the proportions determined by “expert opinion” have been replaced by new proportions using a data-driven approach.
A statistical analysis using very-high resolution imagery was conducted to assess the rates of slash pile burning in BC. In the study, harvest events from around BC were randomly selected and assessed for their association with SPB occurrence. The updated proportions for SPB occurrence developed from the study are 15% for the coast and 59% for the interior, and these new proportions have been applied in BC for NIR2025. The methods and results of this improvement project have been submitted for publication (Nesdoly et al. In preparation)
BC Harvest conditions update 
This project revised the selection criteria for harvesting in BC in order to better reflect the temporal and spatial occurrence of salvage harvesting following the Mountain Pine Beetle (MPB) outbreak. The prior assumption in CBM modelling had been to use a snag-priority harvest rule for all harvesting in BC to represent salvage-focused harvest plans and incentives associated with the MPB outbreak. This update used evidence from the Forestry Practices Board of BC to limit the snag-priority harvesting to the years and spatial areas where MPB had the greatest impact and harvest planning and execution is recorded as being salvage-focused. For the Montane regions of BC, evidence from billing records and the shelf life of beetle-killed wood supported the retention of the snag priority rule between 2002 and 2020, while the remaining years were reassigned to a rule prioritizing highest merchantable carbon stocks. Boreal and Pacific regions of BC, which were not as impacted by the MPB outbreak, were also converted to a merchantable carbon-priority harvest rule. 
Computing architecture update
CBM-CFS3 carbon dynamics, input data, events and record tracking were migrated to a more modern computing architecture that provides advantages in run time and level of detail, while replicating all previous science and model features. Quebec insect classifier update
For multiple years, large areas of Spruce Budworm (SBW) disturbance in Quebec were not realized during modelling, leading to shortfalls between input target areas and what the model represents. SBW disturbances have specific host tree species; however, information on tree species in Quebec is limited. New information has led to improved interpretation of existing information, in turn supporting better matching of SBW events to host tree species. This has helped to reduce the area target shortfalls in Quebec. Although some unrealized disturbances still exist, this work improved representation of SBW disturbances in Quebec. 
Reforestation bug fix
A bug fix was implemented to ensure records selected for reforestation were not eligible for subsequent wildfire or firewood collection disturbances.

 Update to Forest Land and Harvested Wood Products reporting methods
Canada’s 2025 National GHG Inventory Report (NIR2025) is incorporating a major change to its reporting structure for emissions and removals from the managed forest and harvested wood products (HWP) pools. This change is not a modelling change, and is in response to recommendations from the UNFCCC expert review team following their fall 2023 review of Canada’s NIR. However, the change in approach does alter the communication and representation of modelling results. 
Under the previous reporting approach, the transfer of carbon from harvested stands between the managed forest and HWP is not treated as an emission nor removal. Instead, it is counted as a carbon stock transfer from the managed forest carbon pool to the HWP carbon pool. Under the revised approach, the carbon stock change in the forest and HWP components are recognized separately as a carbon stock loss in the forest and a carbon stock gain in HWP. Carbon stock losses can be represented as a positive carbon flux, which is often equated to an emission; the reverse is true for carbon stock gain, represented as a negative carbon flux and equated to a removal. As such, when a forest stand is harvested, the transfer of carbon out of the managed forest carbon pool

sses can be represented as a positive carbon flux, which is often equated to an emission; the reverse is true for carbon stock gain, represented as a negative carbon flux and equated to a removal. As such, when a forest stand is harvested, the transfer of carbon out of the managed forest carbon pool is a positive carbon flux potentially treated as an emission and correspondingly the transfer of carbon into the HWP carbon pool is negative carbon flux potentially treated as a removal. 
This approach significantly changes the component-level timeseries data for emissions from both the managed forest and HWP. However net emissions for the forest sector (i.e. the sum of managed forest and HWP emissions/removals) remain identical under the previous and revised approach.

Updated Waste Incineration Activity Data
Activity data describing waste incineration levels for the period 1941 – 2022 period were provided by ECCC. There were no changes in the wood waste incineration activity from 1990-2021. No waste incineration activity data was provided for 2023, and so waste incineration targets were set to 0 tC for 2023. 
The ‘contemporary’ HWP model scenario that runs from 1990 onward to estimate end-of-life emissions associated with Canada’s domestic harvest since 1990 has been updated to capture the new year (2022) of waste incineration activity data. 
HWP estimates prepared for the NIR include the post-1989 end-of-life emissions from domestic wood products originally harvested as early as 1900. Although the emissions from wood and paper waste incinerated in years 1941 through 1989 do not contribute to the post-1989 HWP emissions, they do alter the C stocks that would otherwise be present in landfills and that would in turn influence post-1989 emissions from landfills. Therefore the ‘historic’ HWP model scenario that runs from 1900 onward to estimate post-1989 end-of-life emissions from pre-1990 HWP-in-use stocks in included, however no changes to the 1941-1989 waste incineration activity data relative to NIR2025 have been made. Anthropogenic GHG Emissions and Removals
As in previous years, the managed forest landbase is partitioned into two components: areas predominantly influenced by natural disturbances (wildfire, windthrow and insect disturbances causing greater than 20% mortality), and areas predominantly influenced by anthropogenic activities (forest management actions, insect attacks causing 20% mortality or less). Figure 4-5 illustrates the partitioning of the FLFL landbase area into anthropogenic and natural components, following the methods described in Kurz et al., 2018. In 2023, the anthropogenic partition area dropped 3.53 million hectares from 166.28 to 162.75. million hectares. This drop is primarily due to the portion of the 7.87 million hectares of wildfires that burned stands in the anthropogenic partition. Other changes to the anthropogenic area are due to insect attack, deforestation, and stand recovery into the anthropogenic partition.

The middle panel shows the incremental contribution of the various NIR2024 improvement projects and activity data updates to the overall differences. The bottom panel shows the net emissions for NIR2025, NIR2024, and the difference between them under the new reporting format. The dominant driver of recalculations from 1990 to 2022 was the improvement to the BC harvest sorting condition. In this improvement, the prior assumption of snag-priority harvest was limited to the years and regions where the mountain pine beetle epidemic occurred. The remaining years and areas were re-assigned to a volume-priority harvest condition. This means that a smaller area was needed to meet the harvest targets, which increase undisturbed productive forest, increased removals, and had the net effect of reducing emissions. Additional recalculations came from increased emissions from the slash-pile burn update as more post-harvest area was burned, and the Quebec spruce budworm update. The latter project caused increased emissions because insect targets were realized more so than in previous NIRs resulting in greater volumes of insect-killed wood and subsequently more emissions from decomposition. The computing architecture update also led to recalculations throughout the time series due to reshuffling of records and changed interpretation of growth curves. The annual impact of the reshuffling varied and didn’t trend towards source or sink overall, so the cumulative impact was negligible

1 Introduction 
This document summarizes the changes to Canada’s National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and 
Reporting System (NFCMARS) for the 2025 national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory submission to the 
United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), covering the reporting period 
1990 – 2023. 
 
NFCMARS methodological updates for the 2025 National Inventory Report (NIR) include the following 
improvement project from the NIR2024 – NIR2026 Improvement Plan1: 
• Project 2021_10: Refine estimates of BC slash burning activity 
 
In addition to the planned improvement to pre-1990 disturbances, the following additional 
improvements were completed: 
• BC harvest sort conditions update 
• Update to insect disturbance classifiers in QC 
• Update to computing architecture 
• Software logic errors related implementation of reforestation 
• Updated residential bioenergy appliance types and emissions factors 
 
The estimates for NIR2025 also include the following changes to activity data: 
• 2023 wildfire activity data update 
• 2015-2022 forest management activity data update, extended to 2023 
• 1990-2023 residential bioenergy activity data update

and removals estimates in greater detail.

2.1 Improvement Project 2021_10 –Refine estimates of BC slash-
burning activity 
Prior to NIR2025, the proportion of harvest area in BC where slash pile burning (SPB) is applied was 
estimated using an “expert opinion” of 15% for coastal regions and 50% for the interior. For NIR2025, 
the proportions determined by “expert opinion” have been replaced by new proportions using a data-
driven approach. 
A statistical analysis using very-high resolution imagery was conducted to assess the rates of slash pile 
burning in BC. In the study, harvest events from around BC were randomly selected and

tions determined by “expert opinion” have been replaced by new proportions using a data-
driven approach. 
A statistical analysis using very-high resolution imagery was conducted to assess the rates of slash pile 
burning in BC. In the study, harvest events from around BC were randomly selected and assessed for 
their association with SPB occurrence. The updated proportions for SPB occurrence developed from the 
study are 15% for the coast and 59% for the interior, and these new proportions have been applied in BC 
for NIR2025. The methods and results of this improvement project have been submitted for publication 
(Nesdoly et al. In preparation) 
2.2 BC Harvest conditions update 
This project revised the selection criteria for harvesting in BC in order to better reflect the temporal and 
spatial occurrence of salvage harvesting following the Mountain Pine Beetle (MPB) outbreak. The prior 
assumption in CBM modelling had been to use a snag-priority harvest rule for all harvesting in BC to 
represent salvage-focused harvest plans and incentives associated with the MPB outbreak. This update 
used evidence from the Forestry Practices Board of BC to limit the snag-priority harvesting to the years 
and spatial areas where MPB had the greatest impact and harvest planning and execution is recorded as 
being salvage-focused. For the Montane regions of BC, evidence from billing records and the shelf life of 
beetle-killed wood supported the retention of the snag priority rule between 2002 and 2020, while the 
remaining years were reassigned to a rule prioritizing highest merchantable carbon stocks. Boreal and 
Pacific regions of BC, which were not as impacted by the MPB outbreak, were also converted to a 
merchantable carbon-priority harvest rule. 
2.3 Computing architecture update 
CBM-CFS3 carbon dynamics, input data, events and record tracking were migrated to a more modern 
computing architecture that provides advantages in run time and level of detail, while replicating all 
previous science and model features. Transitioning to a modern computing architecture sets the stage 
for future improvements that were unable to be implemented in the previous computing architecture 
paradigm.

For multiple years, large areas of Spruce Budworm (SBW) disturbance in Quebec were not realized

disturbances have specific host tree species; however, information on tree species in Quebec is limited. 
New information has led to improved interpretation of existing information, in turn supporting better 
matching of SBW events to host tree species. This has helped to reduce the area target shortfalls in 
Quebec. Although some unrealized disturbances still exist, this work improved representation of SBW 
disturbances in Quebec.

2.7 Update to Forest Land and Harvested Wood Products reporting 
methods 
Canada’s 2025 National GHG Inventory Report (NIR2025) is incorporating a major change to its reporting 
structure for emissions and removals from the managed forest and harvested wood products (HWP) 
pools. This change is not a modelling change, and is in response to recommendations from the UNFCCC 
expert review team following their fall 2023 review of Canada’s NIR. However, the change in approach 
does alter the communication and representation of modelling results. 
 
9 
UNCLASSIFIED - NON CLASSIFIÉ 
Under the previous reporting approach, the transfer of carbon from harvested stands between the 
managed forest and HWP is not treated as an emission nor removal. Instead, it is counted as a carbon 
stock transfer from the managed forest carbon pool to the HWP carbon pool. Under the revised 
approach, the carbon stock change in the forest and HWP components are recognized separately as a 
carbon stock loss in the forest and a carbon stock gain in HWP. Carbon stock losses can be represented 
as a positive carbon flux, which is often equated to an emission; the reverse is true for carbon stock 
gain, represented as a negative carbon flux and equated to a removal. As such, when a forest stand is 
harvested, the transfer of carbon out of the managed forest carbon pool is a positive carbon flux 
potentially treated as an emission and correspondingly the transfer of carbon into the HWP carbon pool 
is negative carbon flux potentially treated as a removal. 
This approach significantly changes the component-level timeseries data for emissions from both the 
managed forest and HWP. However net emissions for the forest sector (i.e. the sum of managed forest 
and HWP emissions/removals) remain identical under the previous and revised approach.

Introduction
This document summarizes the changes to Canada’s National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System (NFCMARS) for the 2025 national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory submission to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), covering the reporting period 1990 – 2023. 

NFCMARS methodological updates for the 2025 National Inventory Report (NIR) include the following improvement project from the NIR2024 – NIR2026 Improvement Plan:
Project 2021_10: Refine estimates of BC slash burning activity

In addition to the planned improvement to pre-1990 disturbances, the following additional improvements were completed:
BC harvest sort conditions update
Update to insect disturbance classifiers in QC
Update to computing architecture 
Software logic errors related implementation of reforestation
Updated residential bioenergy appliance types and emissions factors 

The estimates for NIR2025 also include the following changes to activity data:
2023 wildfire activity data update
2015-2022 forest management activity data update, extended to 2023
1990-2023 residential bioenergy activity data update
2021-2022 industrial bioenergy activity data update, extended to 2023
2023 forest health (insect) activity data update
2023 deforestation activity data update
2019 afforestation activity data update
2022-2023 afforestation and reforestation activity funded under the two billi

gy activity data update
2021-2022 industrial bioenergy activity data update, extended to 2023
2023 forest health (insect) activity data update
2023 deforestation activity data update
2019 afforestation activity data update
2022-2023 afforestation and reforestation activity funded under the two billion trees (2BT) program
2022 waste incineration activity data update
2021-2023: Updated FAO -based HWP commodity conversion parameters
The following sections of this report discuss these updates and the resulting changes in GHG emissions and removals estimates in greater detail.

Methodological Updates 
Improvement Project 2021_10 –Refine estimates of BC slash-burning activity
Prior to NIR2025, the proportion of harvest area in BC where slash pile burning (SPB) is applied was estimated using an “expert opinion” of 15% for coastal regions and 50% for the interior. For NIR2025, the proportions determined by “expert opinion” have been replaced by new proportions using a data-driven approach.
A statistical analysis using very-high resolution imagery was conducted to assess the rates of slash pile burning in BC. In the study, harvest events from around BC were randomly selected and assessed for their association with SPB occurrence. The updated proportions for SPB occurrence developed from the study are 15% for the coast and 59% for the interior, and these new proportions have been applied in BC for NIR2025. The methods and results of this improvement project have been submitted for publication (Nesdoly et al. In preparation)
BC Harvest conditions update 
This project revised the selection criteria for harvesting in BC in order to better reflect the temporal and spatial occurrence of salvage harvesting following the Mountain Pine Beetle (MPB) outbreak. The prior assumption in CBM modelling had been to use a snag-priority harvest rule for all harvesting in BC to represent salvage-focused harvest plans and incentives associated with the MPB outbreak. This update used evidence from the Forestry Practices Board of BC to limit the snag-priority harvesting to the years and spatial areas where MPB had the greatest impact and harvest planning and execution is recorded as being salvage-focused. For the Montane regions of BC, evidence from billing records and the shelf life of beetle-killed wood supported the retention of the snag priority rule between 2002 and 2020, while the remaining years were reassigned to a rule prioritizing highest merchantable carbon stocks. Boreal and Pacific regions of BC, which were not as impacted by the MPB outbreak, were also converted to a merchantable carbon-priority harvest rule. 
Computing architecture update
CBM-CFS3 carbon dynamics, input data, events and record tracking were migrated to a more modern computing architecture that provides advantages in run time and level of detail, while replicating all previous science and model features. Transitioning to a modern computing architecture sets the stage for future improvements that were unable to be implemented in the previous computing architecture paradigm. 
Quebec insect classifier update
For multiple years, large areas of Spruce Budworm (SBW) disturbance in Quebec were not realized during modelling, leading to shortfalls between input target areas and what the model represents. SBW disturbances have specific host tree species; however, information on tree species in Quebec is limited. New information has led to improved interpretation of existing information, in turn supporting better matching of SBW events to host tree species.  Update to Forest Land and Harvested Wood Products reporting methods
Canada’s 2025 National GHG Inventory Report (NIR2025) is incorporating a major change to its reporting structure for emissions and removals from the managed forest and harvested wood products (HWP) pools. This change is not a modelling change, and is in response to recommendations from the UNFCCC expert review team following their fall 2023 review of Canada’s NIR. However, the change in approach does alter the communication and representation of modelling results. 
Under the previous reporting approach, the transfer of carbon from harvested stands between the managed forest and HWP is not treated as an emission nor removal. Instead, it is counted as a carbon stock transfer from the managed forest carbon pool to the HWP carbon pool. Under the revised approach, the carbon stock change in the forest and HWP components are recognized separately as a carbon stock loss in the forest and a carbon stock gain in HWP. Carbon stock losses can be represented as a positive carbon flux, which is often equated to an emission; the reverse is true for carbon stock gain, represented as a negative carbon flux and equated to a removal. As such, when a forest stand is harvested, the transfer of carbon out of the managed forest carbon pool

ses can be represented as a positive carbon flux, which is often equated to an emission; the reverse is true for carbon stock gain, represented as a negative carbon flux and equated to a removal. As such, when a forest stand is harvested, the transfer of carbon out of the managed forest carbon pool is a positive carbon flux potentially treated as an emission and correspondingly the transfer of carbon into the HWP carbon pool is negative carbon flux potentially treated as a removal. 
This approach significantly changes the component-level timeseries data for emissions from both the managed forest and HWP. However net emissions for the forest sector (i.e. the sum of managed forest and HWP emissions/removals) remain identical under the previous and revised approach.

ws the net emissions for NIR2025, NIR2024, and the difference between them under the new reporting format. In this improvement, the prior assumption of snag-priority harvest was limited to the years and regions where the mountain pine beetle epidemic occurred. Background
What is a ‘last-pass disturbance’ (LPD)?
• CBM-CFS3 initialization (Kurz et. al, 2009) :
– links biomass, DOM dynamics and historical disturbance to minimize artifacts appearing 
as changes in soil pools at the beginning of a model run
– populates the biomass and DOM C stocks for each stand
– simulates repeated cycles of growth followed by stand-replacing wildfires at ecozone-
specific fire return intervals until AG + BG DOM stocks vary 1% between rotations
– simulates one final rotation terminated by a ‘last pass’ stand-replacing disturbance 
(harvest or fire), then ages stand to end-of-1989 inventory age to ensure continuity 
between simulation initialization and the simulated DOM dynamics
• When NFCMARS was built in early 2000s, assignment of last disturbance prior to 
stand initiation based on expert judgement and historic data. Choice has small 
impacts on total GHG balance during reporting period.

Background
Why is Canada disaggregating reported GHG fluxes in the managed forest 
into anthropogenic and natural categories?
• To better reflect the impacts of changes in human activities on GHG emissions and 
removals (Kurz et al. 2018).
• Emissions and removals of stands affected by wildfires and other natural

disturbance category.
• The emissions and removals of all remaining lands in the managed forest are 
reported in the anthropogenic category.
• Methods include a region-specific age at which stands that have recovered from

Method – Update Algorithm
• The last pass update algorithm attempts to find suitably aged records to match the historic area harvest (or fire) 
targets. 
• For example. The historic harvest data indicate that 100 hectares were harvested in 1970. The inventory age is 
1990 meaning all records in the inventory are meant to represent the forest conditions in 1990. Therefore in 1990, 
there should be 100 hectares of 20 year old forest (1990-1970 = 20 years). 
• If the inventory is ‘correct’ there are exactly 100 hectares of 20 year old forest and the tool updates the historic 
disturbance from the previous assumption (fire, harvest) to the updated last pass disturbance = harvest.
• Usually there is either more or not enough area to satisfy the target (100 hectares). 
• If there is ‘too much’ 20 year old inventory, only 100 hectares of the total area aged 20 will be set to harvest. 
• If there are less than 100 hectares of total inventory aged 20 in the 1990 inventory, then the tool will set 100% of

Background
What is a ‘last-pass disturbance’ (LPD)?
• CBM-CFS3 initialization (Kurz et. al, 2009) :
– links biomass, DOM dynamics and historical disturbance to minimize artifacts appearing 
as changes in soil pools at the beginning of a model run
– populates the biomass and DOM C stocks for each stand
– simulates repeated cycles of growth followed by stand-replacing wildfires at ecozone-
specific fire return intervals until AG + BG DOM stocks vary 1% between rotations
– simulates one final rotation terminated by a ‘last pass’ stand-replacing disturbance 
(harvest or fire), then ages stand to end-of-1989 inventory age to ensure continuity 
between simulation initialization and the simulated DOM dynamics
• When NFCMARS was built in early 2000s, assignment of last disturbance prior to 
stand initiation based on expert judgement and historic data. Choice has small 
impacts on total GHG balance during reporting period.

disturbance category.
• The emissions and removals of all remaining lands in the managed forest are 
reported in the anthropogenic category.
• Methods include a region-specific age at which stands that have recovered from 
fire are moved from the natural to the anthropogenic category (60 to 100 years).

Subject: NIR2023 and National Forest Sinks Committee Call
Dear XXXX,
[Your province] was one of the provinces for which the CFS Carbon Accounting Team conducted an in-depth review of historic harvest data for the period ~1900 to 1989. 
As you saw in a briefing with your province on [insert month/day] 2022, the changes in historic harvest rates can have large impacts on the partitioning of the reported GHG emissions and removals between the reported human-induced and natural disturbance categories.
This e-mail is to give you an advance notice that the results of the updated historic harvest data will not be included in Canada’s National GHG Inventory Report that will be released on or before April 14th, 2023. That report will, however, include a general statement in the section on “Future Improvements” (Chapter 6) that will state for NIR2024 that:
“The proposed update will result in important reductions in the reported carbon removals that occur in Canada’s managed forest and as a result when the gross emissions from HWP are added, the reported anthropogenic net balance for the whole of the Forest Sector is anticipated to become a net source in all years of the time-series. “
At the National Forest Sinks Committee call on March 29th, we will be providing an update on the status of the work, how the implementation will affect NIR2024, and what information will be released in NIR2023. Note that in the NFSC call we will only present national results and will not speak to the impacts on individual provinces.
As in prior years, provincial-scale summaries of the results from NIR2023 and the impacts of the updated historic harvest data for NIR2024 are available to each province upon request.
Work is continuing on the implementation and assessment of the consequences of these changes in Canada’s National Forest Carbon Monitoring Accounting and Reporting System. A scientific publication is in preparation.
Please forward this e-mail within your organisation as you consider appropriate.
We look forward to the National Sinks Committee call on March 29th.
Best regards,

Method – Update Algorithm
• The last pass update algorithm attempts to find suitably aged records to match the historic area harvest (or fire) 
targets. 
• For example. The historic harvest data indicate that 100 hectares were harvested in 1970. The inventory age is 
1990 meaning all records in the inventory are meant to represent the forest conditions in 1990. Therefore in 1990, 
there should be 100 hectares of 20 year old forest (1990-1970 = 20 years). 
• If the inventory is ‘correct’ there are exactly 100 hectares of 20 year old forest and the tool updates the historic 
disturbance from the previous assumption (fire, harvest) to the updated last pass disturbance = harvest.
• Usually there is either more or not enough area to satisfy the target (100 hectares). 
• If there is ‘too much’ 20 year old inventory, only 100 hectares of the total area aged 20 will be set to harvest. 
• If there are less than 100 hectares of total inventory aged 20 in the 1990 inventory, then the tool will set 100% of 
the area aged 20 in 1990 to harvest and it will then look ahead (21 year old inventory),

• If there are less than 100 hectares of total inventory aged 20 in the 1990 inventory, then the tool will set 100% of 
the area aged 20 in 1990 to harvest and it will then look ahead (21 year old inventory), and behind, (19 year old 
inventory) and assigns available area to harvest until the target is met. 
• The end result is that the total area targeted is achieved by re-setting historic disturbance assumptions of 
inventory that is either at the targeted age, or within a tolerance of the targeted age. 
• Note that the stand ages contained in the forest inventory are never changed, only the last pass disturbance 
assumptions of the inventory records are revised during this process.

Background
Purpose of this review
• To present planned revisions to the data used in Canada’s National Forest Carbon 
Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System (NFCMARS) tentatively planned for 
NIR2023 (mid-May 2022).
• To review assumptions about historic (i.e., 1900 to 1989) stand-replacing 
disturbances that resulted in the initial (1990) forest inventory conditions.
• To preview the impacts of the proposed changes on total GHG emissions and 
removals and their disaggregation into the anthropogenic and natural components.
• To seek feedback about potential additional available data on historic disturbances.

Background
What is a ‘last-pass disturbance’ (LPD)?
• CBM-CFS3 initialization (Kurz et. al, 2009) :
– links biomass, DOM dynamics and historical disturbance to minimize artifacts appearing 
as changes in soil pools at the beginning of a model run
– populates the biomass and DOM C stocks for each stand
– simulates repeated cycles of growth followed by stand-replacing wildfires at ecozone-
specific fire return intervals until AG + BG DOM stocks vary 1% between rotations
– simulates one final rotation terminated by a ‘last pass’ stand-replacing disturbance 
(harvest or fire), then ages stand to end-of-1989 inventory age to ensure continuity 
between simulation initialization and the simulated DOM dynamics
• When NFCMARS was built in early 2000s, assignment of last disturbance prior to 
stand initiation based on expert judgement and historic data. Choice has small 
impacts on total GHG balance during reporting period.

Background
Why is Canada disaggregating reported GHG fluxes in the managed forest 
into anthropogenic and natural categories?
• To better reflect the impacts of changes in human activities on GHG emissions and 
removals (Kurz et al. 2018).
• Emissions and removals of stands affected by wildfires and other natural 
disturbances with greater than 80% stand mortality are reported in the natural 
disturbance category.
• The emissions and removals of all remaining lands in the managed forest are 
reported in the anthropogenic category.
• Methods include a region-specific age at which stands that have recovered from 
fire are moved from the natural to the anthropogenic category (60 to 100 years).
